title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: central question
text: What actually changes when a large language model becomes an agent? It sounds like a simple question. But the word agent is used so loosely that it's worth answering precisely. By the end of this lecture, you will have built the smallest useful agent, and you will know exactly which line of code makes it one.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: principle
text: Agency begins when model decisions can cause actions, whose consequences become observations for subsequent decisions.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: key takeaways
text: An LLM call is not, by itself, an agent. A tool is a capability; software still executes it. The critical transition: Decision $ $ Action $ $ Observation $ $ Next decision. Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control. System quality depends on both the model and the harness around it.

title: Experiment 1 (Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent)
text: So let's run the first experiment. Instead of a real model, we use a ScriptedModel. It's a deterministic stand-in: it returns exactly the text we give it, so every viewer sees the same output. We send the question, we get an answer back, and we compare it with the ground truth, which Python computes for us. The scripted answer is imperfect on purpose, and that's important. This experiment isolates the architecture. It does not measure any real model's arithmetic. Here's the output. The model says thirty-seven times forty-two is approximately fifteen hundred. The ground truth is fifteen fifty-four. Correct: false. So what did this experiment establish? Only that the model produced a response. It does not show that models are bad at arithmetic, and it doesn't show that you need an agent to multiply two numbers. What it gives us is a task with a known right answer, and a capability we can add next.

title: Experiment 2 (Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent)
text: For experiment two, we need a stand-in that reacts to what it sees. That's the PolicyModel. Its policy is simple. It looks for the latest observation in the messages. If there is no observation yet, it asks for the calculator. If there is an observation, it uses it to answer. So the same model makes a different decision depending on its context, and that's exactly the behaviour we need to show the loop. Now, experiment two: from model to agent. We start with the user's question. The model makes a decision: call the calculator. Software runs the calculator. And then comes the key step. We append the result to the messages, as a tool message. Then we call the model again. The output: action, calculator. Observation, fifteen fifty-four. Answer: thirty-seven times forty-two equals fifteen fifty-four. The line that matters is messages dot append. The result goes back into the messages before the second decision is made.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: central question
text: How can probabilistic language safely control deterministic software? A language model produces text, and that text is never guaranteed. Software, on the other hand, needs exact inputs. By the end of this lecture, you will have built the first hard boundary around the model: a contract that every proposal must satisfy before software acts on it.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: principle
text: Never allow probabilistic output to cross a deterministic software boundary without validation.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: key takeaways
text: Natural language is useful for humans but brittle as a software control interface. Parseable output is not necessarily valid output. Schema, semantic and capability validity, and authorization, are different concerns. A model output remains a proposal until deterministic software accepts it. Strict structured generation guarantees shape, not correctness or authority.

title: Experiment 3 (Chapter 2, Structured Decisions)
text: Experiment three is deliberately tiny. It needs no agent loop at all. We take a model-shaped string, and pass it to json dot loads. Then we print the action and the arguments. The output shows the action, calculator, and the arguments, a dictionary with the expression thirty-seven times forty-two. So what changed? Not the model's intelligence. We changed the interface between the model and the program. The decision now has machine-readable structure, with named fields.

title: Experiment 4 (Chapter 2, Structured Decisions)
text: Here is that contract in code. On the left is a small dataclass, the CalculatorDecision, with two fields: an action, and an expression. That's the typed decision that software is willing to act on. On the right is the validate function. If the action is not calculator, it raises an error: unknown action. Then it pulls out the expression, and if that expression isn't a string, it raises another error. Only if both checks pass does it build and return a CalculatorDecision. Now we try it on two proposals. The good one asks for the calculator, with the expression thirty-seven times forty-two. The bad one asks for delete database. The output shows the good proposal turned into a CalculatorDecision. The bad one is blocked, with the message: unknown action. The important event is not that the bad decision was wrong. Models will produce wrong decisions. The important event is that the wrong proposal stopped at a software boundary, rather than becoming an action.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: central question
text: How does an agent continue acting until a goal is complete? By the end of this lecture, you will have built the reusable Agent class that we use throughout the series. And you will know why its step limit is part of the design, rather than cleanup code.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: principle
text: An agent is an LLM inside a controlled feedback system.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: key takeaways
text: An agent loop feeds action consequences back into later decisions. State is what lets a later decision differ because of an earlier event. Valid individual steps can still form a defective trajectory. Stopping conditions are part of control, not optional cleanup. The harness owns execution, validation, state updates, and termination.

title: Experiment 5 (Chapter 3, The Agent Loop)
text: For experiment five, our stand-in model is a PolicyModel, as in lecture one. Its policy collects the tool observations in its messages. If there are none yet, it asks the calculator for twelve times seven. If there is one observation, it takes that value and adds six to it. And once there are two observations, it finishes, and reports the last one as the answer. The important thing is that it decides only from what's in its context. It doesn't secretly know the answer. Here is the loop. For up to ten steps, we ask the model for a decision. If the decision says done, we print the answer, and stop. Otherwise, we execute the action, print the observation, and append it to the messages as a tool message. The trace on the right shows it working. Step one: the calculator computes twelve times seven, and observes eighty-four. Step two: the calculator computes eighty-four plus six, and observes ninety. Step three: done. The answer is ninety. This is the first program in the series that contains the full minimal feedback structure we call an agent loop.

title: Experiment 6 (Chapter 3, The Agent Loop)
text: So in experiment six, we break it on purpose. A ScriptedModel repeats the same single response forever: call the calculator with one plus one. Every individual decision is valid. Every tool call succeeds. And yet, the system as a whole is defective, because it makes no progress towards finishing. The fix is the simplest possible control: a step limit, here set to three. The run function loops for at most three steps, and if no decision has finished the task by then, it raises an error: step limit reached. Here's the output. Step one: one plus one is two. Step two: two. Step three: two. And then: stop, step limit reached. The lesson is that a stopping condition is not merely defensive code. It is part of the agent's control architecture.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: central question
text: When should software decide the path in advance, and when should a model decide the path at runtime? By the end of this lecture, you'll be able to compare a workflow and an agent on the same task, and to place model discretion only where it earns its cost.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: principle
text: Use the least autonomy necessary to obtain the adaptability the task requires.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: key takeaways
text: A workflow substantially predetermines the control path; an agent delegates meaningful runtime control decisions. Runtime discretion buys adaptability but adds cost, latency, variance, and failure trajectories. Simple stable conditions should usually remain deterministic. Hybrids concentrate model reasoning where semantic uncertainty actually exists. Use the least autonomy necessary for the task.

title: Experiment 7 (Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents)
text: Experiment seven builds the same small task family twice. One task is an English report, which is the known path. The other is a French report that needs translation, which is the optional branch. There are three plain functions to use as tools: fetch, translate, and format. Here's the workflow version. The programmer fixed the path. It fetches the document. One explicit rule checks the language, and translates if it isn't English. Then it formats the result. It also records each step in a trace, so that we can compare. And here's the agentic version. A PolicyModel stands in for a model that chooses the next capability at runtime. It looks at what it has already seen. If nothing has been fetched, it asks to fetch. If the data isn't in English, it asks to translate. If nothing has been formatted, it asks to format. And once it has a formatted result, it says it's done. Like our earlier stand-ins, it decides only from the observations in its context. An agent loop, with a limit of six steps, runs it, and counts every model call. Here's the output. On the known path, the workflow simply fetches and formats. The agent goes model, fetch, model, format, model, done. Same answer. Zero model calls against three, and two tool calls each. On the optional branch, the workflow fetches, translates, and formats. The agent makes four model calls to do the same thing. Again, the same answer, and three tool calls each. So both architectures reach the same answer on both tasks. But the agent spends three or four model decisions choosing steps the workflow already knows, and makes exactly the same tool calls.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: central question
text: How does a model gain reliable access to capabilities it does not possess internally? By the end of this lecture, you'll know exactly what a tool is, why its description is part of the control surface, and how to turn a tool failure into a useful observation.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: principle
text: Models choose actions; software executes them.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: key takeaways
text: A tool's executable capability and its model-facing description are different objects. Tool use is selection plus correct invocation. Tool descriptions and schemas shape model behaviour. A correct decision can still meet an execution failure; return it as a structured observation. Expanding the action space also expands the risk surface.

title: Experiment 8 (Chapter 5, Tools)
text: In experiment eight, the model has one possible action: the calculator. Here, the proposal is fixed in the code. In a live system, the model would supply it. It asks for the calculator, with eighteen times seven. Ordinary software looks the tool up by name in the registry, and calls it with the arguments. The output: action, calculator. Result, one hundred and twenty-six. Nothing here requires the model to do arithmetic. Its role is to select a capability, and supply arguments. The deterministic capability does the work.

title: Experiment 9 (Chapter 5, Tools)
text: Experiment nine uses three tiny tasks. Calculate eighteen times seven, which should go to the calculator. What is the weather in Pretoria, which should go to weather. And find information about agent evaluation, which should go to search. We run them twice. Once with clear descriptions. And once with the weather description rewritten to overlap with search: find current information about a city. A fixed script can't show selection getting worse, because it ignores the descriptions. So the stand-in here is a PolicyModel that actually reads the tool descriptions in its context. It picks the tool whose description shares the most words with the goal. And if nothing matches at all, it reports that there's no suitable tool. That's far cruder than a real model. But it makes one real effect visible. Selection depends on the descriptions, not on the functions behind them. With clear descriptions, all three tasks go to the right tool. Three out of three. With overlapping descriptions, the calculator task is still fine. But the weather question no longer matches anything, and the research question goes to weather. Only one out of three. The underlying functions didn't change. Only the model-facing interface did. A live model reads descriptions far better than word overlap, but it faces the same boundary. What it can't distinguish, it can't select reliably. So tool descriptions are part of the control surface. A capability that the model can't reliably distinguish is not well exposed.

title: Experiment 10 (Chapter 5, Tools)
text: In experiment ten, the weather service times out, and we handle that failure in two ways. First, the tempting wrapper, called hidden call. It catches every exception, and returns None. Now the model sees None, and can't tell whether the city was unknown, the service timed out, the credentials failed, or the tool itself crashed. We've destroyed exactly the information needed for the next decision. The fix is structured call. On success, it returns ok, true, with the value. On a timeout, it returns ok, false, an error type of timeout, and retryable, true, plus a message. And on bad arguments, it returns an invalid arguments error that is not retryable. It preserves the failure type, and whether a retry could help, without leaking unnecessary internal details. Here's the output. The hidden version prints None. The structured version prints ok, false; error, timeout; retryable, true; and the message: weather service unavailable. Sent to the model, that's just a small piece of JSON. The failure has become an observation. The agent can now decide whether to retry, use another capability, ask the user, or stop. The full retry and fallback machinery comes much later in the book, because recovery deserves its own engineering model. The lesson: tool results are context, and their design affects the quality of every decision that follows.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: central question
text: What information should the model see at this decision, and what should be left out? By the end of this lecture, you'll be able to tell a context failure from a reasoning failure, and to judge context by whether it's sufficient, rather than by how big it is.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: principle
text: More context is not better context. Better context contains the information needed for the current decision, while controlling noise, cost, risk, and omission.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: key takeaways
text: Information can exist in the system without being visible to the model. Context engineering is broader than prompt wording. Context must be sufficient before it can be considered efficient. Selection policies can cause failures independently of model reasoning. Ordering, provenance, trust, and budget are part of context design.

title: Experiment 11 (Chapter 6, Context Engineering)
text: Experiment eleven uses a toy refund decision. The question: can order seventeen be refunded? The relevant facts: the purchase was twelve days ago, and the refund window is thirty days. Then there are distractors: the customer's tier, preferred language, last login, shipping method, newsletter status, and warehouse. We compare three contexts. A minimal one, with just the two required facts and no distractors. One with the relevant facts plus lots of noise. And a large but incomplete one, which has lots of noise, but leaves out the refund window. The measurement at the heart of the experiment is required-fact coverage. It's a one-line function in the companion code: the fraction of required facts that are present in the context. The decision is a deterministic refund rule, which can only use the facts it's given. If coverage is below one, it can't decide. Otherwise, it compares the purchase age with the refund window, and returns refund, or no refund. Here's the output. The minimal context has full coverage, two fields, no distractors, and the answer is refund. Relevant plus noise also has full coverage, eight fields and six distractors, and the answer is still refund. But the large, incomplete context has coverage of only one half. Seven fields, six distractors, and the result: cannot decide. So the largest context isn't the best one, and the third context is large, yet useless for this decision. Be careful about what this shows. The rule is deterministic, so the noisy context still gives the right answer here. This experiment does not measure how a live model reacts to distraction. What it does is expose the variables a live benchmark must control: required-fact coverage, context size, and distractor count. Context size is not a proxy for context quality.

title: Experiment 12 (Chapter 6, Context Engineering)
text: In experiment twelve, each candidate fact gets a simple relevance score, and we keep the top two. The selection policy is just a sort and a slice: rank by score, and take the first few. We run the same policy twice. Once with sensible scores, where the purchase age and the refund window both score one. And once with a deliberately corrupted ranking, which scores the customer tier above the refund window. With the good ranking, the selector keeps the purchase age and the refund window. Required-fact coverage: two out of two. We've halved the context, and it's still sufficient. With the corrupted ranking, it keeps the purchase age and the customer tier. Coverage: one out of two. The context is just as small, and apparently well ranked, but the refund rule is gone. It's insufficient. That's the failure mode. A context selector can fail before the model ever reasons.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: central question
text: How do we find useful evidence in a large knowledge source, and turn it into a grounded answer? By the end of this lecture, you will have built a transparent retriever, a small RAG pipeline, and a reranker. And you will know why retrieval quality and answer quality are two different problems.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: principle
text: Retrieval is not truth. And two inequalities to remember. Retrieval quality is not answer quality: a good retriever can feed a poor generator, and a strong generator cannot reliably use evidence it never receives. And similarity is not relevance: semantic closeness is evidence for candidate selection, not proof that a document is the right authority for the task.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: key takeaways
text: Retrieval generates candidate evidence; it does not generate the final answer. RAG couples retrieval, context construction, and generation. Similarity does not establish relevance, authority, currency, or truth. Reranking cannot recover a relevant item absent from the candidate set. Measure retrieval failures and generation failures separately. Citations should support claims, not merely accompany them.

title: Experiment 13 (Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG)
text: Experiment thirteen runs that retriever. We have three short documents, and the query, refund days. We print the query terms, the score of every document, and the single best candidate. Tokenization matters more than it looks. If we split on spaces alone, we would get tokens like days with a full stop, and refunds with an s, and the query words would match nothing at all. So the tokenizer strips punctuation and drops a trailing plural s, as a stand-in for real stemming. Here's the output. The query terms are refund and day. The refund policy scores one point zero. The shipping document shares one term, day, so it scores in between, at zero point seven one. And the gold customer document scores zero. What did we establish? An interface. Retrieve takes a query, documents and k, and returns ranked candidates. Later, we can swap the representation and the ranking method without changing that contract.

title: Experiment 14 (Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG)
text: Experiment fourteen makes the knowledge source more realistic. There are two refund policies: thirty days, effective twenty twenty-five, and fourteen days, effective twenty twenty-six. The two texts differ only in the number, so a similarity retriever scores them identically. The generator is a PolicyModel stand-in that quotes the number of days in whatever evidence it receives. It cannot invent anything. That isolates the one question this experiment asks: which evidence reached the generator? The generate function builds a prompt from one document and the question, calls the model, and prints the answer and the year of its source. We retrieve the top two candidates. Then we select in two ways. The naive way takes the top-ranked candidate. The metadata way takes the policy with the newest effective year. Both candidates arrive with equal similarity. The naive selection answers thirty days, from the twenty twenty-five policy. The metadata selection answers fourteen days, from the twenty twenty-six policy. Both answers are faithful to their evidence. The naive one is still wrong, and no amount of generator quality would fix it. The lesson: retrieval provides evidence, metadata and selection decide which evidence should govern, and generation turns the selected evidence into an answer.

title: Experiment 15 (Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG)
text: Experiment fifteen starts with three documents: a refund history note, the current refund policy, and a shipping note. The rerank score gives one point for mentioning refund, and two points for mentioning current. So a task-aware score prefers an explicit current policy. These keyword rules stand in for a learned reranker, such as a cross-encoder, which reads the query and the candidate together. First, we rerank all three. Before reranking, history is first. After reranking, current moves to the top. Then we break it on purpose. We remove the current policy before reranking. Now the reranker can only order history and shipping. Nothing can bring the current policy back. That is the failure boundary. Reranking can improve the ordering inside the candidate set. It cannot repair zero recall.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: central question
text: What should an agent preserve from the past, and when should that information influence the present? The answer we'll arrive at is that memory is not a database. Memory is a policy around persistence and recall.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: principle
text: Memory is a write policy, plus a store, plus a retrieval policy. The diagram puts it together. An experience reaches the write policy, which either rejects it or persists it to the store. The retrieval policy selects memories into the current context, and the context informs a new decision.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: key takeaways
text: Working memory preserves task state inside a trajectory. Episodic memory records events; semantic memory records durable facts; procedural memory records reusable methods. Persistence requires an explicit write policy. Recall is context selection over persisted state. Forgetting, expiry, and supersession are useful memory operations. The memory write policy is also a security boundary.

title: Experiment 16 (Chapter 8, Memory)
text: Working memory is the simplest kind: it preserves information needed across the steps of the current task. The task state holds a goal, multiply twelve by seven and then add six, and a list of observations. The first step runs the calculator on twelve times seven, and records the result in that list. The second step needs that result. The product from function searches the observations for the twelve times seven entry, and returns its result. The second step takes the product, adds six, and records that too. Then we break working memory on purpose, by replacing the observations list instead of accumulating it. The output shows eighty-four, then a final answer of ninety. But after the replacement, the question, is twelve times seven still available, prints false. The earlier observation is gone, even though the run has not ended. The lesson: working memory is task state selected for continued use. It is not necessarily the entire interaction history.

title: Experiment 17 (Chapter 8, Memory)
text: For experiment seventeen, the kernel provides a deliberately small store, called Memory. Every record is a dictionary with a type, a text, and a source. Write appends a record. Retrieve returns records of a given type whose text contains the query, up to a limit. Notice what the store does not do. It keeps whatever it is given. Deciding what deserves to be written is not the store's job. That belongs to a write policy outside it. So here are two write policies. The naive policy returns true for everything: persist it all. The durable policy rejects requests that announce their own short lifetime. It looks for markers such as this one, just this, or for now. For each policy, we create a fresh memory. We store one episode, the user asked for a Python example of RAG, and one semantic fact, the user prefers concise explanations. Then a one-off request arrives: use pirate language for this one joke. We ask the write policy whether to persist it. Finally, we print what retrieval returns for episodes and for semantic memories. Under the naive policy, the pirate instruction is now stored as a durable semantic fact, right next to the real preference. Under the durable-only policy, it was rejected. So every future explanation request, under the naive policy, retrieves the pirate instruction. The keyword rule is crude, and a model-assisted classifier could replace it. But the point stands: the write policy, not the store, decided what the future will see. This is the failure mode. Persistence can turn a temporary observation into a long-lived error.

title: Experiment 18 (Chapter 8, Memory)
text: Experiment eighteen has two procedures. The good one: read the failing assertion, edit the smallest responsible unit, and rerun the test. The bad one: when any test fails, delete the test. The model is a stand-in that follows whatever procedure it is shown. If the context says delete the test, it deletes the test. If it mentions the smallest responsible unit, it inspects and then edits. With no procedure, it rewrites the whole module. That property, following whatever it's shown, is exactly what makes procedural memory both powerful and dangerous. We run three cases: no procedure, the good procedure, and the bad procedure. In each case, we write the procedure to memory with the source, past runs. We retrieve procedural memories with the query, test fails. We inject them into the context as system messages, and let the model decide. With no procedure, the model rewrites the module. With the good procedure, it inspects and edits the refund window function. With the bad procedure, it deletes the test. The bad procedure was retrieved by the same query, and injected by the same code, as the good one. The memory system can now make future behaviour consistently worse. Persistence amplifies both good and bad abstractions. The lesson: procedural memory turns past learning into future control policy. So it deserves stronger validation than an ordinary, transient observation.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: central question
text: How do we make growing context smaller, without removing information that future decisions still need? By the end of this lecture, you'll judge a compressor not by how short its output is, but by whether the next decision can still be made correctly.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: principle
text: Compression is successful when it reduces representation cost, while preserving the information required for future decisions. The diagram shows the whole lifecycle. Raw interaction becomes working context. Working context is compressed into compact working state. Selected items persist into memory. And memory is consolidated into durable facts or skills.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: key takeaways
text: Compression is a lossy transformation; evaluate it by downstream utility. Critical constraints, permissions, provenance, and uncertainty may need explicit preservation. Shorter context is not automatically better context. Compression and memory persistence solve different problems. Consolidation creates reusable abstractions from multiple experiences. Recoverable compression can preserve access to original evidence.

title: Experiment 19 (Chapter 9, Context Compression)
text: Experiment nineteen represents the context as structured facts, so we can see exactly what survives. The compress function in the kernel is a single line. It keeps only the fields declared necessary for the next phase. The context has seven fields: the task, a word limit, the audience, the successful source, the failed searches, the approval constraint, and some small talk. The keep list names the five fields the next phase needs, including send requires approval. Now we add a harness rule, may send now. It reads the approval constraint, and, like many real checks, treats a missing constraint as no constraint at all. We run two compressors. The good one uses the full keep list. The broken one uses the same list, minus the approval constraint. For each, we print the compression ratio, the compressed state, and whether the agent may send without approval. The good compressor keeps one hundred and thirty-seven of one hundred and ninety-four characters, about seventy-one percent. The approval constraint is still there, so the agent may not send without approval. The broken compressor keeps only one hundred and five characters, fifty-four percent. That's a better ratio. But the approval constraint is gone, and now the agent may send without approval. Nothing in the compressed state looks wrong. The constraint is simply absent. That's the failure mode: a shorter context can be operationally worse, if compression deletes a constraint.

title: Experiment 20 (Chapter 9, Context Compression)
text: Experiment twenty compares two consolidators. First, a small keyword classifier reads the preference in each episode: concise if it mentions concise or shorten, detailed if it mentions detailed. The blind consolidator ignores the evidence entirely. It always says the user prefers concise responses. The guarded consolidator collects a vote from every episode. If the votes disagree, it refuses to write a fact, and reports the conflict. If there are fewer than two votes, it says there isn't enough evidence. Only otherwise does it write the preference. We run both consolidators on two sets: a consistent set of three concise episodes, and a conflicting pair, one asking for a concise answer and one for a detailed explanation. On the consistent set, the two agree. Both write, user prefers concise responses. Three event records become one reusable fact. On the conflicting set, the blind consolidator still writes that the user prefers concise responses. It has erased the contradiction. The guarded consolidator writes no fact, and reports one concise and one detailed episode. Consolidation needs thresholds, scope, provenance and conflict handling. The keyword classifier here stands in for whatever judgment a real system uses. The lesson: consolidation is abstraction, not mere summarization.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): central question
text: How can an agent discover and invoke external capabilities through a standard interface, instead of a custom integration for every system? By the end of this lecture, you will have traced every message involved in one MCP tool call. And you'll know which questions the protocol answers, and which it leaves to the host.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): principle
text: MCP standardizes capability access. It does not create agency. In lecture five, a dictionary of tools gave us local discovery and execution. Now, tools list and tools call do that through a server. The abstraction did not change. The integration boundary did.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): key takeaways
text: MCP standardizes an integration boundary; it is not itself an agent. MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 with an initialize handshake, capability negotiation, and stdio or Streamable HTTP transports. Servers offer tools, resources, and prompts; clients may offer roots, sampling, and elicitation. A failed tool returns isError: true; an unprocessable request returns a JSON-RPC error. Protocol authorization governs access to a server; per-action permission remains host policy. Tool definitions are untrusted input: they can be poisoned, changed, or collide across servers.

title: Experiment 21 (Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP))
text: Experiment twenty-one makes this contract visible, without hiding it inside a library. It simulates both sides of the exchange in one process. It is not the MCP SDK, and it uses no transport. Each request is serialized to JSON text, as stdio or HTTP would carry it, and passed straight to the server's handle function. The server declares the protocol version and one tool, the calculator, with its input schema. The implementation is the kernel's safe evaluator from lecture five, so no eval is involved. Here is the part of the server's handle function that deals with tool calls. Earlier branches answer initialize and tools list, and ignore notifications. If the requested tool exists, the server runs it. On success, it returns a normal result with the value as text, and is-error false. If the tool raises an error, it still returns a normal result, but with the message, invalid arithmetic expression, and is-error true. If the tool name is unknown, it returns a JSON-RPC error instead, with code minus thirty-two thousand, six hundred and two. And any unknown method gets a method-not-found error. After initialize and tools list, a stand-in for the model makes three proposals. A good one: calculate eighteen times seven. A schema-valid but meaningless one: the calculator with the expression, delete all invoices. And a call to a tool the server never listed: delete invoice, with id seven. For each proposal, the client sends tools call, and prints either the protocol error, or the content and the is-error flag. After the handshake, discovery finds the calculator. The first call returns one hundred and twenty-six, with is-error false. The second runs the calculator and fails, so it returns invalid arithmetic expression, with is-error true. The third never reaches a tool. It gets a protocol error: unknown tool, delete invoice. The arithmetic is deliberately uninteresting. What matters are three boundaries. Discovery and invocation go through messages, not through direct knowledge of a Python function. A tool that runs and fails returns a normal result with is-error true. And a request the protocol cannot honour returns a JSON-RPC error.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: central question
text: When does alternating model decisions with external observations improve performance over answering in one shot? By the end of this lecture, you'll see that ReAct earns its cost only when actions create new information that can change the next decision.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: principle
text: ReAct is useful because actions create new information that can change the next decision.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: key takeaways
text: ReAct alternates decisions, actions, and observations. Its value comes from new feedback that can change later decisions. The harness needs observable actions, observations, and state transitions; reasoning text, whether ReAct thoughts or hidden reasoning, is optional rather than an interface. A structurally valid loop can still ignore evidence or fail to make progress. Iterative reasoning adds model calls, cost, latency, and possible failure trajectories. Reasoning architectures should be tested against simpler baselines.

title: Experiment 22 (Chapter 11, ReAct)
text: Experiment twenty-two uses a task whose second action depends on the first observation: find the current value of X, then calculate X times one point one five. A one-shot system must either already know X, or guess it. A ReAct-style system can first look X up, and then calculate with the observed value. The environment holds X equals eighty. There are two tools: a lookup, and the calculator. And the decisions come from deterministic stand-ins, not from a language model. Here is the ReAct stand-in. Its next decision depends only on what it has observed so far. If it hasn't seen any tool results yet, it asks to look up X. With one observation, it builds the expression from the value it saw, times one point one five, and calls the calculator. With two observations, it answers with the latest one. The run function is the agent loop again, with printing, a step limit of four, and one extra switch, called feed back. Each step asks the model for a decision and appends it. If the model is done, the run ends. Otherwise, the action is executed and printed. And only if feed back is on is the observation appended to the messages. We run it three times. First, a one-shot scripted model with no tools. Second, the ReAct loop. And third, the same loop with feed back switched off. Here's the output. The one-shot stand-in has no tool, so it can only guess. It assumes X is one hundred, and answers one hundred and fifteen. The ReAct loop looks up X and observes eighty. Then it calculates eighty times one point one five, and observes ninety-two. And it answers ninety-two. In the broken run, the lookup executes and returns eighty, four times in a row. The model never sees the result, so it keeps asking for it, until the step limit stops the run after four model calls. ReAct answers ninety-two because the environment supplied information after step one that was not available before the action. The key event is not that the model thought more.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: central question
text: When does deciding a sequence before acting improve an agent, and when does following that sequence become a liability? By the end of this lecture, you will have validated and executed a plan, you will have watched a fixed plan fail when the world changes, and you will have compared three controllers: reactive, plan-first, and plan plus replan.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: principle
text: A plan is a hypothesis about the future. So planning should be judged by the improvement it creates in task performance, coordination or resource use. Not by how sophisticated the generated plan looks.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: key takeaways
text: Planning creates an intermediate representation of intended future work. Plans can expose dependencies, coverage, and opportunities for coordination. Validate a plan against known capabilities and constraints. Execution tests the assumptions embedded in a plan. Replanning needs an explicit trigger. Measure planning quality and execution quality separately. More planning is not automatically better.

title: Experiment 23 (Chapter 12, Planning)
text: Experiment twenty-three uses a task with an explicit dependency. Find the price of three units of product A, the price of two units of product B, then compute the total. The plan is written by hand, standing in for a planner's output. Each step names a tool, its arguments, and where to save the result. The first two steps look up prices. The third step calls the calculator with the expression three times A plus two times B, where A and B are placeholders filled from earlier results. The same file defines a bad plan, which inserts a step that calls a currency converter. We'll come back to that one. Before anything runs, the plan is validated. The validate function walks through the steps and records a problem for every step that names a tool the system does not have. The main loop then runs both plans. If validation finds problems, the plan is rejected before execution. Otherwise, it is executed, and the total is printed. The executor keeps a state dictionary. For each step, it fills the placeholders from the state, calls the tool, and stores the result. In the output, the good plan looks up A, ten, and B, seven. The calculator then receives three times ten plus two times seven, and the total is forty-four. The bad plan is rejected before execution, because step three names a tool that does not exist. Notice that the calculator step cannot even be formatted until both prices are in the state. The plan's contribution is coordination, not extra prose about reasoning.

title: Experiment 24 (Chapter 12, Planning)
text: Experiment twenty-four makes that failure concrete with a travel-like toy task. The goal is to reach destination D. Route A is shortest, and route B is longer. So the natural plan is: take route A, then continue to D. But after the first decision, the environment reports that route A is blocked. We run three controllers against this same world. Route A is blocked, but none of them knows that at the start, and each controller gets at most four actions. Here is the heart of the experiment. One driver loop runs all three controllers, until the agent reaches D or uses up its four actions. The reactive controller makes a fresh decision every step. The others take the first step of their plan. When an observation says blocked, the route is recorded as known to be blocked, and only the plan plus replan controller then makes a new plan. Its trigger is a failed action. Everything here is plain code, not model output, so the run is fully deterministic. Here are the results. The reactive controller succeeds in three actions, wasting one. Plan-first tries route A four times, and spends its whole budget on a blocked road. Plan plus replan succeeds in three actions, wasting one, after making two plans. Notice that in this toy, reactive does just as well as replanning. The plan contains only one real decision, so global structure buys nothing. Planning earns its cost when a task has dependencies that local decisions would discover too late, as in experiment twenty-three.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: central question
text: Does letting an agent critique its own output actually improve the result? By the end of this lecture, you will have watched reflection repair a wrong answer, and break a correct one. And you will have seen how a verification gate keeps the repair, and removes the regression.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: principle
text: Reflection adds another probabilistic component. Its errors must be measured just like the errors of the original generator. Or, more briefly: a critic is another fallible component, not an oracle.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: key takeaways
text: Reflection adds a critic and a revision stage; it does not guarantee improvement. A critic is fallible: measure its precision and recall. Critique proposes a defect; verification tests whether it is real. Reflection can regress already-correct outputs. Gate it. Reflection loops need budgets, stopping rules, and resource-equivalent baselines.

title: Experiment 25 (Chapter 13, Reflection)
text: Experiment twenty-five uses a task with an objective check: calculate seventeen times six. The draft is scripted to be wrong. It says ninety-six. The critic points out that the multiplication is incorrect, and that the answer is one hundred and two. The revision applies the correction. In this case, reflection helps. But the interesting experiment begins when the draft is already correct, or when the critic is wrong. So the experiment runs two scripted critics, a good one and a bad one, against a wrong draft and a correct draft. And it uses two revision policies. Always applies every critique. Verified applies a critique only when a calculator confirms the proposed value. The critics are simple lookup tables, from a draft to a critique. The good critic corrects ninety-six to one hundred and two, and finds nothing wrong with one hundred and two. The bad critic claims that the answer should be one hundred and twelve, whatever the draft says. The outcome function compares the revision with the correct answer, computed by the calculator. A wrong draft becomes either an improvement or no useful repair. A correct draft is either preserved, or it becomes a regression. And here are the two policies. Revise simply applies whatever the critic proposes, unless the critic found nothing. Verified revise is more careful. It changes the draft only if a tool, here the calculator, confirms the proposed value. Otherwise, it keeps the draft. So one policy trusts the critic. The other asks a tool before changing anything. Here's the output. Under the always policy, the good critic repairs the wrong draft, and preserves the correct one. But the bad critic turns the correct draft into one hundred and twelve. That's a regression. So always gives one improvement and one regression. Under the verified policy, the improvement survives, and the regression disappears, because the calculator rejects the invented defect. One improvement, zero regressions. But notice that verification cannot rescue the wrong draft when the only critique on offer is also wrong. It filters bad changes. It does not create good ones.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: central question
text: When is exploring multiple candidate paths better than committing to the first plausible path? By the end of this lecture, you will have run beam search on a small puzzle, watched a misleading evaluator prune the only winning branch, and seen what a better evaluator really costs.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: principle
text: Search is useful only when alternatives can be evaluated. And remember that search amplifies whatever the evaluator rewards. It can amplify competence, and it can amplify evaluator bias.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: key takeaways
text: Search delays commitment by keeping several candidate paths open. It needs a state, a generator, an evaluator and a search policy, bounded by a budget. More candidates help only if viable alternatives are generated and can be evaluated. Pruning saves resources but can discard the eventual best branch. Best-of-N searches answers; trees search intermediate states. Prefer external verification; compare with simpler baselines.

title: Experiment 26 (Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning)
text: Experiment twenty-six uses a transparent toy problem. Transform two into thirteen, using exactly two operations. The operations are plus three, times two, and plus nine. The first move gives five, four, or eleven. A greedy strategy that scores states by how close they are to thirteen prefers eleven. But from eleven, no single operation reaches thirteen. You get fourteen, twenty-two, or twenty. Another branch succeeds. Two times two is four, and four plus nine is thirteen. The example is deliberately simple. It shows that evaluating only the current state can differ from evaluating the future potential of a branch. Here's the code. Expand applies every operation to a state, and records the path. Then there are two evaluators. Closeness is the greedy heuristic: the negative distance to the target, right now. Lookahead is smarter. It expands the state through all the remaining steps, and returns the best closeness still reachable. The search itself is beam search. At each depth, every state in the beam is expanded, and the expansions are counted. The candidates are then sorted by the evaluator's score, and only the best few, the beam width, are kept. At the end, any state equal to the target is a solution. The experiment runs widths one, two and three, under each evaluator, and reports the expansions and any solution found. Here are the results. The first moves score minus eight for five, minus nine for four, and minus two for eleven. So closeness ranks four last. With closeness, widths one and two both fail. Width two keeps eleven and five, and still prunes four. Only width three finds two times two plus nine, and in this tree, width three is exhaustive search. The lookahead evaluator lets even width one succeed. But it is not free. It quietly expands the rest of the tree for every candidate it scores, which is affordable only because this tree is tiny. Better evaluation often means spending computation inside the evaluator, instead of inside the search.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: central question
text: How should an agent decide which capability, workflow, or model should handle a task? By the end of this lecture, you will have scored routers both by their accuracy and by the cost of their mistakes. And you will have compared fixed, oracle, predicted, and cascade model routing.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: principle
text: Routing maps an observed task, plus system state, through a routing policy to a capability, model or workflow, and then to an outcome. So here is the principle from this chapter. Routing is resource allocation under uncertainty. Judge it by downstream outcomes, not by the sophistication of the router.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: key takeaways
text: Routing allocates tasks to capabilities, workflows, models, or control paths. Routing errors can have asymmetric cost and risk. Router accuracy and end-to-end system quality are different metrics. Model routing trades quality against cost and latency. Cascades replace perfect prediction with failure detection and escalation. Compare with simple baselines: always-strong, deterministic rules.

title: Experiment 27 (Chapter 15, Routing)
text: Experiment twenty-seven starts with three transparent routes: math goes to the calculator, policy goes to policy retrieval, and write goes to the writing workflow. There are five labeled tasks, each with its correct route. Notice that one of them, Calculate three plus four, starts with a capital letter. And each kind of mistake has a cost. Sending a policy question to the writer costs five, because it risks an unsupported answer. The other misroutes cost one. Three routers are compared. The rule router is minimal and deterministic. If the task starts with calculate, it goes to math. If it mentions policy, it goes to policy. Everything else goes to writing. The misroute function deliberately sends every task to the writing workflow. And SEMANTIC is a scripted stand-in for a model-based router: a fixed table of predictions. It gets one thing wrong. It sends the refund policy question to the writer. Here's the output. The rule router gets four out of five. It fails on the capitalised request, because starts with is case-sensitive. Its one misroute costs one. Always-write gets one out of five, with a misroute cost of twelve. The semantic router also gets four out of five. Same accuracy as the rules. But its mistake was a policy question, so its misroute cost is five. The point is not that keyword routing is sophisticated. It exposes the boundary cleanly. Routing chooses. The destination executes.

title: Experiment 28 (Chapter 15, Routing)
text: Experiment twenty-eight routes between two models. A fast model costs one unit, and a strong model costs ten. There are five arithmetic tasks, two labelled easy and three labelled hard. The call model function encodes an explicit assumption: the fast model is right on easy tasks only, and the strong model is right on all of them. The verifier is exact: it compares the answer with the calculator. And choose model is the deployable router. It cannot see the difficulty label, which only the oracle may read. So it predicts difficulty from an observable feature: long expressions are predicted to be hard. The cascade tries the fast model first. If the verifier rejects the answer, it escalates to the strong model, and pays for both calls. Then there are five strategies in total. Always fast. Always strong. The oracle, which uses the true difficulty label. The length router. And the cheap-first cascade. Here are the results. Always fast solves two out of five, for a cost of five. Always strong solves all five, for fifty. The oracle solves all five for thirty-two. It is not deployable, but it is an upper-bound reference. The length router solves four for twenty-three. Ninety-nine times ninety-nine is short, so it is predicted easy, and the fast model gets it wrong. The cascade solves all five for thirty-five. Every hard task pays for a failed fast attempt first, but no advance prediction of difficulty is needed. Every strategy is trying to preserve quality, while avoiding the cost and latency of using the strongest model for every request.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: central question
text: When can independent work run concurrently, and how should multiple results be recombined into one reliable outcome? By the end of this lecture, you will have overlapped independent waits, broken a dependency by parallelising it, and watched a bad fan-in throw away three good reviews.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: principle
text: Parallelise independent work. Preserve ordering where dependencies exist. Parallelism changes time. Fan-out and fan-in change both time and coordination.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: key takeaways
text: Parallelism is valid only where dependencies permit it. Concurrency can cut latency without reducing total work. Critical-path and straggler latency matter. Fan-out creates branches; fan-in defines how they become a result. Evaluate aggregation separately. Shared writes and side effects need stronger coordination. Parallel designs need limits, failure policies, cancellation and budgets.

title: Experiment 29 (Chapter 16, Parallelism)
text: Experiment twenty-nine needs three independent facts from three services. Each call takes two simulated seconds. Call service records the call, waits using asyncio sleep, and then advances a simulated clock. The waits really overlap, but the clock makes the printed times exact and repeatable. The sequential version awaits each fetch in turn. The concurrent version passes all three to asyncio gather, which runs them at the same time. Here's the output. Both versions return the same three facts, and both make three calls. But sequential takes six seconds, and concurrent takes two. So only the elapsed time differs. Sequentially, the time is the sum of the three. In parallel, it is roughly the longest of the three, plus some overhead. The total work is the same. One practical detail. Each fetch must be an async coroutine. Ordinary blocking functions passed to gather would run one after another, before gather even starts. And so, a key distinction. Lower latency is not lower compute, or lower cost.

title: Experiment 30 (Chapter 16, Parallelism)
text: Experiment thirty asks three reviewers to inspect the same proposal, open a second warehouse in Q3, from three different perspectives: financial, risk, and operations. Fan out runs all three reviewers concurrently with gather. Notice return exceptions is set to true, so a failed branch becomes a result, instead of an exception that hides the others. The reviewers return fixed findings: the margin assumption is unsupported, there is a dependency on one supplier, and the timeline is infeasible. A second run makes the operations reviewer time out. Then we compare two fan-in policies on the same branch results. The bad fan-in over-summarises. It keeps only issues that at least two reviewers agree on. If there are any, the proposal needs revision. Otherwise, it looks acceptable. The complete fan-in keeps every finding, together with its reviewer, and lists any branch that failed. If a branch is missing, the verdict is incomplete. Otherwise, it is revise if there are issues, and accept if there are none. Here's what happened. The bad fan-in says: proposal looks acceptable. All three reviewers found valid issues. But no two reviewers raised the same issue, so the over-summarising aggregator dropped every one of them. The branches succeeded. The system failed at aggregation. The complete fan-in says revise, and lists all three findings. And in the partial-failure run, it says incomplete, names operations as missing, and keeps the two findings it did get. That's the failure mode. Good parallel work can be destroyed by a bad fan-in policy.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: central question
text: What changes when one agent can invoke another agent, through the same action interface used for ordinary tools? Multi-agent systems can sound like a whole new field. In this lecture we'll see that they start from something we already have. By the end, you will have wrapped a child agent as a tool, watched it hide a loop from its parent, and you'll know which limits must cross the delegation boundary.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: principle
text: Multi-agent systems begin when an agent becomes a capability exposed to another controller. The figure shows the transition. In chapter five, an agent called a tool. In chapter seventeen, an agent calls an agent-as-tool. The outer contract is the same: select, invoke, observe. The novelty is inside the capability.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: key takeaways
text: An agent can be exposed through the same invocation contract as a tool. Agent-tools differ operationally: their path, cost, latency and failures can vary. Delegated autonomy should include explicit budgets and permissions. Structured failure allows the parent to retain control. Delegation is also context engineering and a security boundary. Nested traces should expose the work hidden behind parent calls.

title: Experiment 31 (Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool)
text: Let's make it concrete. Experiment thirty-one gives the parent a goal that needs both research and arithmetic: find the reported value of X, then calculate X times one point one. The parent first delegates the information subtask. Its action is a call to the researcher, asking what is X. The observation comes back as a small structured object: status complete, answer eighty, steps used two. Then the parent uses a deterministic tool. It calls the calculator with eighty times one point one, and observes eighty-eight. Here is the child's run method from the companion code. Both levels, parent and child, are built from the same agent loop we wrote back in chapter three. The child creates its own agent, with its own scripted model and its own search tool, and with a step limit that the parent passes in. If the loop finishes, the status is complete. If the child hits its step limit, the loop raises an error, and the child reports the status incomplete, with no answer. Either way, it returns a structured result that includes how many steps it used, rather than a bare string. And this is the parent's policy. With no observation yet, it asks the researcher what X is. When a structured result comes back, it checks the status. If the status is not complete, the parent stops and escalates, instead of calculating with a value it doesn't have. If the status is complete, it builds the expression and calls the calculator. And once the calculator's observation arrives, it answers. The experiment runs twice. The second run gives the child a model that searches forever. Here's the output. With the cooperative specialist, the researcher returns complete, with answer eighty. The parent's actions are researcher, then calculator. The child made one hidden search, and the answer is eighty-eight. With the looping specialist and a delegated limit of five steps, the researcher returns incomplete, with a null answer and five steps used. The parent took only one action. Behind it, the child made five searches. And the parent's answer is: escalate, research incomplete. Notice that nothing in the parent loop needed special multi-agent syntax. The specialist is simply an action whose implementation happens to contain another model-driven process.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: central question
text: When does a coordinator improve a team of specialist agents, and when does another management layer merely add overhead and information loss? By the end of this lecture, you will have run a supervisor over three workers, and a two-level hierarchy, and you'll have seen exactly where each one fails.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: principle
text: Coordination must earn its layer. A supervisor is valuable only when decomposition, assignment, monitoring, or integration are real problems. A hierarchy is valuable only when reducing coordination complexity outweighs the extra hops and the information loss.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: key takeaways
text: Supervision combines decomposition, assignment, scheduling, monitoring, integration and recovery. Worker competence cannot compensate for every supervisor error. Shared task state should preserve continuity without broadcasting unnecessary context. Hierarchy reduces coordination span by introducing abstraction boundaries, and those boundaries can lose critical information. Budgets, permissions, delegation depth and traces must stay enforceable across the hierarchy.

title: Experiment 32 (Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers)
text: Experiment thirty-two gives the system a goal that needs three distinct skills: produce a short, evidence-based comparison of A and B. The supervisor decomposes it into three tasks. Research comparable facts about A and B. Analyze the differences. And write the final comparison. But these tasks are not independent. The analyst needs the researcher's evidence, and the writer needs the analyst's findings. So the supervisor has to coordinate state, not just choose workers. Here are the three workers. They're scripted, so the run is deterministic. Each one reads a shared state, and returns an update. The researcher returns evidence about A and B. The analyst turns evidence into findings: A is cheaper, and B is rated higher. But if there's no evidence, it returns no findings. And look at the writer. If there are no findings, it still writes something: A and B are broadly comparable. That's a fluent draft, with nothing behind it. It's marked in the code as unsupported. Now the supervisor. A plan is just an ordered list of worker names, and there are two ways to run it. The naive supervisor simply takes the next worker in the plan. The dependency-aware supervisor looks, at each step, for the first pending worker whose inputs already exist in the state. If no worker is ready, it reports that it's blocked. Either way, it runs the worker, and merges its update into the shared state. Here's the output. With the good decomposition, the order is researcher, analyst, writer, and the draft says A is cheaper, and B is rated higher. With the bad decomposition, the naive supervisor runs the writer first. The writer has no findings, so it produces the unsupported draft: A and B are broadly comparable. The researcher and analyst run afterwards, but nothing revisits the draft. With the same bad plan, the dependency-aware supervisor reorders the work, and gets the right answer. So the repair lives in the coordinator, not in the workers. Worker competence cannot repair a structurally bad decomposition.

title: Experiment 33 (Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers)
text: Now suppose one supervisor has too many different workers. We can introduce an intermediate layer. The root delegates broad subgoals to a research lead and a build lead, and each lead coordinates its own workers. Experiment thirty-three compares a flat team, where the root reads all four worker reports directly, with this two-level hierarchy. It counts the root's span of control, and the messages exchanged. It runs the hierarchy twice: once with lossy leads that forward only findings, and once with structured leads that also forward caveats. And one research worker reports that option A is cheaper, but that its source confidence is low. Here are the leads and the root. The lossy lead returns only the findings from its workers' reports. The structured lead returns the findings too, but also a separate list of caveats. The root's decision rule is simple. If any caveat reaches it, it says: verify before choosing. Otherwise, it chooses option A. Here's what happened. The flat team: the root's span is four, eight messages are exchanged, and the decision is to verify first, because the confidence is low. The hierarchy with lossy leads: the span drops to two, the messages rise to twelve, and the root chooses option A. It never saw the caveat. The hierarchy with structured leads: same span, same twelve messages, and the root correctly asks for verification. So the hierarchy halves the root's span of control, and adds four messages. With lossy leads, the caveat is lost. The structured field carries it across both boundaries.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: central question
text: Can several agents make a better decision than one? And what happens when their errors are correlated, or when the most persuasive answer is wrong? By the end of this lecture, you will have watched a vote repair one error and confirm another, and you'll have seen a judge reward rhetoric, until it is grounded in a tool.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: principle
text: Collective intelligence requires error diversity. More agents help only when they contribute sufficiently independent information, and the system can aggregate that information reliably. Consensus by itself is not evidence of truth.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: key takeaways
text: Voting aggregates positions; it does not establish truth. Consensus is valuable only to the extent that opinions contain useful independence. Shared evidence and shared blind spots can create false consensus. Debate can expose errors, but can also reward persuasion and create anchoring. A judge is another fallible evaluator; ground it where possible. Measure error correlation, Oracle@N, selection accuracy, regression, cost and latency.

title: Experiment 34 (Chapter 19, Debate and Voting)
text: Experiment thirty-four uses a binary question whose answer we know: B. Each scripted worker answers from the one source it reads. A filing and an analyst note both say B. A promotional blog says A. The majority function returns the most common answer. And if there's an exact tie, it reports a tie, instead of breaking it at random. The file also reports Oracle at N, meaning: was at least one worker right? And it counts how many distinct sources sat behind the votes. Four scenarios. First, independent errors: three workers read three different sources. The votes are B, B, A. The majority is B, which is correct. The one wrong worker was outvoted. Second, correlated errors: two workers read the same blog. Now the votes are A, A, B, and the majority is wrong. Third, nine voters, but still drawing on the same two sources: seven say A and two say B. Still wrong. And fourth, an even split, which is reported as a tie. Look at the correlated case. Oracle at three is true: the correct answer was right there in the votes. But the vote picked the wrong one. A vote has no mechanism for recognising that the minority is correct.

title: Experiment 35 (Chapter 19, Debate and Voting)
text: The experiment compares two judges. The rhetoric judge is a deliberately crude stand-in for a judge that can't verify anything: the longest argument wins. The grounded judge computes the answer itself, with the calculator tool. It accepts only a candidate whose answer matches. And if none matches, it refuses to force a choice. Here's the output. In the normal debate, both judges pick B, and both are correct. But that's luck for the rhetoric judge: B happened to write the longer argument. Now the persuasion variant. The wrong agent gives a long, confident, polished argument for ninety-six. The correct agent just says one hundred and two. The rhetoric judge now picks A, and it's wrong. The grounded judge still picks B. So the rhetoric judge's accuracy depends on presentation, not on the arithmetic. That's the failure mode. Debate can optimize persuasiveness rather than truth, when the judge cannot verify the disputed claim.

title: Chapter 20, Shared State: central question
text: What happens when several agents coordinate by reading and writing the same workspace, rather than passing every message directly? By the end of this lecture, you will have built a blackboard that keeps conflicting claims, rejects a stale write, and lets only one agent claim a task.

title: Chapter 20, Shared State: principle
text: Shared state is shared influence. A blackboard simplifies information exchange by making state reusable. That same reuse magnifies stale data, conflicts, unauthorized writes, and bad evidence. So shared state needs explicit write, version, provenance, and trust policies.

title: Chapter 20, Shared State: key takeaways
text: Shared state and model context are different abstractions. A blackboard lets agents coordinate indirectly through persistent task state. Structured state should preserve provenance and uncertainty. Last-write-wins is not a truth-resolution policy. Versioning detects stale computations; task claims need concurrency control. Write permissions and validation make shared state a security boundary.

title: Experiment 36 (Chapter 20, Shared State)
text: Experiment thirty-six gives three specialists a common goal: work out the total cost of an order, from a product price, a quantity, and a shipping fee. The board starts with the goal, an empty set of facts, and three tasks: find the price, find the shipping, and calculate the total. The price worker publishes a unit price of eighty, and a quantity of three. The shipping worker independently publishes a shipping fee of fifteen. The calculation worker waits until all the facts it needs exist on the board: unit price, quantity and shipping. Once they do, it computes the total: eighty times three, plus fifteen, which is two hundred and fifty-five. Notice that no worker needed a direct message from any other. The shared state carried the coordination. A plain dictionary is enough to show readiness, but it hides the failures we care about. So the experiment's blackboard stores each fact as a list of claims, each with its source. Each source has an authority. A newer catalog ranks highest, then the older catalog, the carrier's API and the calculator, and a cached web page ranks lowest. When claims conflict, the current value is resolved by source authority, not by timing. The most authoritative claim wins, whenever it was written. Here's how the board publishes. Every write appends a claim and increases a version number. A writer can also say which version it read. If the board has moved on since then, the write is rejected as stale. The version check and the write happen together, inside a lock. It's a compare-and-swap. The script then runs four steps in order: the readiness check, a conflicting write, an exclusive task claim by two agents, and a stale write. Here's the output. After pricing, the total is not ready. Once shipping arrives, it is, and the total is two hundred and fifty-five, computed at version three. Next, a cached page writes a price of ninety. In a plain dictionary, the last write wins, and the price becomes ninety. But the board kept both claims, and resolves the price by authority back to the catalog's eighty. Then agent A claims the calculation task, and succeeds. Agent B tries, and is refused. Finally, a price correction lands in the middle of the calculation. The commit of two hundred and fifty-five is rejected as stale: it read version four, but the board is at version five. The recomputed total of two hundred and eighty-five is accepted.

title: Chapter 21, Agent-to-Agent Communication: central question
text: How can independently implemented agents discover capabilities, delegate work, exchange status and artifacts, and preserve trust across a system boundary? By the end of this lecture, you will have run a tiny remote agent that deduplicates retries, rejects an unknown caller, and completes a task with an artifact nobody can use.

title: Chapter 21, Agent-to-Agent Communication: principle
text: A communication protocol can standardize exchange. It cannot create shared meaning, or trust, by itself.

title: Chapter 21, Agent-to-Agent Communication: key takeaways
text: Agent-to-agent communication crosses an explicit agent/service boundary. Discovery describes capabilities; authorization decides whether they may be used. Tasks need lifecycle semantics; artifacts need structured, versioned contracts. Shared syntax and schema do not guarantee shared semantics. Delegation does not automatically transfer trust or authority. Remote outputs are untrusted inputs until validated at the receiving boundary.

title: Experiment 37 (Chapter 21, Agent-to-Agent Communication)
text: Experiment thirty-seven builds two tiny agents. A coordinator needs research. A remote research agent publishes a card with one skill. Notice what the coordinator does not do. It doesn't choose a task ID, and it doesn't call a skill by name. As in A2A, it sends a message with its own message ID, and the server decides whether to create a task, and assigns the task ID. In the server's send message method, a message ID it has already seen is a retry, so it returns the existing task. Otherwise it creates a new, submitted task. And if the caller isn't on the allowed list, the task is rejected. For an allowed caller, the task moves to working. The result comes back as an artifact, made of typed parts, here a single data part. And the task completes. On the caller's side, the comparison is validated independently. The artifact must contain an integer price, and the currency must be US dollars. The experiment also builds a second, drifted remote agent, that returns a field called amount, containing the text eighty dollars. Here's the output. One skill is discovered: company research. Task one goes from submitted, to working, to completed. The retry of message one returns task one again, and only one task is stored. The intruder's request creates task two, which is rejected. The artifact is valid. And the drifted agent? Its task completes, but its artifact is not valid. So the whole mechanism is visible without a networking framework: discover, send a message, track the task status, and receive an artifact. A retry is recognised by its message ID, an unknown caller is rejected, and a task can complete with an artifact the caller cannot use.

title: Chapter 22, Evaluation: central question
text: How do we determine whether an agentic system succeeds, why it fails, and whether a proposed architectural improvement is actually better? By the end of this lecture, you will be able to score outcomes, trajectories and model judges. And you will know why a single headline score is rarely enough.

title: Chapter 22, Evaluation: principle
text: Evaluate at the failure layer. Measure final outcomes, but also evaluate the components and trajectories that produce them. Otherwise, a good score can hide a fragile system, and a bad score can lead to the wrong fix.

title: Chapter 22, Evaluation: key takeaways
text: Begin with the engineering question being tested. Outcome, trajectory, component, resource and control are distinct layers. Use objective evaluators whenever practical; baselines and slices make comparisons meaningful. Prefer trajectory invariants over one supposedly perfect path. LLM-as-judge is a scalable evaluator, not ground truth: calibrate it and swap the order. Keep held-out tests and turn discovered failures into regression cases.

title: Experiment 38 (Chapter 22, Evaluation)
text: Experiment thirty-eight begins with the simplest objective task: arithmetic with known answers. The kernel provides two comparison functions. Exact match is true only when the raw output equals the reference exactly. Numeric match parses the output as a number, and compares it with the reference within a small tolerance. If the output can't be parsed, it returns false. The agent is a fixture that answers in text, just as a language model does. The experiment scores the same answers twice, once with each comparison. There are three cases. The fixture gets one wrong: it says twenty-five plus nineteen is forty-five. And it gets one right, but formats it as nine point zero. Exact match scores zero out of three. Numeric match scores two out of three. So the evaluator is a design decision. Ground truth is known here, and the evaluator is deterministic. But comparing the text one hundred and two with the integer one hundred and two scores a correct answer as wrong. Normalize outputs deliberately, and record how you did it.

title: Experiment 39 (Chapter 22, Evaluation)
text: Experiment thirty-nine looks not only at the answer, but at the path that produced it. There are three authorized tools: search, retrieve and calculator. Only retrieve and calculator are relevant. There's a single reference path, retrieve then calculator, and a limit of six steps. Two trajectories both end with the correct answer, one hundred and two. The wasteful one calls search, then a weather tool, then the calculator. The direct one goes straight to the calculator. Each is checked against the reference path, and against a set of invariants. The invariant checks ask whether the required tool was used, how many calls were irrelevant or unauthorized, and whether the run stayed within the step limit. The wasteful trajectory made two irrelevant calls, and one of them was to a tool it was never authorized to use. The direct trajectory is clean on every check. But look at the reference match. It's false for both. The reference-path check rejects the direct trajectory too, even though it's a perfectly good solution.

title: Experiment 40 (Chapter 22, Evaluation)
text: Some outputs have no exact-match evaluator. A model can score them against a rubric: two for correct, complete and grounded, one for partially correct, and zero for incorrect or unsupported. That's useful because it scales subjective evaluation. It's risky because the evaluator is itself a model. Experiment forty makes the risk concrete without calling any model. It uses two stand-in judges with known biases. One rewards long answers. The pairwise judge always prefers whichever answer comes first. The judge is checked against four answers with trusted labels, and the pairwise judge is run in both orders. Against the trusted labels, the judge agrees on only one answer out of four, and it over-scores two. The long, confident answer with the wrong revenue figure gets the top score, while the short, correct and sourced answer is marked down. The swap test shows the second bias.
