title: Preface: opening
text: Why This Book Exists The motivation Agentic systems are becoming more capable faster than our explanations of them are becoming clearer. This book starts with the smallest possible mechanisms, breaks them deliberately, and then engineers the controls that make autonomy useful.

title: Preface: Artificial intelligence crossed a boundary
text: For most of the modern history of machine learning, we built systems that predicted. A model classified an image, estimated a probability, forecast a time series, ranked alternatives, or generated text. The model produced an output. Software around the model decided what happened next. Large language models began to blur that boundary. They could write code, interpret instructions, reason over documents, choose between alternatives, and describe sequences of actions. It was natural to take the next step: give the model tools and allow it to act. A model could search. It could query a database. It could execute code. It could use a browser. It could call another model. It could remember what happened previously. It could make a plan, execute part of it, inspect the result, revise the plan, and continue. The model was no longer merely producing an answer. It was participating in a process. And that changed the engineering problem.

title: Preface: From models to agents
text: The term AI agent quickly came to describe an enormous range of systems. A chatbot with a calculator was called an agent. A retrieval system was called an agent. A workflow containing several model calls was called an agent. Systems that planned, reflected, delegated work to other models, controlled computers, wrote software, or operated continuously were all described using the same word. Around them grew an equally large vocabulary: tools, function calling, memory, RAG, ReAct, reflection, planning, routing, orchestration, supervisors, workers, multi-agent systems, MCP, A2A, computer use, agent skills, context engineering, human oversight, guardrails, evaluators, judges, sandboxes, checkpoints, durable execution, and self-improvement. Each idea is useful. Together, they can make the field appear considerably more mysterious than it is. Frameworks make the problem worse for someone trying to understand the fundamentals. A few lines of framework code may create an apparently sophisticated agent, but those few lines can hide hundreds or thousands of lines of machinery. The program works. But the reader cannot necessarily explain why. What exactly made it an agent? What information was passed to the model? Who executed the tool? Where was state stored? What caused another model call? Why did the loop stop? What would happen if the tool failed? What prevented the model from calling a capability it should not have? What changed when another agent was added? Which part of the system should be blamed when the result was wrong? Those questions are much easier to answer when the machinery is small enough to see. That observation became the motivation for this book.

title: Preface: Start with the smallest possible experiment
text: The central teaching philosophy of this book is simple: every important idea in agentic AI should be understandable through the smallest program that can demonstrate it. We will therefore not begin with an agent framework. We will begin with a model call. Then we will change one thing. We will give the model an action. Then we will return the result of that action as an observation. That gives us a feedback loop. Later we will add structured decisions. Then state. Then multiple tools. Then retrieval. Then memory. Then planning. Then reflection. Then other agents. Then evaluation, recovery, permissions, security, budgets, computer use, and learning. At every stage, we will ask the same question: What changed? The progression is deliberately incremental because complexity is easiest to understand when we can identify exactly where it entered the system. The first implementation of an idea should therefore be small enough to fit on a screen whenever possible. Not because production systems should be tiny. They should not. But because explanations should be.

title: Preface: Run it. Then break it.
text: There is another important principle behind the experiments in this book. We will not stop when the code works. We will deliberately break it. If we add a tool, we will remove the tool and allow the model to request it anyway. If we add memory, we will store something that should not have been remembered. If we add retrieval, we will retrieve irrelevant evidence. If we add planning, we will change the environment after the plan has been created. If we add reflection, we will let the critic make a correct answer worse. If we add multiple agents, we will make them confidently agree on the same wrong answer. If we add retries, we will create a retry storm. If we add computer use, we will move the button after the agent has observed it. If we add self-improvement, we will give the agent a metric it can exploit. This is not merely a teaching device. Failure reveals architecture. A successful demonstration tells us that a system can work. A carefully constructed failure tells us why it works, what assumptions it depends on, and where its boundaries lie.

title: Preface: From Agentic AI to Agentic Engineering
text: Building useful agents is not primarily about discovering increasingly elaborate prompts. It is a systems engineering problem. A useful working decomposition is: Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control The model proposes decisions. Context determines what information is available when those decisions are made. Actions determine what the system is capable of doing. State determines what persists across decisions. Control determines what is allowed to happen, how execution proceeds, and when it stops. Almost every major concept in modern agentic systems can be understood as engineering one or more of these five components. RAG changes context. Memory combines state with context selection. Tools add actions. MCP standardizes access to actions and resources. ReAct changes control by feeding observations into subsequent decisions. Planning changes how control allocates future actions. Reflection adds another feedback mechanism. Multi-agent systems make other agents available as capabilities and introduce new coordination structures. Human approval constrains control. Sandboxing constrains actions. Budgets constrain resources and continuation. Computer use introduces perception and action grounding. Self-improvement allows parts of the system itself to change across tasks. Seen this way, the apparent collection of unrelated agent techniques begins to form a coherent engineering discipline. Agentic Engineering is the discipline of designing, building, evaluating, and operating software systems in which models dynamically choose actions toward goals while engineering constrains their context, state, capabilities, resources, risk, and autonomy.

title: Preface: The model is not the system
text: Modern models are extraordinarily capable, and their capabilities will continue to improve. But an agent is not merely its model. The same model can behave very differently depending on the system surrounding it. Give it irrelevant context and performance can deteriorate. Give it an unreliable tool and correct reasoning can still produce failure. Give it unlimited memory and obsolete or malicious information can influence future decisions. Give it unlimited steps and a perfectly valid sequence of actions can continue forever. Give it broad computer access and a grounding mistake can become an external side effect. Give it a badly designed reward and a capable system may become very effective at optimizing the wrong objective. This motivates another recurring idea in the book: Agent Quality Model Quality + Harness Quality This is intentionally not a numerical equation. It is an engineering reminder. The harness determines what the model sees, what it can do, what information persists, what feedback returns, what authority it receives, what happens when something fails, and when execution must stop. As models become stronger, the harness does not become irrelevant. In many applications it becomes more important.

title: Preface: Autonomy creates obligations
text: Giving an agent more capability is easy to describe as progress: more tools, more memory, more reasoning, more agents, more time, more access, more independence. But increasing autonomy changes the risk surface of the system. A model that only generates text can produce a bad answer. A model that can send an email can produce a bad answer and send it. A model that can execute code can produce a bad decision and execute it. A persistent agent can carry a bad assumption into future tasks. A multi-agent system can propagate a mistake through several components. A self-improving system can potentially preserve a bad change. For this reason, a second proposition runs through the entire book: Autonomy Control Requirements Tools require permissions. Memory requires provenance and write policies. Planning requires budgets and stopping conditions. Delegation requires accountability. Persistence requires recovery. Computer use requires grounding and verification. Self-improvement requires independent evaluation and rollback. The objective of Agentic Engineering is therefore not maximum autonomy. It is useful autonomy under appropriate control.

title: Preface: More is not always better
text: Many experiments in this book challenge intuitions that sound reasonable but fail under measurement. More context does not necessarily produce better decisions. More reasoning does not necessarily produce better answers. More agents do not necessarily produce more intelligence. More reflection does not necessarily improve a correct result. More memory does not necessarily create better memory. More autonomy does not necessarily create a better system. Every mechanism has both a benefit and a cost. We will therefore repeatedly ask not merely whether a technique works, but whether it earns the resources and complexity it introduces. Where appropriate, experiments will consider several dimensions: success, cost, latency, reliability, and autonomy or risk. These dimensions should not automatically be collapsed into a single score. A system can become more accurate while becoming slower. It can become cheaper while becoming less reliable. It can complete more tasks while requiring dangerously broad authority. Engineering means making those trade-offs visible.

title: Preface: No magic
text: There is a temptation in fast-moving fields to explain new capabilities using new terminology. This book takes the opposite approach. Whenever possible, we will reduce a technique to ordinary software concepts. An agent loop is a loop. A tool call is a proposed function invocation. Memory is a write policy, a store, and a retrieval policy. Routing is resource allocation under uncertainty. A supervisor is a coordinator. Shared state is shared influence. A retry is another attempt whose side effects must be understood. A checkpoint is persisted recoverable state. Human approval is an authorization boundary. Computer use is perception, grounding, action, and verification. Self-improvement is optimization followed by evaluation and controlled promotion. The models are unusual components. The engineering principles around them are often surprisingly familiar. This is good news. It means that decades of software engineering, distributed systems, security, control, testing, optimization, and machine learning remain relevant. Agentic systems do not replace those disciplines. They bring them together in a new configuration.

title: Preface: Primitive $\rightarrow$ Engineered $\rightarrow$ Framework
text: The examples in this book operate at three levels. First comes the primitive implementation. This is the smallest code that exposes the mechanism. Then comes the engineered implementation. Here we introduce validation, typing, retries, permissions, logging, evaluation, budgets, security, or whatever the primitive requires to become more dependable. Only then do we consider the framework implementation. Frameworks are valuable. They save enormous amounts of engineering effort. But a framework is much easier to understand after we know what it is doing for us. By the time you encounter a sophisticated agent framework, I want you to be able to look through its abstractions and recognize the machinery underneath. Where is the model? What context is being constructed? What actions exist? Where is state stored? What controls the next step? Once those questions become natural, frameworks become implementation choices rather than sources of mystery.

title: Preface: Why deterministic examples come first
text: Agentic systems contain probabilistic components. That makes them interesting. It can also make them frustrating teaching instruments. If the first experiment depends on a live model, two readers may run identical code and observe different behavior. A provider may update a model. Sampling may change an answer. An example that worked when the book was written may behave differently when the reader runs it. For that reason, the examples use tiny deterministic stand-ins for the model: ScriptedModel, which replays fixed responses, and PolicyModel, which decides from what it sees in its context. This is intentional. The deterministic example demonstrates the mechanism. A separate empirical experiment measures the model. We should not confuse the two. When the question is architectural—What does feedback do? What happens if an observation is removed? Why does a stopping condition matter?—deterministic examples let us isolate the variable we care about. When the question is empirical—Does reflection improve accuracy? Does a stronger model need fewer planning steps? Does multimodal grounding survive UI variation?—we must run repeated experiments against real models and report the methodology. This book does both, and keeps them apart. Every numbered experiment is deterministic and runs without an API key. Nine chapters then add a Live run: the same question asked of real, pinned model snapshots over repeated trials, reported with 95% intervals, token use, and the date of the run. Some live results confirm the mechanism, some do not reproduce it, and one shows a model judging no better than chance; all are reported as recorded. A single small run is evidence about one model on one day, not a law, and Chapter 22 shows how to design a larger evaluation.

title: Preface: What I want the reader to be able to do
text: My goal is not for you to memorize a catalog of agent patterns. Frameworks will change. Model APIs will change. Protocol implementations will change. Some of today's terminology will disappear and new terminology will take its place. The underlying engineering questions will remain. After working through the experiments in this book, you should be able to encounter an unfamiliar agent architecture and ask: What information can the model see? What can it do? What persists? What controls the next decision? What evidence is being used? Where can failure occur? What authority does the system possess? How is success measured? How much can it spend? How does it recover? When does a human intervene? When does it stop? And if it changes itself, what independent evidence shows that the change was actually an improvement? Those questions are more durable than any framework.

title: Preface: The journey ahead
text: We will begin with perhaps the smallest possible question: What actually changes when an LLM becomes an agent? From there, the book progressively adds capability. We will give agents tools. Then context. Then retrieval and memory. We will let them reason through feedback, make plans, search alternatives, route work, and execute tasks in parallel. We will allow agents to use other agents. Then we will confront the engineering consequences: evaluation, observability, failure recovery, human approval, security, permissions, budgets, and stopping. Finally, we will give agents some of their broadest capabilities: writing software, controlling computers, perceiving multimodal environments, and learning from experience. At every step, we will add one mechanism and ask what new failure it makes possible. By the end, we will arrive back at a deceptively simple architecture: Model + Context + Actions + State + Control But those five words will mean considerably more than they did at the beginning.

title: Preface: A short manifesto for Agentic Engineering
text: An agent is not a model with a clever prompt. It is a software system in which a model participates in decisions that can affect an environment. As we give that system more context, tools, memory, time, collaborators, persistence, and authority, we increase its autonomy. Every increase in autonomy creates an engineering obligation. Tools require permissions. Memory requires provenance. Planning requires stopping. Delegation requires accountability. Persistence requires recovery. Computer use requires verification. Self-improvement requires independent evaluation. The purpose of Agentic Engineering is therefore not to maximize autonomy. It is to engineer autonomy that is useful, observable, bounded, recoverable, and justified. And the best way to understand how to do that is to build the smallest possible agent— and then break it.

title: How to Use This Book: opening
text: A practical guide to the experiments, code, measurements, and reading paths The shortest version Read the idea. Run the smallest experiment. Break it deliberately. Measure what changed. Engineer the failure. Only then reach for a framework. This book is designed to be executed, not merely read. Its 30 chapters contain 59 deliberately small experiments, and a closing case study combines them in one system. Each experiment isolates one mechanism so that you can see what it contributes, how it fails, and what engineering is required to make it dependable. You do not need to build every production extension to benefit from the book. But whenever possible, run the primitive example before reading the engineered solution. Seeing a failure occur is more instructive than being told that the failure is possible.

title: How to Use This Book: 1. The recurring chapter pattern
text: Stage | What you should do IDEA | Understand the single mechanism being introduced. CODE | Read or type the smallest useful implementation. RUN | Predict the result, then execute it. BREAK | Change the condition identified in the chapter and reproduce the failure. WHY? | Explain the failure in architectural terms. ENGINEER IT | Add the smallest control that addresses the mechanism. PATTERN | Learn the standard research/industry terminology. SCALE | Map the primitive to a production implementation or framework. Do not skip BREAK. The failure experiment is often the point of the chapter.

title: How to Use This Book: 2. One experiment, one variable
text: The examples are intentionally smaller than normal applications. Their purpose is causal clarity. If a 20-line program can demonstrate a mechanism, a 300-line application usually makes the lesson harder to see. Repository rule Every first-principles experiment is a single short file, printed in full in its chapter together with its real output. The code lives at .

title: How to Use This Book: 3. The three implementation levels
text: Level | What it teaches | Typical characteristics Primitive | The mechanism | Minimal Python, deterministic fixtures, few dependencies Engineered | The controls | Validation, types, retries, authorization, tracing, tests, budgets, security Framework | The mapping | Equivalent concepts in contemporary agent frameworks and protocols Progression Primitive → Engineered → Framework

title: How to Use This Book: 4. Deterministic examples and live-model experiments
text: The book deliberately separates architectural demonstrations from empirical model evaluation. Mode | Use it when | What it tells you Deterministic scripted model | You are learning a mechanism | Whether the architecture behaves as claimed Live LLM | You are measuring model behavior | How a particular model performs under that architecture Benchmark / repeated trials | You are comparing alternatives | Whether an apparent gain survives variance and held-out evaluation A deterministic model is not pretending to be intelligent. It is a controlled fixture. It lets two readers reproduce the same feedback loop, routing decision, reflection failure, or stopping defect.

title: How to Use This Book: 5. Do not treat example results as universal claims
text: When a chapter shows that a mechanism can improve or degrade a result, the primitive experiment demonstrates possibility and mechanism—not a universal empirical effect. Claims about model performance require repeated trials, explicit datasets, model/version information, and appropriate baselines.

title: How to Use This Book: 6. The recurring scorecard
text: Measure several dimensions Q = (S, C, L, R, A): a vector of success, cost, latency, reliability, and autonomy/risk. These dimensions are intentionally not collapsed into one universal number. When you modify an experiment, record which dimensions improve and which deteriorate.

title: How to Use This Book: 7. Suggested Python level
text: The primitive examples assume basic Python familiarity: functions, dictionaries, lists, loops, classes, exceptions, and reading small test files. Advanced Python is not required to understand the core architecture. If you can read a 20–50 line Python script, you can follow the primitive experiments. Type hints, dataclasses, async execution, testing, and packaging appear more often in engineered versions. Framework-specific knowledge is intentionally not a prerequisite.

title: How to Use This Book: 8. Environment setup
text: python -m venv .venv # macOS / Linux source .venv/bin/activate # Windows PowerShell .venv .ps1 # The agentic kernel and test runner (Python 3.10+) python -m pip install -e . python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python chapters/01/01_llm_call.py python -m pytest # Optional: LangChain / LangGraph companions (Python 3.12+) python -m pip install -r requirements-frameworks.txt python -m framework_examples.02_llm_to_agent Start with git clone https://github.com/agentic-engineering-book/code and run these commands from the repository root. The first-principles experiments need only the standard library and the small agentic kernel. The framework companions pin exact versions in requirements-frameworks.txt; requirements-frameworks-live.txt adds the optional provider package used by the live mode of Experiments 2 and 22. Each chapter folder has a README listing its files.

title: How to Use This Book: 9. Provider-neutral model interface
text: Where possible, examples reason about a small provider-neutral interface rather than making one vendor API part of the concept. The repository implements this interface with deterministic stand-ins (ScriptedModel and PolicyModel in agentic/model.py) and with OpenAIModel in agentic/live.py, which connects the same loop to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted or local (Chapter 3). The live experiments in live/ need python -m pip install openai and an OPENAI_API_KEY; they make paid requests and are optional. This keeps the architectural lesson stable even when APIs change.

title: How to Use This Book: 10. Repository organization
text: The companion code is available at . Figure: Layout of the companion code repository. The shared package stays deliberately small. Chapters should introduce only the machinery required for the concept at hand.

title: How to Use This Book: 11. The 59-experiment numbering
text: Experiment filenames are numbered globally rather than restarting in every chapter. This makes the repository mirror the conceptual progression of the book. For example, Chapter 1 contains 01_llm_call.py and 02_llm_to_agent.py; Chapter 30 ends with 57_self_improvement.py, 58_experience_learning.py, and 59_reward_optimization.py.

title: How to Use This Book: 12. Predict before you run
text: For each experiment, pause before execution and write down what you expect to happen. This small habit turns a code example into an experiment. When the result differs from your prediction, you have found something worth understanding.

title: How to Use This Book: 13. Change one thing at a time
text: If you replace the model, prompt, tool set, context, stopping policy, and evaluator simultaneously, you may get a better system without learning why. The primitive experiments encourage controlled changes. Figure: A controlled experiment changes one mechanism at a time.

title: How to Use This Book: 14. Keep the failure
text: When you engineer a fix, preserve the failing case as a test. The book’s failure examples are natural seeds for regression suites.

title: How to Use This Book: 15. Safe execution
text: Some later experiments involve code execution, computer use, external content, memory, or consequential actions. Use controlled fixtures and sandboxes while learning. Prefer fake services, recorded UI states, temporary directories, and narrowly scoped credentials over live consequential systems. Safety rule A teaching experiment should not require broad real-world authority to demonstrate a concept.

title: How to Use This Book: 16. Reading path: software engineers
text: Software engineers can read the book linearly, but may want to pay particular attention to the transition from primitive behavior to engineered control. Part I for the agent loop and architecture. Part II for tool, context, memory, and interface design. Part V for validation, observability, recovery, authorization, security, and budgets. Chapters 28–30 for coding, computer use, and self-improvement.

title: How to Use This Book: 17. Reading path: ML and AI engineers
text: Part I to separate model behavior from agent architecture. Part III for reasoning/control patterns and their empirical evaluation. Chapter 22 for task, trajectory, and judge-based evaluation. Chapters 29–30 for multimodal perception and learning across tasks. Run live-model variants after the deterministic mechanism is clear.

title: How to Use This Book: 18. Reading path: researchers
text: Treat each experiment question as a hypothesis template. Replace deterministic fixtures with controlled model trials and repeated runs. Preserve baselines and report cost/latency alongside task metrics. Use held-out evaluation for self-improvement claims. Distinguish architecture effects from model/version effects.

title: How to Use This Book: 19. Reading path: technical leaders and architects
text: You can understand the core thesis without implementing every experiment. Focus on the architecture, failure, and engineering sections. Introduction and Chapters 1–4 for the autonomy spectrum. Chapters 5–10 for capability and context boundaries. Chapters 17–21 for delegation and multi-agent coordination. Part V in full for production governance. Chapter 30 for the control implications of systems that learn or modify themselves.

title: How to Use This Book: 20. Reading path: executives
text: You do not need to run the experiments to make sound decisions about agents. Start with the briefing written for you, then read the chapters that shape the decisions only leaders can make. In every chapter, the central question at the start and the principle and key takeaways at the end can be read on their own. Read | Why Agentic Engineering for Executives | The decisions, numbers, risks, and checklist in one place 1 — From an LLM to an Agent | What actually changes when a model can act 4 — Workflows vs Agents | When autonomy is worth paying for, and when it is not 22 — Evaluation | What evidence to ask for before approving a system 25 — Human-in-the-Loop | How approval and permissions really constrain an agent 26 — Security | Why untrusted content must never become trusted control 27 — Budgets and Stopping | How cost and risk are bounded before they are spent Conclusion | The principles of the book in one place Every chapter also has a narrated video lecture, and every experiment can be run and watched step by step in a web browser, with no programming, at .

title: How to Use This Book: 21. Reading path: time-constrained readers
text: If you want the shortest path through the book, read the following chapters first: Chapter | Why 1 — From an LLM to an Agent | The fundamental feedback loop 4 — Workflows vs Agents | When autonomy is justified 5 — Tools | How decisions become consequences 6 — Context Engineering | What the model sees 8 — Memory | What persists 12 — Planning | Future structure under uncertainty 17 — An Agent Is Just Another Tool | Delegation as composition 22 — Evaluation | How to know whether the system works 25 — Human-in-the-Loop | Authority and approval 26 — Security | Information is not authority 27 — Budgets and Stopping | Why autonomy must end 30 — Self-Improving Agents | Why change is not automatically improvement

title: How to Use This Book: 22. How to use frameworks with this book
text: Do not avoid frameworks. Delay them just long enough to understand what they are doing. After completing a primitive experiment, reproduce the same behavior in the framework you use professionally and map its abstractions back to Model, Context, Actions, State, and Control.

title: How to Use This Book: 23. Keep a lab notebook
text: For each experiment, record a compact result table. Field | Example Question | Does reflection improve this task? Baseline | one model call Change | draft → critique → revision Success | 8/10 → 9/10 Cost | 1 call → 3 calls Latency | 1.2 s → 3.5 s Regression | 1 previously correct answer became wrong Conclusion | useful on this slice; not universally beneficial The numbers above are illustrative only. Your notebook should contain measured results from your own run.

title: How to Use This Book: 24. When a result surprises you
text: Do not immediately add more prompting. First identify the failure layer: Model, Context, Actions, State, or Control. Then ask what evidence would distinguish competing explanations.

title: How to Use This Book: 25. When to move from primitive to engineered
text: Move on when you can explain the primitive mechanism and reproduce its failure. The engineered version should answer a specific failure—not add production complexity for its own sake.

title: How to Use This Book: 26. When to move from engineered to framework
text: Move on when you can name the responsibilities you want the framework to assume: state persistence, orchestration, tracing, tool schemas, durable execution, human approval, or another explicit need.

title: How to Use This Book: 27. A chapter-completion checklist
text: - I can state the experiment’s question in one sentence. - I can explain the mechanism without naming a framework. - I ran or traced the primitive example. - I reproduced the deliberate failure. - I can classify the failure as Model, Context, Actions, State, or Control. - I understand what the engineered fix changes. - I know what the fix costs in complexity, latency, or resources. - I can recognize the same mechanism inside a framework. - I know which empirical claims would require a real benchmark rather than the deterministic example.

title: How to Use This Book: 28. The most important habit
text: Ask this repeatedly What changed? Whenever the system gains a new capability, memory, reasoning step, agent, protocol, permission, or learning mechanism, ask what changed in the five-part architecture—and what new failure became possible.

title: How to Use This Book: 29. Then ask the second question
text: The engineering question What control does this new autonomy require? Those two questions—What changed? and What control does it require?—are enough to guide you through the entire book.

title: How to Use This Book: Ready
text: With the method established, the next step is intentionally small: make one model call, add one action, feed the observation back, and watch a model become part of an agent loop.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: opening
text: A briefing for leaders who will approve, fund, and answer for agentic systems The short version An agent is software that lets a model's decisions cause actions. Grant it the least autonomy that achieves the result, start where outcomes can be checked and actions undone, measure cost per completed task, put a named person in charge of every agent, and expand only on evidence. The rest of this book is written for the people who build agents. This briefing is written for the people who decide whether they should be built, where, and under what control. It assumes no programming knowledge and takes about forty minutes to read. Executive books on artificial intelligence explain well why AI matters and how organisations should change around it. They say less about the engineering facts that decide whether an agent project pays off: when an agent is better than a simpler workflow, what really drives its cost, which failures to expect, and what "under control" means in practice. Those facts are what this book measures. Each recommendation below is tied to the chapter, and usually to the experiment, that demonstrates it, so you can hand the chapter reference to your technical team and ask them to show you. Figures from outside the book are dated and sourced, because this field moves quickly. Treat them as the state of evidence at that date, not as permanent truths.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 1. The decisions that are yours
text: Most decisions about agents belong with engineers. A small number cannot be delegated, because they set the level of risk the organisation accepts. Decision | Why it sits with leadership | Section Where to use agents | It commits budget and people, and it decides which processes change. | 4 How much autonomy | It sets how much can go wrong before a person notices. | 3 What it may cost | Agent costs grow with every step, retry, and escalation. | 5 Who is accountable | An agent cannot be held responsible; a person must be. | 7 What counts as success | Without agreed measures, demos substitute for evidence. | 8 Buy, build, or partner | It decides whether the capability stays in the organisation. | 10 When to stop | Many projects fail because nobody defined the exit. | 11

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 2. What an agent is, in one page
text: A language model on its own produces text. It can describe an action, but it cannot take one. An agent is a software system in which a model's decisions can cause actions, and the results of those actions come back to the model as new information for its next decision. That loop of decision, action, and observation is the whole difference (Chapter 1). Every agent, however it is marketed, is made of five parts: Part | What it is | The executive question Model | The language model that proposes the next step. | Which model, from whom, and at what cost per call? Context | The information the model sees when it decides. | Is the information current, permitted, and sufficient? Actions | The tools and systems the agent can change. | What exactly can it change, and can that be undone? State | What it remembers between steps and between tasks. | What does it keep, for how long, and who can see it? Control | The rules that limit, check, and stop it. | Who set the limits, and what happens when they are reached? It helps to place agents next to the systems you already know: System | Who decides the next step Rule-based automation (RPA) | A programmer, in advance, for every case. Workflow with an AI step | A programmer fixes the path; a model handles one step, such as reading a document. Chatbot or copilot | A person, after reading the model's answer. Agent | The model, at run time, within limits that software enforces. How to spot "agent washing" Ask one question: does a model's decision cause an action whose result the system then observes and acts on again? If not, it may be useful, but it is not an agent. In June 2025 Gartner estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic products offered genuinely agentic capabilities [1].

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 3. The autonomy decision
text: Autonomy is not a property of the model. It is a decision you make about how much the system may do before a person looks. It helps to think of it as a ladder. Figure: The autonomy ladder. Each step up removes a human check, so each step up must add a software control in its place. The central rule of this book applies directly to leadership decisions: Least autonomy Use the least autonomy necessary to obtain the adaptability the task requires (Chapter 4). Many tasks do not need an agent at all. If the steps are known in advance, a fixed workflow is cheaper, faster, and easier to audit. Gartner made the same observation when it predicted, in June 2025, that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027: many use cases presented as agentic do not require agentic implementations [1]. Evidence from the book (Chapter 4, Experiment 7) A report-summarising task is solved twice: once by a fixed workflow, once by an agent. Both produce the same answers. The workflow uses no model calls; the agent uses three for an English report and four for a French one that needs translating. When the path is known, autonomy adds cost and variability without adding value. Autonomy earns its place where the right next step genuinely depends on what was just found out: investigating an incident, reconciling records that disagree, repairing code until its tests pass. Even then, the step up the ladder should be taken deliberately, one rung at a time, with the matching control in place first.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 4. Where the value is
text: Adoption is not the problem. Results are. In June 2025 McKinsey reported that nearly eight in ten companies it surveyed use generative AI, yet just as many report no significant bottom-line impact, a gap it called the "gen AI paradox" [2]. In August 2025 MIT's NANDA initiative reported that about 95% of the enterprise generative AI pilots it studied delivered no measurable profit-and-loss impact, based on 150 interviews, a survey of 350 employees, and an analysis of 300 public deployments [3]. The 95% figure comes from an early research programme and has been debated, but its explanation is more useful than the number: the tools did not learn from, or fit into, the way work was actually done. Both reports point to the same lesson. Value comes from redesigning a process around what agents do well, not from attaching an agent to a process designed for people. MIT also found that the largest returns came from back-office work, while more than half of budgets went to sales and marketing tools [3]. Good first uses share a recognisable profile: Property | Why it matters The outcome can be checked | You can tell automatically whether the agent succeeded (Chapter 22). Coding agents thrive because tests can be run (Chapter 28). Actions can be undone | A mistake becomes a correction, not an incident. The volume is high | Small savings per task add up; the cost of evaluation is spread wide. The path varies from case to case | Otherwise a workflow is the better tool (Section 3). Someone owns the process | A named owner decides what good looks like and answers for it. The data is reachable and permitted | An agent can only decide well on what it is allowed to see (Chapter 6). Figure: Prioritising a portfolio of agent opportunities by business value and by the consequence of a wrong action.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 5. The economics
text: The price of a single model call is the wrong number to manage. The useful number is the cost per completed task, including everything that task required. - Steps. An agent calls the model once per decision. A task that takes eight decisions costs eight calls, and longer contexts make each call dearer (Chapters 3 and 6). - Retries and failures. Failed attempts still cost money. Unbounded retries multiply load (Chapter 24). - Escalation. Routing hard cases to a stronger model raises quality and cost together (Chapter 15). - Evaluation and oversight. Test suites, monitoring, and the time people spend reviewing and approving are part of the cost, not overhead to be ignored. - Incidents. The expected cost of a wrong action belongs in the business case. Three levers keep the economics sound. Use a workflow wherever the path is known. Route each task to the cheapest model that can be shown to handle it, escalating only when a check says so (Chapter 15). And enforce budgets before each action rather than discovering overspend afterwards (Chapter 27). Evidence from the book (Chapter 27, Experiment 51) An agent searches for an answer that its sources never contain. With no limits, it makes 100 searches, spends 3.00 cost units, and still has no answer. With a budget checked before every action, it stops after three searches, at 0.09 of a 0.10 limit, and reports why it stopped: BUDGET_EXHAUSTED. Costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls are exactly the three reasons Gartner gave for its prediction that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 [1]. All three can be addressed before a project is approved.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 6. What goes wrong
text: Agents fail in characteristic ways. None of these failures is exotic; each is reproduced deliberately in this book so that the matching control can be engineered. You do not need the details, but you should expect your teams to have an answer for every row. Failure | What it looks like | Control (chapter) Invalid action | The model proposes an action that does not exist or has the wrong inputs. | Validation before execution (2) Runaway loop | Every step looks fine, but the task never finishes. | Step limits and budgets (3, 27) Prompt injection | Text in an email or web page instructs the agent to do something else. | Authority kept outside content (26) Poisoned memory | A false "fact" is stored and trusted later. | Write policies for memory (8, 26) Agreeing on the same mistake | Several agents or votes confirm a shared error. | Independent evidence and checks (19) Gaming the measure | The system optimises a score instead of the goal. | Hard rules beside the score (30) Approval misuse | A person approves one action and another is executed. | Approval bound to the exact action (25) Silent failure | Nobody can reconstruct what happened or why. | Tracing and audit trails (23) One rule connects them all, and it is the closest thing this book has to a law: The control law As autonomy increases, control requirements increase. The objective is not maximum autonomy. It is useful autonomy under appropriate control.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 7. Accountability and governance (part 1 of 2)
text: An agent cannot be held responsible for anything. A person must be. Research published in Harvard Business Review in May 2026 found, in a large-scale experiment, that describing AI as an employee rather than as a tool shifted accountability away from the people involved [4]. Treat agents as governed tools with human owners, not as colleagues. Governance for agents needs a few concrete elements: - A named owner for every agent, who answers for its outcomes and can stop it. - A register of agents: what each one is for, what it may change, which data it may see, and who owns it. - Permissions granted per task, not per agent, and enforced by software rather than by instructions to the model (Chapters 25 and 26). - Approvals bound to the exact action, so that what a person approved is what runs (Chapter 25). - An audit trail that records which decision caused which action (Chapter 23). - Governance in proportion to autonomy. A drafting assistant and an agent that moves money need different controls. Gartner warned in May 2026 that applying the same governance to every agent, regardless of its autonomy and scope, leads to failure [5]. Regulation is moving in the same direction. Under Article 26 of the EU AI Act, organisations that deploy high-risk AI systems must use them according to the provider's instructions, assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training, and authority, monitor the system and report risks, and keep its automatically generated logs for at least six months [6]. As of October 2026 these duties apply from 2 December 2027 for most high-risk uses; check the current dates and whether your use case is classed as high-risk. Note the word authority: an overseer who can watch but not intervene does not meet the requirement.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 7. Accountability and governance (part 2 of 2)
text: Trust is still scarce. In a survey of 603 business and technology leaders conducted in July 2025, Harvard Business Review Analytic Services found that only 6% of companies fully trust AI agents to run core business processes, and only 12% said their risk and governance controls were fully in place [7]. Governance is not what slows agents down; its absence is what keeps them out of core processes.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 8. Measuring whether it works
text: A demonstration shows that something can work once. A decision to deploy needs evidence that it works reliably, on cases the system has not seen, at a known cost. Evaluate at the failure layer Measure final outcomes, but also the steps that produce them. Otherwise a good score can hide a fragile system, and a bad score can lead to the wrong fix (Chapter 22). A small set of measures is enough for an executive dashboard: Measure | What it tells you Task success rate | How often the agent achieves the goal, on held-out cases. Cost per completed task | The full cost, including retries, escalation, and review. Escalation rate | How often it hands work to a person, and whether that is falling. Intervention rate | How often a person has to correct or stop it. Incidents | Wrong actions that reached a customer, a system, or a record. Time to completion | Whether the process is actually faster end to end. Be wary of measures that can be satisfied without doing the work, and of checks that agree with each other because they share the same blind spot. Evidence from the book (Chapters 13, 19, and 30) Letting a model critique its own answer repaired a wrong answer and broke a correct one; only an independent check kept the repair and removed the damage (Experiment 25). A majority vote repaired one error and confirmed another, because the voters shared the same mistake (Experiment 34). An easy-to-measure reward selected exactly the wrong behaviour until a hard rule was added (Experiment 59).

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 9. People and organisation
text: Agentic systems change what people do more than how many people are needed. The work moves towards setting goals, defining what good looks like, reviewing exceptions, and improving the system. Three capabilities matter most: - Owners in the business who define outcomes, accept risk, and answer for results. - Evaluation skills: building the test cases and measures that tell you whether an agent works. In the July 2025 survey above, 44% of organisations were prioritising training staff to oversee agents [7]. - A platform team that provides shared models, tools, permissions, logging, and evaluation, so that each new agent does not rebuild the controls. Prefer open standards for connecting agents to tools and to each other, such as the Model Context Protocol and agent-to-agent protocols (Chapters 10 and 21). They reduce dependence on a single vendor. They do not, on their own, create trust: a standard connection still needs the permissions and checks described in Section 7.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 10. Buy, build, or partner
text: In the MIT study, solutions bought from specialised vendors or built with partners succeeded about 67% of the time, while internally built tools succeeded about a third as often [3]. Buying is not automatically safer, however. In September 2026 Gartner predicted that by 2028, 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built for them by vendor engineers embedded in their organisation, because costs rise and the customer cannot evolve the system on its own [8]. Whichever route you choose, make sure your organisation can run, measure, and change the system without depending on someone else. Ten questions to put to any vendor or internal team: - What exactly can the agent change, and what is it forbidden to change? - How are permissions granted, and are they enforced by software or by instructions to the model? - Which actions require a person's approval, and is the approval tied to the exact action? - What is logged, for how long, and can we reconstruct why any action was taken? - What evidence shows it works on cases like ours, measured on cases it was not tuned on? - What does a completed task cost, including retries and escalations, and how are budgets enforced? - What happens when it fails, when a tool is unavailable, or when it is unsure? - How does it resist instructions hidden in documents, emails, or web pages? - Which open standards does it support, and how would we leave? - Who in our organisation will be able to change it after the project ends?

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 11. A first ninety days
text: Weeks | Do | Decide 1–2 | Choose one or two processes from the "start here" quadrant. Name an owner. Measure today's cost, time, and error rate. | Is the path variable enough to need an agent, or would a workflow do? 3–6 | Build the evaluation first: real, held-out cases and the measures in Section 8. Then build the smallest system that could pass. | Does it beat the baseline on held-out cases, at an acceptable cost? 7–10 | Run it in a limited scope, at rung 2 or 3 of the ladder, with budgets, approvals, and an audit trail. | Are incidents, escalations, and interventions within the limits agreed in advance? 11–13 | Review the evidence with the owner and the risk function. | Scale, adjust, or stop, against criteria written down in week 1. Write the stop criteria before the project starts. A project that cannot fail cannot be evaluated either.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 12. The executive checklist
text: Before approving an agent, you should be able to answer every question with a yes. - Is the task's path genuinely variable, so that a fixed workflow would not do? - Is there a named owner who will answer for the agent's outcomes and can stop it? - Is the autonomy level chosen deliberately, with the matching controls in place? - Can the outcome be checked, and can wrong actions be undone or contained? - Is success defined, measured on held-out cases, and compared with today's process? - Is the cost per completed task known, with budgets enforced before actions? - Are permissions granted per task and enforced by software? - Are consequential actions approved by a person, bound to the exact action? - Can we reconstruct what the agent did and why, from its audit trail? - Has it been tested against hidden instructions, bad data, and unavailable tools? - Do we meet our regulatory duties, including human oversight with real authority? - Are the stop criteria written down, and do we have the capability to change the system ourselves?

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 13. Principle and key takeaways
text: Briefing principle Autonomy is a business decision, not a model capability. Grant it only where value can be measured, actions can be controlled, and a person is accountable. - An agent is a model whose decisions cause actions, with software in control of what is allowed. - Use the least autonomy that achieves the result; many "agentic" use cases are workflows. - Start where outcomes are checkable, actions reversible, and volume high; redesign the process rather than attaching an agent to it. - Manage cost per completed task, and enforce budgets before actions, not after. - Every agent needs a named human owner, task-scoped permissions, approvals bound to actions, and an audit trail. - Approve on held-out evidence, not on demonstrations. - Whether you buy or build, keep the ability to run, measure, and change the system yourselves.

title: Agentic Engineering for Executives: 14. Where to go next
text: The reading path for executives in How to Use This Book lists the chapters that matter most for leaders. Each chapter opens with a central question and ends with a principle and key takeaways, which can be read on their own. Every chapter also has a narrated video lecture, and each of the book's 59 experiments can be run and watched step by step in a web browser, with no programming, at .

title: Introduction: opening
text: A conceptual map for the 59 experiments that follow The central idea Much of modern agentic AI can be understood as progressively engineering five components around a model: Model + Context + Actions + State + Control. The easiest way to build an AI agent is to start with a large language model and give it a tool. The easiest way to misunderstand an AI agent is to stop there. Consider a model connected to a calculator. The model receives a question such as “What is 37 × 42?” Instead of answering directly, it proposes a calculator action. Software executes that action, returns 1554, and the model uses the observation to produce the final answer. Something important has happened. The model did not merely generate text. Its output caused software to perform an action, and the result of that action changed the information available to the model’s next decision. Figure: An action's observation feeds the model's next decision. That loop is the seed from which almost everything in this book grows. Add more actions and we have richer tool use. Add retrieved information and we have RAG. Preserve information across tasks and we have memory. Generate future actions before executing them and we have planning. Generate alternatives and compare them and we have search. Ask the system to inspect its previous output and we have reflection. Allow one agent to invoke another and we have multi-agent systems. Give the agent pixels and we have multimodal perception. Give it a mouse and keyboard and we have computer use. Allow lessons from one task to alter behavior on later tasks and we have learning. The field can appear to contain dozens of unrelated ideas. Much of it can instead be understood as progressively engineering a small number of components around a model. Working definition Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control

title: Introduction: 1. The five components
text: Model. The model proposes decisions. It may answer, select a tool, choose a route, generate a plan, criticize an answer, decide whether a task is complete, or delegate work. The model is an important decision component; it is not necessarily the entire decision system. Context. Context is what the model can see when making a decision: the goal, instructions, prior messages, tool descriptions and results, retrieved documents, memories, plans, images, source code, or errors. Selecting what enters context is therefore an engineering decision. Actions. Actions are what the system can cause to happen: search, calculate, query, write, send, execute, click, or delegate. Actions connect decisions to an environment and create the possibility of external consequences. State. State is information that survives long enough to influence later decisions. It can include message history, working memory, long-term memory, task state, checkpoints, shared state, artifacts, and experience. Control. Control determines how execution proceeds: whether another step occurs, whether an action is valid and authorized, whether to retry, route, escalate, approve, stop, or spend more resources. Information available to the system ≠ Information visible to the model

title: Introduction: 2. The model is inside a harness
text: A useful agent can be pictured as a model embedded inside ordinary software. The surrounding software—the agent harness—constructs context, exposes tools, validates decisions, manages state, controls authority, traces execution, enforces budgets, and decides when autonomy ends. Figure: The model sits inside a harness that turns goals into context and observations back into state. Systems principle Agent Quality Model Quality + Harness Quality. This is not a numerical identity; it is a reminder that system behavior depends on both the model and the machinery surrounding it.

title: Introduction: 3. Why the feedback loop matters
text: Figure: A conventional model call ends at its output. A conventional model call ends at output. An agent introduces feedback: Figure: An agent repeats decide, act, observe and update until the goal is done. The observation changes the next decision. This matters because plans can be wrong, searches can fail, APIs can reject requests, code can fail tests, other agents can fail, and interfaces can change. The environment supplies evidence; the agent uses that evidence to decide what to do next.

title: Introduction: 4. The smallest controlled agent loop
text: Element | Role model() | Model messages | Context + State execute() | Actions validate() | Control authorize() | Control MAX_STEPS | Control Almost everything else in the book expands one of these ideas.

title: Introduction: 5. A conceptual autonomy ladder
text: The following levels are a book-specific reasoning tool, not an industry standard. Level | System | What changes 0 | Model | Input → model → output 1 | Tool user | The model can select an external capability 2 | Multi-step agent | Decisions adapt to observations 3 | Persistent agent | State survives across tasks or time 4 | Multi-agent system | Agents delegate, coordinate, or share state 5 | Self-improving system | Experience can alter future instructions, memory, programs, or policy Control law Autonomy Control Requirements

title: Introduction: 6. The autonomy envelope
text: Autonomy is not a single switch. It can be bounded along several dimensions: capabilities, permissions, resources, time, and risk. Important distinction Capability ≠ Permission ≠ Approval. The existence of an action does not authorize its use.

title: Introduction: 7. Workflow or agent?
text: If the path is known in advance, a deterministic workflow may be easier to test, cheaper to run, and safer to operate. Agency becomes useful when the path must change in response to observations. Figure: A known path is fixed in advance; an adaptive path chooses its next step after observing. Architecture principle Use the least autonomy necessary for the required adaptability.

title: Introduction: 8. Translate metaphors into mechanisms
text: Metaphor | Mechanism Remember | write → store → retrieve Reflect | draft → critique → revise Plan | goal → proposed future actions Collaborate | delegate → exchange state → aggregate Learn | experience → candidate change → evaluation → promotion Once expressed as mechanisms, agentic ideas become testable. Once they become testable, they become engineering.

title: Introduction: 9. The experimental method
text: Stage | Purpose IDEA | Explain one concept CODE | Implement the smallest useful program RUN | Observe what happens BREAK | Violate an assumption deliberately WHY? | Identify the failure mechanism ENGINEER IT | Add the smallest useful control PATTERN | Connect to research/industry terminology SCALE | Map to production architectures and frameworks Book method Concept → Experiment → Failure → Engineering

title: Introduction: 10. One experiment, one question
text: Every experiment should answer a question. Does reflection improve an answer? Does planning improve task completion? When does majority voting outperform one agent? Does more context help? Does memory improve future tasks? Can a computer-use agent recover when the interface changes? Does a self-generated change improve performance on unseen tasks? This keeps the experiments scientific rather than decorative. A technique must demonstrate what it buys us.

title: Introduction: 11. Measure benefit and price
text: Recurring scorecard Q = (S, C, L, R, A), a vector where S = success, C = cost, L = latency, R = reliability, and A = autonomy/risk. The dimensions should normally remain visible rather than being collapsed into a fabricated universal score. A technique can improve accuracy while worsening latency, cost, reliability, or risk.

title: Introduction: 12. More is not automatically better
text: More Context ≠ Better Context More Agents ≠ Better Intelligence More Reasoning ≠ Better Answers More Memory ≠ Better Memory More Autonomy ≠ Better Systems Agentic patterns are hypotheses. They should be evaluated.

title: Introduction: 13. Mechanism versus model performance
text: Foundational examples often use deterministic scripted models so that the mechanism is reproducible. Live-model benchmarks answer a different question: how well does a particular model behave under the architecture? Figure: Deterministic experiments test the mechanism; live-model benchmarks measure empirical behavior.

title: Introduction: 14. Primitive $\rightarrow$ Engineered $\rightarrow$ Framework
text: Level | Purpose Primitive | Minimal Python; expose the mechanism Engineered | Add types, validation, retries, permissions, logging, tests, tracing, budgets, and security Framework | Express the same architecture using contemporary agent infrastructure Frameworks become easier to understand once their abstractions are recognizable as mechanisms we have already built.

title: Introduction: 15. The 59 experiments
text: The book contains 59 minimal experiments across 30 chapters, followed by a case study that builds one complete system from them. They are not 59 unrelated applications. They form one conceptual progression from a model call to controlled systems that can act, coordinate, perceive, recover, and learn.

title: Introduction: 16. The six-part journey
text: Part | Question | Topics I — What Is an Agent? | What changes when a model becomes an agent? | Model call, structured decisions, loop, workflow vs agent II — Giving Agents Abilities | What should the agent know and do? | Tools, context, RAG, memory, compression, MCP III — Making Agents Think and Work | How should computation be allocated? | ReAct, planning, reflection, search, routing, parallelism IV — Agents Working Together | When does coordination create value? | Agent-as-tool, supervisors, voting, debate, shared state, A2A-style communication V — Engineering Reliable Agents | How do we bound and diagnose autonomy? | Evaluation, observability, recovery, HITL, security, budgets VI — Advanced Agentic Engineering | What happens when agents act broadly and learn? | Coding, computer use, multimodality, self-improvement

title: Introduction: 17. A failure map
text: Layer | Typical failure Model | Poor decision Context | Missing, irrelevant, stale, or adversarial information Action | Capability fails or produces an unexpected result State | Information is stale, lost, duplicated, poisoned, or inconsistent Control | Wrong action allowed, recovery fails, resources run away, or stopping is wrong Diagnostic principle Evaluate at the failure layer. Do not label every agent failure a model failure.

title: Introduction: 18. A security map
text: Security principle Untrusted Information ≠ Trusted Control A webpage, retrieved document, image, or memory may contain instructions. That does not grant those instructions authority. Information flow and authority flow must remain separate.

title: Introduction: 19. The economics of agency
text: An agent can dynamically decide to retrieve, call another model, invoke tools, ask another agent, reflect, retry, or verify. Cost therefore becomes a trajectory property, and budgets become part of control. Stopping principle Autonomy must earn continuation.

title: Introduction: 20. Agentic systems allocate resources under uncertainty
text: Planning, reflection, routing, search, collaboration, and verification all answer a related question: where should the system spend its next unit of computation? Act, think again, retrieve, search another branch, ask a stronger model, ask another agent, verify, ask a human, or stop?

title: Introduction: 21. The trajectory is the unit of engineering
text: Evaluation principle Outcome Quality ≠ Trajectory Quality A system can reach a correct answer through an unsafe or wasteful process. It can also fail safely when success is impossible. Agent evaluation therefore asks not only whether the answer was correct, but whether tools were selected correctly, actions were authorized, observations were incorporated, failures were recovered, constraints were respected, and stopping was appropriate.

title: Introduction: 22. From demos to engineering
text: A demo proves possibility. Engineering deals with repeated reality: timeouts, malicious retrieval, conflicting state, revoked permissions, changing interfaces, runaway loops, bad lessons, and imperfect evaluators.

title: Introduction: 23. A discipline of controlled autonomy
text: Definition Agentic Engineering is the discipline of designing, building, evaluating, and operating software systems in which models dynamically choose actions toward goals while engineering constrains their context, state, capabilities, resources, risk, and autonomy.

title: Introduction: 24. What remains after frameworks change
text: What does the model know? What can the system do? What persists? Who has authority? What evidence supports the next decision? What can fail and how will it recover? How much may it consume? How will success be measured? When should a human intervene? When should the agent stop? If the system learns, what independent evidence shows that the change is better?

title: Introduction: 25. The experiment begins
text: We are now ready to remove almost everything: no orchestration graph, planner, vector database, memory system, browser, multi-agent framework, computer control, or self-improvement. Just one model call. Then we add exactly one capability: a calculator. That tiny transition contains the architectural seed of the entire book. Chapter 1 question What actually changes when a large language model becomes an agent?

title: Conclusion: opening
text: The Discipline of Agentic Engineering What the experiments illustrate about useful autonomy The final question After adding context, tools, memory, planning, collaborators, persistence, computer use, and learning, what remains invariant—and what must we engineer as autonomy increases?

title: Conclusion: Return to the smallest agent
text: We began with almost nothing: a model, a goal, and a calculator. The important transition was not the calculator itself. It was the feedback path: Decision → Action → Observation → Next decision The model proposed an action. Software executed it. The consequence returned as new information. The next decision could therefore depend on what actually happened rather than only on what the model predicted would happen. From that small loop, the rest of the book grew. Tools expanded what the system could do. Context engineering changed what the model could see. Retrieval connected decisions to external knowledge. Memory allowed the past to influence the future. Planning organized future actions. Reflection introduced retrospective feedback. Search created alternatives. Routing allocated work. Parallelism overlapped independent work. Other agents became capabilities, collaborators, and sources of state. Then the engineering consequences accumulated. Evaluation asked whether the system succeeded. Observability asked why. Recovery made failure survivable. Human approval and permissions constrained authority. Security separated untrusted information from trusted control. Budgets constrained continuation. Coding agents showed how much executable feedback is worth, and how easily a weak evaluator can be gamed. Computer use made perception part of control. Self-improvement made the system itself part of the environment being changed. The architecture became richer, but the fundamental loop remained visible underneath it.

title: Conclusion: The five-component model, revisited
text: At the beginning of the book we proposed a deliberately simple decomposition: Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control After thirty chapters, those five terms carry more weight. The model is a decision component, not the whole system. Context is not everything the system knows. It is the information selected for a particular decision. Actions are not merely tools. They are capabilities whose consequences may escape the model and affect an external environment. State is not merely chat history. It includes working state, long-term memory, shared state, checkpoints, artifacts, and learned experience. Control is not an implementation detail. It determines what may execute, how resources are allocated, what happens after failure, when authority is required, and when the system must stop. This decomposition is useful precisely because it survives changes in frameworks, protocols, and model providers. New agent technologies usually modify one or more of these five components rather than replacing the underlying engineering problem.

title: Conclusion: What the experiments illustrated
text: The book's experiments are small and deterministic. They use scripted models and fixtures so that each mechanism can be seen clearly; they do not measure how often real models fail. What they do show, again and again, is that the intuition "adding more agentic machinery must improve a system" has concrete counterexamples. More context can distract. More reasoning can amplify a bad premise. More memory can preserve stale or malicious information. More agents can create correlated error and coordination overhead. More retries can multiply load or repeat side effects. More autonomy can make the same mistake more consequential. More adaptation can optimize the wrong objective. The recurring lesson is not that these mechanisms are bad. It is that every mechanism is conditional. It creates value under some assumptions and failure under others. Agentic patterns should therefore be treated as hypotheses to test, not rituals to adopt. Nine principles the book keeps returning to - More Context ≠ Better Context - More Reasoning ≠ Better Answers - More Memory ≠ Better Memory - More Agents ≠ Better Intelligence - More Autonomy ≠ Better Systems - Adaptation ≠ Improvement - Outcome Quality ≠ Trajectory Quality - Capability ≠ Permission - Consensus ≠ Truth Each of these is a hypothesis the experiments make vivid, not a measured law. Testing them on your own tasks, with real models and real data, is the work the book hands back to you.

title: Conclusion: Resource allocation under uncertainty
text: Planning, reflection, routing, search, delegation, model selection, verification, and stopping initially appeared to be different topics. Across the experiments, a common structure emerged. Each asks where the system should spend its next unit of computation, time, money, attention, or authority. Should it act now or gather more evidence? Should it retrieve another document? Search another branch? Ask a stronger model? Delegate to a specialist? Run another test? Request human approval? Retry? Stop? Agentic systems are therefore not only reasoning systems. They are resource-allocation systems operating under uncertainty. This perspective explains why more reasoning is not automatically better. Reasoning consumes resources. It should continue only when its expected value justifies its cost and risk. The same principle applies to autonomy. Authority is also a resource. It should be allocated deliberately.

title: Conclusion: The control law of Agentic Engineering
text: As capability increased throughout the book, another relationship became increasingly difficult to ignore. A model that produces text needs relatively little operational control. A model that invokes tools needs permissions. A persistent agent needs state governance. A planning agent needs stopping rules. A coding agent needs sandboxed execution and tests it cannot rewrite. A multi-agent system needs delegation boundaries and accountability. A computer-use agent needs current perception, grounding, and post-action verification. A self-improving system needs independent evaluation, promotion gates, lineage, and rollback. This gives us the central control law of the book: Autonomy Control Requirements This is not an argument against autonomy. It is an argument against unengineered autonomy. The goal is not to minimize what agents can do. The goal is to expand capability while preserving appropriate control.

title: Conclusion: The harness matters
text: A powerful model can make an agent better. But chapter after chapter, the failures the experiments staged were fixed in the harness, not in the model: model quality is only part of system quality. The harness determines what the model sees, which tools exist, how tool arguments are validated, what authority is granted, what state persists, how failures are handled, what gets measured, when humans intervene, and when execution stops. That is why the book used the conceptual relationship: Agent Quality Model Quality + Harness Quality This is not a numerical formula. It is a reminder about where engineering leverage exists. When a system fails, replacing the model may help. But so might better context selection, a narrower tool interface, a stronger verifier, a safer memory write policy, an idempotent action, a checkpoint, a budget, or a permission boundary. A mature agent architecture makes those possibilities visible.

title: Conclusion: Better models do not eliminate Agentic Engineering
text: It is tempting to imagine that sufficiently capable models will make much of this engineering unnecessary. Some scaffolding will disappear. Better models may require fewer examples, fewer retries, simpler routing, less explicit planning, or less elaborate prompting. Capabilities that currently require several components may collapse into one model call. But increased model capability also expands the set of tasks we are willing to delegate. A model that is more reliable may receive more tools. A model that reasons better may receive longer-running goals. A model that operates computers well may receive access to consequential interfaces. A model that writes better software may be permitted to modify larger systems. A model that learns effectively may be allowed to adapt across tasks. The engineering problem therefore moves rather than disappears. As competence increases, the feasible autonomy envelope expands. And as the autonomy envelope expands, questions of evaluation, authorization, observability, security, recovery, and stopping become more consequential. Agentic Engineering is not a workaround for weak models. It is the discipline required when model decisions are embedded in systems that can act.

title: Conclusion: From capability to useful autonomy
text: Capability is valuable, but capability alone is not the objective. The objective is useful autonomy. Useful autonomy means that the system has enough freedom to adapt where deterministic software would be too rigid, but enough control that its behavior remains measurable, bounded, recoverable, and appropriate to the consequences of its actions. This is why the book repeatedly separated concepts that are easy to conflate: Capability ≠ Permission. Permission ≠ Approval. Similarity ≠ Relevance. Consensus ≠ Truth. Critique ≠ Verification. Action success ≠ Task success. Outcome quality ≠ Trajectory quality. Adaptation ≠ Improvement. The distinctions matter because agentic systems convert information into decisions and decisions into consequences. Capability added | New opportunity | Engineering obligation Tools | Act on external systems | Permissions + validation Memory | Use past experience | Provenance + write policy Planning | Coordinate future actions | Budgets + replanning + stopping Multiple agents | Delegate and specialize | Authority + accountability Code execution | Act on software and get test feedback | Sandbox + protected evaluator Persistence | Continue across time | Recovery + revocation + freshness Computer use | Operate human interfaces | Grounding + verification Self-improvement | Change future behavior | Independent evaluation + rollback

title: Conclusion: The Agentic Engineering checklist
text: When confronted with a new agent architecture, framework, research paper, or product proposal, the following questions provide a compact way to reason about it. - What is the goal? Define success before choosing the architecture. - What does the model see? Identify the context, its provenance, freshness, and selection policy. - What can the system do? Enumerate capabilities and their possible external consequences. - What persists? Identify working state, long-term memory, shared state, checkpoints, and learned artifacts. - What controls execution? Make routing, validation, retries, approvals, budgets, and stopping explicit. - What authority does it have? Separate capability, permission, and approval. - What adversarial inputs can redirect it? Trace untrusted content to every privileged action it could reach. - How is success measured? Evaluate the outcome and, where necessary, the trajectory. - What can fail? Classify failures at the model, context, action, state, and control layers. - How does it recover? Design retries, idempotency, fallback, checkpointing, and escalation before failure occurs. - What are the resource and risk limits? Bound steps, cost, time, tool use, privileges, and consequential actions. - What evidence justifies another step? Autonomy should earn continuation. - If the system changes itself, what proves the change is better? Require held-out evaluation, controlled promotion, lineage, and rollback. These questions are intentionally framework-independent. They are meant to remain useful after today's APIs and libraries have changed.

title: Conclusion: The future of the discipline
text: The specific shape of agentic systems will continue to change. Agents will become more persistent. Tool and agent interfaces, already converging on shared protocols such as the Model Context Protocol, will continue to standardize. Agent-to-agent interaction will become more common. Models will perceive richer environments. Coding agents will operate across larger software lifecycles. Systems will learn from increasingly structured experience. Some parts of the harness itself may become learned or generated. Agents may increasingly act as infrastructure rather than applications: long-running components that negotiate tasks, maintain state, invoke services, supervise other agents, and adapt over time. That future will create new patterns and new terminology. But it will not remove the fundamental questions. What information influenced the decision? What authority did the system possess? What happened after the action? What state survived? How was success established? What limited the system? Who or what could stop it? What evidence justified a change? Those questions define a discipline more durable than any particular generation of agent technology.

title: Conclusion: Engineering the autonomy
text: The smallest useful agent is easy to write. A loop, a model, and a tool can fit on one screen.
