That simplicity is worth preserving because it reveals something important: the difficult part of agentic systems is not creating the first action loop. The difficult work begins when we give that loop more context, more tools, more memory, more time, more collaborators, more persistence, more authority, and eventually the ability to change itself. Each addition creates capability. Each capability creates new possible trajectories. Each new trajectory creates new ways to succeed—and new ways to fail. The purpose of Agentic Engineering is not to suppress that autonomy. It is to make autonomy useful. Observable enough to understand. Bounded enough to trust. Recoverable enough to operate. Measured well enough to improve. And justified by the value it creates. Build autonomy that can justify itself An agentic system should be able to show what evidence it used, what action it chose, what authority permitted it, what resources it consumed, what happened afterward, and why continued autonomy remains justified.

title: Conclusion: One final diagram
text: Capability → Autonomy → Control → Useful Autonomy More models More context More tools More memory More agents More persistence More learning [3pt] [2pt] AUTONOMY [2pt] [3pt] Evaluation Observability Permissions Security Recovery Budgets Human oversight Stopping [3pt] [2pt] USEFUL AUTONOMY Building the agent is only the beginning. Engineering its autonomy is the discipline.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.1 A model can answer. An agent can act.
text: Suppose we ask a language model a simple question: "What is 37 × 42?" The model receives text and returns text. It may answer correctly. It may answer incorrectly. Either way, nothing outside the model has changed. No calculator has been called, no file has been read, no database has been queried, and no observation from the world has returned to influence a second decision. That distinction is the starting point for this book. A large language model is a powerful generator and decision component, but generation alone is not agency. Agency appears when a model is embedded in software that can translate a decision into an action, observe the consequence, and use that observation to decide what to do next. This is useful software, but its architecture is still one-way: The model can describe an action—"I should use a calculator"—without actually causing one. Giving a model instructions about tools is not the same thing as connecting those instructions to executable capabilities. Experiment 1 — A model call. Our first experiment is deliberately tiny. We use a deterministic stand-in for a model so that every reader sees exactly the same output. The stand-in returns an imperfect arithmetic answer. This is not intended to measure the arithmetic ability of any current model. It isolates the architecture. Running it produces: MODEL: 37 x 42 is approximately 1,500. GROUND TRUTH: 1554 CORRECT: False What did this experiment establish? Only that the model produced a response. It did not establish that models are generally bad at arithmetic, nor that an agent is required for multiplication. The arithmetic task gives us a ground truth and a capability we can add in the next experiment.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.2 Add an action
text: Now give the software a calculator. The model no longer needs to be the component that performs the arithmetic. Its job can change from answering the mathematical question directly to choosing an appropriate action. The companion kernel's calculator parses the expression and evaluates only numbers and arithmetic operators, with limits on expression length and exponent size. A model-supplied string therefore cannot run arbitrary code or tie up the machine with an enormous power. Never pass model output to Python's eval: the expression is untrusted input, whoever wrote the prompt. The model can now propose a structured decision: "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "37*42" But even now the model has not performed the action. Ordinary software receives that proposal, looks up the capability, executes it, and returns the result. The value 1554 is an observation produced by the environment, not a fact invented by the model. Experiment 2 — From model to agent. This time the stand-in for the model is a PolicyModel: a small function that looks at the messages it receives and decides from them. It is still deterministic, but unlike a fixed script it reacts to its context. Asked a question with no observation available, it requests the calculator; once an observation is present, it answers from it. The deterministic run produces: ACTION: calculator OBSERVATION: 1554 ANSWER: 37 x 42 = 1554.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.3 The important line is not the calculator
text: It is tempting to say that the second program is an agent because it has a tool. That is close, but it misses the most important mechanism. A tool is only a capability. The architectural transition is the feedback path: Decision → Action → Observation → Next decision The result of the action becomes information available to the model's next decision. Once that feedback path can repeat, we have the core of an agent loop. This is why a chatbot that merely describes actions is different from an agent that can perform them. The difference is not personality, verbosity, or whether the prompt contains the word agent. The difference is executable coupling to an environment.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.4 A first definition
text: We can now introduce the working model that will organize the rest of the book: Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control Model decides. Context is what the model can see now. Actions are what the system can do. State preserves information across steps. Control determines what may happen, when another step occurs, and when execution stops. At this point those five terms are intentionally broad. We will engineer each one separately. Context will grow into retrieval and context engineering. State will grow into memory and checkpoints. Actions will grow into tools, protocols, coding, and computer use. Control will grow into ReAct, planning, routing, evaluation, permissions, budgets, and human approval. Component | In this chapter | Later in the book Model | Chooses an answer or action | Model routing, critics, judges Context | Messages supplied to the model | RAG, compression, context engineering Actions | Calculator | Tools, MCP, coding, computer use State | Tool result appended to messages | Memory, shared state, checkpoints Control | One decision followed by another | Loops, planning, budgets, permissions

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.5 The model is not the whole system
text: This leads to one of the book's central themes: agent performance is a property of a system, not only a model. Two applications can use the same underlying model and behave very differently because one gives it better context, safer actions, stronger validation, more useful feedback, or better stopping rules. We will eventually summarize that idea as: [ Agent quality ; ; Model quality + Harness quality ] The symbol is conceptual, not a numerical equation. The point is that the surrounding software—the harness—can improve or destroy the usefulness of the model. A stronger model does not remove the need for engineering around it.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.6 Deliberately break it
text: Every important mechanism in this book will be broken on purpose. Failure makes the boundary of an abstraction visible. Break Experiment 2 by removing the calculator while leaving the model free to request it. The model can still produce: "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "37*42" but the software cannot execute the request. The model's decision may be perfectly sensible while the system still fails. This distinction—reasoning success versus execution success—will return throughout the book.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.7 What should we measure?
text: For these deterministic demonstrations, the measurements are simple: lcc Measure | Model only | Tool-using agent Task success | No in our scripted run | Yes Model calls | 1 | 2 Tool calls | 0 | 1 These are demonstration results from deterministic scripts, not empirical claims about current models. Measuring a live model needs repeated trials and adds tokens, cost, latency, reliability, and risk; Chapter 22 shows how to design that evaluation.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.8 The smallest useful agent
text: We can now strip the architecture down to its essence. Ignore provider SDKs, tracing systems, databases, frameworks, and deployment infrastructure. The conceptual machine is: That loop is intentionally incomplete. It has no validation, no step limit, no error handling, no permissions, and no cost budget. Those omissions are not mistakes in the pedagogy. They are the agenda for the rest of the book. Chapter principle Agency begins when model decisions can cause actions whose consequences become observations for subsequent decisions.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.9 Before we add more
text: It would be easy to keep adding tools and call the result increasingly agentic. We will not do that yet. The next chapter addresses a more basic problem: the model communicates in probabilistic natural language, while software needs dependable contracts. Before an agent can safely control tools, we need to answer: How can probabilistic language control deterministic software?

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.10 Live run: Arithmetic with and without a tool
text: Experiments 1 and 2 used a stand-in that was scripted to be wrong. Here a real model gets twenty five-digit by four-digit multiplications, once on its own and once inside the Chapter 3 agent loop with the calculator as a tool. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Exact answer, model alone | 0/20 | 0.00 | [0.00, 0.16] Exact answer, model + calculator | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Runs that called the calculator | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Unaided, the model gave a plausible but wrong number every time: for 27611 × 2033 it answered 56,120,063 instead of 56,133,163. With the tool it called the calculator on every task and every answer was exact. The run used provider defaults, without an extended reasoning budget, which may score higher unaided; the point is that the tool makes exactness independent of the model's arithmetic. Model gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 60 requests, 7,238 input and 993 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch01_tool_vs_no_tool (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.11 Exercises
text: - Change Experiment 1 so that the scripted model returns the correct answer. Does that make it an agent? Explain why or why not. - Add a second tool called square. What new problem appears when the model must choose between capabilities? - Remove the tool observation from messages before the second model call in Experiment 2, then run it. What does the policy model do instead of answering, and what information has the system lost? - Replace the calculator with a function that returns the current time. Which component of Model + Context + Actions + State + Control changed? - Write one example of a system that uses an LLM but should remain a deterministic workflow rather than an agent. We will revisit your answer in Chapter 4.

title: Chapter 1, From an LLM to an Agent: 1.12 Chapter 1 checklist
text: - An LLM call is not, by itself, an agent. - A tool is a capability; software still executes the capability. - The critical transition is Decision → Action → Observation → Next decision. - Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control. - System quality depends on both the model and its surrounding harness.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.1 Natural language is a poor API
text: At the end of Chapter 1, our model could choose a calculator. We quietly assumed that software could understand the choice. Real model output makes that assumption dangerous. "I think I should probably use the calculator on 37 times 42." A human understands this immediately. Software has awkward questions. Is the action called calculator, calculate, or use_calculator? Where do the arguments begin? Is “37 times 42” an expression or prose? Did the model actually request execution, or merely discuss the possibility? We could attack the sentence with regular expressions and string matching. That works until the wording changes. The better move is to change the interface. Ask the model to produce a decision that software can parse. "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "37*42" This is the first hard boundary we draw around the model. Natural language remains useful inside the system, but the point where probabilistic output controls deterministic software gets a contract. Experiment 3 — Structured output. The smallest useful experiment needs no agent loop. It only proves that a model-shaped string can be converted into a software object with named fields. Output: ACTION: calculator ARGUMENTS: 'expression': '37*42' What changed? Not the model's intelligence. We changed the interface between the model and the program. The decision now has machine-readable structure.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.2 Structure removes ambiguity---not uncertainty
text: JSON solves a syntactic problem. It does not prove that the decision is sensible, safe, authorized, or even usable. "action": "delete_database", "arguments": That object is excellent JSON. A parser will happily accept it. If our only gate is json.loads, we have converted an invalid request into a beautifully structured invalid request. First distinction Parseable ≠ valid. There are several boundaries worth separating: Question | Example failure | Layer Can I parse it? | Missing quote / malformed JSON | Syntax Does it match the expected shape? | arguments missing; expression is a list, not text | Schema Do the values make sense? | expression is "1/0" or "x+1" | Semantic validation Does this capability exist? | delete_database is unknown | Capability validation May this agent use it? | real tool, insufficient permission | Authorization This chapter implements the first four ideas far enough to make the boundary visible. Authorization becomes a full engineering concern later, especially in Chapters 25–27.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.3 Validation is ordinary software
text: A common mistake is to ask the model to validate itself and then treat the second model answer as enforcement. A model can help repair or interpret a bad proposal, but the hard gate should live in ordinary deterministic software whenever the rule can be expressed deterministically. The complete file for Experiment 4 below defines the contract and then tries one good and one bad proposal: Notice the allocation of responsibility. The model proposes values. The validator does not ask whether the model “really meant” them. It checks a contract. Experiment 4 — Reject an invalid decision. Running the file above prints: GOOD: CalculatorDecision(action='calculator', expression='37*42') BLOCKED: Unknown action The important event is not that the bad decision was wrong. Models will produce wrong decisions. The important event is that the wrong proposal stopped at a software boundary rather than becoming an action.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.4 Proposal is not execution
text: Figure: A model proposal passes parsing, validation, and authorization before anything executes. This diagram establishes a design rule that will survive every later chapter: a model's output is a proposal until trusted software accepts it. Chapter principle Never allow probabilistic output to cross a deterministic software boundary without validation.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.5 Break it three different ways
text: Breaking structured decisions reveals why a single “valid/invalid” label is too crude. Failure A — Malformed syntax. "action":"calculator","arguments":"expression":"37*42" The closing brace is missing. Parsing fails before we can discuss the action at all. Failure B — Valid syntax, wrong shape. "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": ["37", "*", "42"] This parses, and it even names a valid action. But our contract requires the expression to be a string. Failure C — Valid structure, invalid capability. "action": "delete_database", "arguments": Again, perfect JSON. But our program exposes no such capability. The validator rejects it before any executor sees it. Later we will add a fourth failure: a capability can exist and still be forbidden to this agent. That is the difference between capability and permission.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.6 What should happen after rejection?
text: Rejecting a bad proposal is only half the design. The caller needs a policy for what happens next. Policy | Useful when | Risk Fail closed | Action is consequential or ambiguity is unacceptable | Task may stop unnecessarily Repair deterministically | Error has an obvious mechanical fix | Repair logic can become complex Ask model to retry | Schema/argument failure may be recoverable | Extra cost; repeated invalid output Fallback | Alternate capability/model can perform task | Different behavior or quality Escalate to human | Consequence or uncertainty is high | Latency and human workload The correct policy depends on consequence. A malformed weather query and a malformed payment instruction should not share the same recovery policy.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.7 Structured generation is not validation
text: Modern model APIs can constrain outputs to a declared JSON Schema. In their strict modes, constrained decoding guarantees that a completed response matches the schema; the remaining exceptions are refusals and responses cut off by a length limit. That removes most parsing and shape failures. But generation-time structure and execution-time validation solve different problems. Structured generation: "Please produce this shape." Validation: "I will independently verify the proposal before software acts on it." Even a schema-valid object can contain a wrong account number, an unsupported tool, a dangerous file path, or an action that exceeds the user's authority. The closer an action gets to the outside world, the less we should confuse formatting guarantees with correctness or permission.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.8 The software boundary is part of the harness
text: Chapter 1 introduced the idea that agent quality depends on the harness around the model. Validation is our first concrete harness component. Figure: The validator applies deterministic policy between the model's proposal and the executor. A stronger model may reduce the frequency of invalid proposals. It does not eliminate the need for the boundary. Reliable engineering does not depend on a probabilistic component never making a mistake.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.9 What should we measure?
text: Once decisions are structured, several quantities become measurable. Metric | Question Parse rate | What fraction of outputs can be parsed? Schema-valid rate | What fraction match the required structure? Capability-valid rate | What fraction request known actions? Argument-valid rate | What fraction contain usable arguments? Execution success | What fraction of accepted proposals actually succeed? These metrics diagnose different failures. A low parse rate suggests an output-format problem. A high schema-valid rate with low execution success suggests the problem lies later—in semantics, the tool, the environment, or the task itself.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.10 The smallest safe boundary
text: The complete pattern for this chapter can be reduced to four lines of architecture: In a consequential system we will eventually insert authorization between validation and execution. We will also add tracing, retries, budgets, and human approval. But the essential separation is already visible. Engineering takeaway The model may propose an action. Deterministic software decides whether the proposal satisfies the contract before execution.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.11 Bridge to Chapter 3
text: We can now safely represent one decision. But an agent becomes interesting when one action produces an observation that changes the next decision. How does an agent continue acting until a goal is complete? Chapter 3 turns our validated one-step decision into the book's first reusable agent loop.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.12 Live run: Prompted JSON versus a strict schema
text: A small model turns twenty short arithmetic requests into calculator decisions, once with the JSON format described only in the prompt and once with a strict JSON Schema enforced by the provider. Each output is parsed, checked against the contract, and evaluated with the calculator. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Parses, prompted | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Schema-valid, prompted | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Computes the right value, prompted | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Parses, strict schema | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Schema-valid, strict schema | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Computes the right value, strict schema | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] On these easy requests, prompting alone was already fully reliable for this model, so strict mode bought nothing measurable. That is a useful negative result rather than a reason to skip validation: the guarantee of strict mode matters for larger schemas, weaker models, long outputs and the long tail of production traffic, and neither mode can check that the expression is the right one; the validator and the calculator did that. Model gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 40 requests, 3,258 input and 811 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch02_structured_output (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.13 Exercises
text: - Modify Experiment 3 so that arguments is missing. Which line fails: parsing or later access? What does that tell you about parsing versus validation? - Extend validate to reject an empty expression string. Is that a syntax, schema, or semantic rule? - Add a second allowed action called weather. How would you represent action-specific argument schemas without filling the executor with if statements? - Imagine the system really does have a delete_file tool. Write one example where the action is structurally valid but should still be denied. - Design a retry policy for invalid calculator arguments. When should the system stop asking the model to repair its proposal?

title: Chapter 2, Structured Decisions: 2.14 Chapter 2 checklist
text: - Natural language is useful for humans but brittle as a software control interface. - Parseable output is not necessarily valid output. - Schema validity, semantic validity, capability validity, and authorization are different concerns. - A model output should remain a proposal until deterministic software accepts it. - Strict structured generation can guarantee the shape of a response, but not its correctness or authority, so it does not replace execution-time validation.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.1 One action is not enough
text: Chapter 2 gave us a safe boundary around one model decision. We can parse a proposal, validate it, and execute it. But many useful tasks cannot be completed with one action. Consider this request: Multiply 12 by 7, then add 6. A calculator can perform either operation. The interesting problem is sequencing. The result of the first operation—84—must become available before the second operation can be chosen and executed. Figure: Sequencing: the result of the first operation must exist before the second can be chosen. We could hard-code those two operations. But then our program would know the solution path in advance. To build an agent, we instead let the model choose the next action after seeing the latest state.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.2 Repeat the decision boundary
text: Take the architecture from Chapter 2: Figure: The Chapter 2 decision boundary: the model proposes, and deterministic code parses, validates and executes. and feed the resulting observation back into the model: Figure: Feeding the observation back into the model turns the Chapter 2 boundary into a loop. Now add one more possible model decision: done. The model can either request another action or declare that the goal is complete. "done": false, "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "12*7" "done": true, "answer": "The answer is 90." The core control problem At each step, the system must decide whether to act again or stop. Experiment 5 — The smallest agent loop. The stand-in model is a PolicyModel (Chapter 1) that decides only from the observations in its context: multiply, then add 6 to whatever it observed, then finish. The harness executes each requested action, prints the step, and appends the observation to the message history. The trace is: STEP 1 ACTION: calculator("12*7") OBSERVATION: 84 STEP 2 ACTION: calculator("84+6") OBSERVATION: 90 STEP 3 DONE: The answer is 90. This is the first program in the book that contains the full minimal feedback structure we will call an agent loop.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.3 Observe $\rightarrow$ decide $\rightarrow$ act $\rightarrow$ observe
text: The loop can be described without mentioning language models at all: Figure: The observe, decide, act cycle, described without reference to language models. The model occupies the decision role. Tools connect decisions to an environment. State carries observations forward. Control determines whether another iteration is allowed. Agent component | Role in Experiment 5 Model | Chooses calculator action or done Context | Goal plus accumulated observations Actions | Calculator State | Message history Control | Loop, step limit, and the executor's unknown-action check This makes our Chapter 1 decomposition concrete: Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control The loop is where these five components begin operating as a system.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.4 State is what makes the next decision different
text: Suppose we execute 12*7 but do not return 84 to the model. The second model call sees essentially the same world as the first. The environment changed from the program's perspective, but the model received no new observation. The feedback loop is broken. Delete the messages.append call from Experiment 5 and run it: the policy model sees no observation, so it requests 12*7 again at every step until the loop runs out. This gives us a useful operational definition of state for now: information preserved across steps so that later decisions can depend on earlier events. Later, state will become richer: working memory, persistent memory, checkpoints, shared multi-agent state, and external databases. But a list of messages is enough to expose the mechanism.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.5 The dangerous line: while True
text: A first implementation of an agent often looks like this: The code is elegant—and incomplete. What if the model never returns done? What if a tool result causes the model to repeat the same action forever? What if every iteration costs money? Autonomy without a stopping policy is an unbounded resource request. Experiment 6 — The agent that never finishes. Break the agent by scripting the same valid action forever. ScriptedModel repeats its last response once the script runs out, so a one-response script never finishes. Every individual decision is valid. Every tool execution succeeds. Yet the system as a whole is defective because it makes no progress toward termination. The fix is the simplest possible control, a step limit: The broken run becomes: STEP 1: calculator("1+1") -> 2 STEP 2: calculator("1+1") -> 2 STEP 3: calculator("1+1") -> 2 STOP: Step limit reached Engineering lesson A stopping condition is not merely defensive code. It is part of the agent's control architecture.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.6 There is more than one way to stop
text: A step limit is useful because it is easy to reason about, but real agents usually need several stopping conditions. Stopping condition | Example | What it controls Goal completion | Model returns done | Task completion Step budget | Maximum 20 iterations | Runaway loops Cost budget | Maximum $1 equivalent | Financial resources Token budget | Maximum context/generation use | Inference resources Time budget | Maximum 120 seconds | Wall-clock resources No-progress rule | Same state/action repeated | Stagnation Human stop | Operator cancels | External control Chapter 27 will turn these ideas into explicit resource budgets. For now, the key insight is that “done” is only one termination signal.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.7 Local correctness does not imply system correctness
text: Experiment 6 gives us an important engineering pattern. Each component can look correct in isolation: model decision ✓ valid tool call ✓ succeeds observation ✓ returned next decision ✓ valid system behavior ✗ useless loop Agentic systems are sequential systems. Their failures can live in trajectories rather than individual steps. This is why later evaluation must inspect both final outcomes and the path taken to reach them.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.8 The harness owns the loop
text: The model may propose that the task is complete, but ordinary software controls execution. The harness decides: - whether the decision is valid; - whether an action is allowed; - whether the action is executed; - what observation returns to context; - whether another iteration is permitted; - when budgets or policies force termination. This is a major conceptual shift. The model is the adaptive decision component. The harness is the control system around it. Figure: The harness wraps the model in a loop: context feeds the model, decisions are validated and executed, observations return to context, and the harness decides whether to stop or continue. Chapter principle An agent is an LLM inside a controlled feedback system.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.9 A reusable minimal Agent
text: We can now write the class that will recur throughout the book. It is the companion kernel's agentic/agent.py: it records each decision as an assistant message and each observation as a tool message, and it refuses to run past its step limit. This class is intentionally missing most production concerns. We will not hide those concerns inside a framework yet. We will add them one at a time so the reader can see exactly what problem each abstraction solves.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.10 Plugging in a real model
text: The stand-ins are deliberate, but the loop does not depend on them. Any object with a generate(messages) method that returns the same decision dictionaries can drive it. The companion kernel's agentic/live.py is that object for any provider that speaks the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions protocol with tool calling, including OpenAI and local servers such as Ollama. Three details matter more than they look. A real model answers a tool request with a call identifier, and the next request must send the tool result back under that identifier; to_api keeps that pairing so the Chapter 3 loop does not have to. Arguments arrive as a JSON string that can be malformed, so the adapter reports malformed_arguments instead of crashing, and Chapter 2's validator decides what happens next. And every request records its tokens and latency, which later chapters turn into cost and budget measurements. Running the same Agent with a real model needs only a different model object: Pin a dated model snapshot rather than an alias, record what you ran, and expect the wording of the answer to vary between runs. Selected chapters end with a Live run section that repeats an experiment against real models and reports the recorded results with 95% intervals. They make paid requests and are optional; every deterministic example still runs without an API key.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.11 What should we measure?
text: Loops create measurements that single calls do not have. Metric | Question Task success | Did the run achieve the goal? Steps | How many decisions were required? Tool calls | How many external actions occurred? Repeated actions | Did the agent get stuck? Termination reason | Goal, budget, error, or human stop? Cost / latency | What did the trajectory consume? For Experiment 5, the deterministic trace completes in two tool actions and a final decision. For Experiment 6, the step budget—not task completion—terminates the run. These are mechanism demonstrations, not empirical model benchmarks.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.12 More autonomy means more trajectories
text: A one-shot model call has a small execution surface: input arrives, output returns. An agent loop creates many possible paths. Figure: A single call has one path from input to output; an agent loop branches into many possible trajectories. Every additional decision point creates useful flexibility and additional failure paths. That trade-off will become central to Agentic Engineering: autonomy is valuable when it buys adaptation that justifies its added control requirements.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.13 Bridge to Chapter 4
text: We now have an agent. But that does not mean every task should use one. If the sequence of steps is already known, a deterministic workflow may be cheaper, faster, easier to test, and more reliable. The next chapter therefore asks a question that should come before almost every agent project: When should we use an agent at all?

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.14 Exercises
text: - Modify Experiment 5 so that the second operation subtracts 6 instead of adding it. Which parts of the harness change? - Remove the observation from state after the first calculator call (delete the messages.append call in Experiment 5). Predict the failure before running the program, then run it. - Add a no-progress rule that stops after the same action and arguments occur twice in a row. - Design a termination record with fields for reason, steps, and last_observation. Why is a boolean done insufficient for debugging? - Give an example where a 3-step limit is too restrictive and another where 100 steps is dangerously permissive.

title: Chapter 3, The Agent Loop: 3.15 Chapter 3 checklist
text: - An agent loop feeds action consequences back into later decisions. - State is what lets a later decision differ because of an earlier event. - Valid individual steps can still form a defective trajectory. - Stopping conditions are part of control, not optional cleanup. - The harness owns execution, validation, state updates, and termination.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.1 Now that we can build an agent, should we?
text: Chapter 3 gave us a reusable loop. It is tempting to put that loop around every LLM application. But an agent is not automatically a better workflow. It exchanges predictability for adaptability. Suppose every customer request must follow exactly three steps: 1. validate_input() 2. calculate_quote() 3. format_response() If those steps are always required and always occur in that order, asking a model to rediscover the sequence on every run adds a decision where none is needed. Figure: A fixed workflow follows a predetermined path, while an agent chooses each next step after observing the result of the last. The second architecture is more flexible. It also introduces more model calls, more possible trajectories, more latency, more cost, and more opportunities for a wrong choice.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.2 A workflow encodes the path; an agent chooses it
text: Working distinction A workflow has a substantially predetermined control path. An agent delegates meaningful runtime control decisions to a model. This is not a binary taxonomy for all software. Real systems mix deterministic and agentic regions. A fixed workflow may contain one agentic routing step. An agent may call deterministic workflows as tools. The useful question is where runtime discretion is valuable. Architecture | Who chooses the next step? | Strength | Cost Fixed workflow | Programmer / code | Predictability | Less adaptive Conditional workflow | Rules / code | Controlled branching | Rules must anticipate cases Agentic control | Model at runtime | Adaptation to novel state | More uncertainty and overhead Hybrid | Code + model | Targeted flexibility | More design work

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.3 Three kinds of task
text: To compare architectures fairly, we need tasks that differ in how much runtime uncertainty they contain. Task class | Example | What is known in advance? Known path | Always fetch → format | Entire sequence Optional branch | Fetch; translate only when needed | Most sequence; one branch Novel path | Choose among several capabilities based on request | Path depends on runtime meaning These three classes create a simple hypothesis: as path uncertainty increases, the value of runtime model control may increase. That is a hypothesis to test, not a law to assume. Experiment 7 — Workflow vs agent. The repository experiment implements the same small task family twice: an English report (the known path) and a French report that needs translation (the optional branch). The workflow encodes the path, with one explicit rule for the branch. The agentic version asks a PolicyModel which capability to use next, deciding only from the observations it has seen, and counts its model calls. Output: KNOWN PATH workflow: fetch->format agent: model->fetch->model->format->model->done same answer: True | model calls: 0 vs 3 | tool calls: 2 vs 2 OPTIONAL BRANCH workflow: fetch->translate->format agent: model->fetch->model->translate->model->format->model->done same answer: True | model calls: 0 vs 4 | tool calls: 3 vs 3 Both architectures reach the same answer on both tasks. But the agent spends three or four model decisions choosing steps the workflow already knows, and it makes exactly the same tool calls. For an optional branch, the workflow remains attractive if the condition is cheap and explicit. We do not gain much by replacing a reliable boolean condition with an expensive probabilistic decision. The interesting case is a request whose required capability cannot be cleanly encoded as a small stable rule set. Runtime interpretation may now earn its overhead.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.4 Deliberately over-agent the problem
text: The easiest way to understand the trade-off is to build an obviously excessive agent. Goal: add 6 to 84 Agent decisions: 1. Should I calculate? 2. Which tool should I use? 3. Should I call the calculator? 4. Is 84+6 the right expression? 5. Should I stop after seeing 90? A deterministic program needs one line: Failure mode Agentic overhead can dominate the task itself. This is not an argument against agents. It is an argument against spending intelligence on decisions that software can make more cheaply and reliably.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.5 Deliberately under-agent the problem
text: The opposite mistake is to force an open-ended task through an exploding rule tree. If users continually produce novel combinations and the correct path depends on meaning rather than a stable machine-readable field, runtime model reasoning may simplify the control problem. Failure mode Determinism becomes brittle when the environment contains meaningful variation the rules cannot economically enumerate.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.6 Autonomy has a price
text:
Chapter 3 showed that each decision point creates possible trajectories. Chapter 4 adds the economic view. Every model-controlled decision consumes resources and introduces uncertainty. Value of autonomy = benefit from adaptation
- cost of additional control Treat this as a design decomposition, not a literal universal equation. The costs include more than inference spend. Dimension | Question Success | Does runtime discretion improve task completion? Cost | How many model/tool resources are consumed? Latency | How much wall time does extra decision-making add? Reliability | How variable is behavior across equivalent runs? Risk | What additional actions or trajectories become possible? These dimensions will become the formal Agentic Engineering Scorecard in Part V. We introduce them now because architecture decisions should never be judged on success rate alone.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.7 The least-autonomy principle
text: A useful default is to place deterministic control around everything that is known and delegate only the uncertain decision to the model. Bad default: Model decides everything. Better default: Code handles known structure. Model handles semantic uncertainty. Code validates and constrains the result. Design principle Use the least autonomy necessary to obtain the adaptability the task requires. Least autonomy does not mean minimum intelligence. It means allocating model discretion where it creates value rather than where deterministic software already has a dependable answer.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.8 Hybrid systems are usually more interesting
text: The workflow-versus-agent framing can sound like a choice between two mutually exclusive architectures. In practice, strong systems often combine them. Figure: A hybrid system: deterministic stages surround a model router that dispatches to fixed flows or bounded agentic investigation. Here the model does not own the whole application. It owns a bounded decision region. This pattern will recur throughout the book: model discretion inside deterministic scaffolding.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.9 How to choose
text: Before adding an agent loop, ask five questions. Question | If YES, lean toward Is the path known and stable? | Workflow Can branching be expressed with cheap reliable rules? | Workflow Does the correct path depend on unstructured meaning? | Agent or hybrid Will novel situations appear that rules cannot economically enumerate? | Agent or hybrid Are wrong actions highly consequential? | More deterministic control / approval These are design heuristics, not a scoring formula. The architecture should be validated on representative tasks rather than selected by terminology.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.10 Benchmark the architecture, not the demo
text: A single impressive agent run cannot answer whether an agent is the better architecture. Compare workflow and agentic versions across task classes, on the same tasks, with the same tools. Experiment 7 fills in the cells a deterministic fixture can fill: Workflow vs agent | Known path | Optional branch | Novel path Same answer | Yes | Yes | Not in fixture Model calls | 0 vs 3 | 0 vs 4 | Not in fixture Tool calls | 2 vs 2 | 3 vs 3 | Not in fixture Latency, cost | 3XNeed a live model: the stand-in has no latency or price Variance across runs | 3XNeed repeated live runs: the stand-in is deterministic The novel-path column is deliberately empty: a fixture with a known answer cannot contain a path nobody anticipated, and that is exactly where runtime model control might pay for itself. Filling it requires representative real requests, repeated trials with a pinned model, and the evaluation design of Chapter 22. Until then, the expected shape of the trade-off remains a hypothesis: workflows should be strong when paths are known, and agentic control may become more valuable as semantic or path uncertainty increases. Report measured results rather than numbers chosen to fit that story.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.11 A spectrum of control
text: More predetermined More adaptive Workflow – Conditional flow – Router – Agent loop – Open-ended agent | | | | | low runtime discretion high runtime discretion Thinking in a spectrum is more useful than arguing about whether a system “is an agent.” The engineering question is how much control has been delegated, over which decisions, under what constraints, and with what measurable benefit.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.12 Part I synthesis
text: We began Part I with a model that could only return text. Four chapters later, the architecture has acquired action, contracts, feedback, state, stopping rules, and an explicit choice about autonomy. Figure: What each chapter of Part I added to the architecture. Together they produce the first layer of Agentic Engineering: Part I thesis Agency is controlled runtime discretion: models choose actions toward goals, while software defines the capabilities, validates decisions, preserves state, and bounds execution.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.13 What we have not built yet
text: Our agent is still deliberately weak. It has almost no useful knowledge, only a tiny action set, no long-term memory, no retrieval, and no standard interface for external capabilities. Part II therefore changes the question from: What is an agent? to: What should an agent be able to know and do? We begin with the most direct way to expand agency: tools.

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.14 Exercises
text: - Take a three-step process from your own work. Mark every step whose order is known in advance. Which decisions, if any, genuinely require runtime interpretation? - Rewrite an agentic example from Chapter 3 as a fixed workflow. What flexibility is lost? What complexity disappears? - Design a hybrid customer-support architecture where a model chooses among three deterministic workflows but cannot directly execute consequential actions. - Give an example of an optional branch that should be ordinary code rather than an LLM decision. Explain why. - Define a small benchmark with five known-path and five novel-path tasks. Which measurements would you require before deciding between a workflow and an agent?

title: Chapter 4, Workflows vs Agents: 4.15 Chapter 4 checklist
text: - A workflow substantially predetermines the control path; an agent delegates meaningful runtime control decisions. - Runtime model discretion buys adaptability but adds cost, latency, variance, and possible failure trajectories. - Simple stable conditions should usually remain deterministic. - Hybrid architectures can concentrate model reasoning where semantic uncertainty actually exists. - Use the least autonomy necessary for the task.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.1 A model cannot call your function
text: Part I ended with a controlled agent loop. Its actions were intentionally tiny. We now expand the action space—but first we need to be precise about what a tool actually is. Suppose our Python program contains: The language model does not magically acquire a pointer to this function. It cannot reach into Python memory and invoke it. The application must describe the capability to the model, receive a proposed invocation, map that proposal back to executable code, and return the result. Figure: From a Python capability to an observation the model can use. Four distinct objects 1. The real function or API. 2. Its model-facing description/schema. 3. The proposed invocation. 4. The execution result.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.2 The tool registry
text: The smallest useful implementation is a dictionary that maps stable names to executable functions. The registry is software's source of truth about what can actually execute. Separately, the model receives a description such as: "name": "calculator", "description": "Evaluate a basic arithmetic expression.", "parameters": "type": "object", "properties": "expression": "type": "string" , "required": ["expression"] The parameters value is a JSON Schema object. Providers name the field differently (parameters, input_schema, or inputSchema in MCP), but the schema inside follows the same standard. These two representations serve different audiences. The function is for the runtime. The schema is for the model and validator. Experiment 8 — One tool. Give the model one possible action: calculator. It proposes an invocation; ordinary software resolves the name and executes the function. Output: ACTION: calculator RESULT: 126 Nothing in this experiment requires the model to perform arithmetic. Its role is to select a capability and supply arguments. The deterministic capability performs the operation.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.3 Tool calling is delegation
text: A useful mental model is that tool use delegates a subproblem from the probabilistic model to another system. Figure: Tool calling delegates a subproblem from the model to a deterministic system. The delegated system need not be deterministic. A tool might be a search engine, database, payment API, browser, another model, or—as we will see in Part IV—another agent. The architectural contract remains input → execution → result.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.4 More tools create a selection problem
text: With one tool, selection is trivial. Add three capabilities: Now the model must infer which capability best matches the goal. Tool use has become two problems: 1. Select the right tool. 2. Call the selected tool correctly. A system can fail at either stage. A perfectly formed call to the wrong tool is still wrong. Experiment 9 — Tool selection. Use three tiny tasks: Goal | Expected capability Calculate 18 times 7. | calculator What is the weather in Pretoria? | weather Find information about agent evaluation. | search A fixed script cannot show selection degrading, because it ignores the descriptions. The stand-in here is a PolicyModel that reads the tool descriptions in its context and picks the tool sharing the most words with the goal. That is far cruder than a real model, but it makes one real effect visible: selection depends on the descriptions, not on the functions behind them. The experiment runs the same three tasks twice, once with clear descriptions and once with the weather description rewritten to overlap with search. Output: CLEAR DESCRIPTIONS Calculate 18 times 7. -> calculator ok What is the weather in Pretoria? -> weather ok Find information about agent evaluation. -> search ok selection accuracy: 3/3 OVERLAPPING DESCRIPTIONS Calculate 18 times 7. -> calculator ok What is the weather in Pretoria? -> none WRONG Find information about agent evaluation. -> weather WRONG selection accuracy: 1/3 The underlying functions did not change; only the model-facing interface did. With overlapping descriptions the weather question no longer matches anything, and the research question ties between two tools. A live model is far better at reading descriptions than word overlap, but it faces the same boundary: what it cannot distinguish, it cannot select reliably. Engineering lesson Tool descriptions are part of the control surface. A capability the model cannot distinguish reliably is not well exposed.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.5 Tool schemas are affordances
text: The description tells the model what a capability is for. The schema tells it how the capability may be used. "name": "weather", "description": "Get current weather for a city.", "parameters": "type": "object", "properties": "city": "type": "string", "minLength": 1 , "required": ["city"] A good interface narrows the model's decision problem. Instead of inventing arbitrary text, the model chooses among named capabilities and fills constrained arguments. But schemas do not guarantee semantic correctness. city="37*42" is still a string. The same distinction from Chapter 2 remains: structure is not meaning.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.6 Correct selection can still fail
text: So far, a valid tool call has always produced a useful result. Real capabilities fail independently of the model. Figure: A correctly selected tool can still fail. This is an important separation of responsibilities. The model can make the correct decision and the system can still fail because the network, API, credential, dependency, or external service failed. Experiment 10 — Tool failure. The weather service times out. The experiment handles the same failure twice: a wrapper that hides it, and one that turns it into a structured observation. Output: HIDDEN: None STRUCTURED: ok: False error: timeout retryable: True message: weather service unavailable The failure becomes an observation. The agent may later decide whether to retry, use another capability, ask the user, or stop. We defer the full retry/fallback machinery to Chapter 24 because recovery deserves its own engineering model. Key distinction Decision failure ≠ execution failure.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.7 Do not hide tool errors
text: hidden_call is the tempting wrapper: it converts every exception into None. Now the model sees None but cannot tell whether the city was unknown, the service timed out, credentials failed, or the tool itself crashed. We have destroyed information needed for the next decision. structured_call preserves the failure type and whether a retry could help, without leaking unnecessary internals. Sent to the model, the observation is plain JSON: "ok": false, "error": "timeout", "retryable": true Tool results are context. Their design affects the quality of subsequent reasoning.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.8 Tools expand both capability and risk
text: A calculator changes little outside the process. An email tool can communicate with another person. A payment tool can move money. A shell tool can modify a machine. Figure: Each tool expands what the agent can do, and what it can change. Adding a tool therefore changes more than usefulness. It expands the set of world states the agent can cause. Design principle The action space is also a risk surface. This is why later chapters separate capability from permission. A system may technically possess a tool without granting every agent authority to use every operation.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.9 Tool design is API design for a probabilistic caller
text: Traditional APIs are usually called by software written against documentation. Agent tools are called by a probabilistic decision-maker interpreting natural-language descriptions. That changes interface design. Poor interface | Better interface | Why do_it(x) | get_current_weather(city) | Intent is explicit One giant admin tool | Small scoped operations | Reduces action ambiguity Free-form string arguments | Typed constrained fields | Narrows valid calls Raw exception text | Structured error result | Supports recovery Overlapping descriptions | Distinct capability descriptions | Improves selection The goal is not to make every tool microscopic. It is to expose meaningful capabilities at a level where the model can choose them reliably and policy can govern them clearly.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.10 Tool selection is itself an evaluation target
text: Once several tools exist, we can measure the interface rather than relying on a few demos. Metric | Question Selection accuracy | Did the model choose the appropriate capability? Argument validity | Were required fields usable? Execution success | Did the tool complete? Unnecessary calls | Did the agent invoke tools it did not need? Recovery success | Did it respond appropriately to tool failure? These metrics separate model-interface problems from runtime problems. If selection accuracy is high but execution success is low, changing the prompt may be the wrong intervention.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.11 What the model sees vs what the runtime owns
text: MODEL VIEW RUNTIME VIEW name: calculator Python function description: arithmetic credentials schema: expression:string network client timeout retries permissions secrets The model should receive enough information to make a good decision, not every implementation detail required to execute it. This separation becomes increasingly important as tools connect to sensitive systems.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.12 The minimal tool pipeline
text: Figure: The minimal tool pipeline, from goal to an observation that re-enters the context. Chapter principle Models choose actions; software executes them.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.13 Bridge to Chapter 6
text: Tools expand what an agent can do. But the model can only choose well using information visible in its current context. If we give it too little context, it lacks necessary facts. If we give it everything, important information may be buried in noise while cost and latency increase. What information should the agent see right now? That is the problem of context engineering.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.14 Live run: Tool selection with overlapping descriptions
text: Experiment 9 showed a stand-in model losing accuracy when two descriptions overlap. Here a small real model chooses among the same three tools for twenty requests, with clear descriptions, with overlapping descriptions, and with overlapping descriptions and the same argument name for every tool. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Correct tool, clear descriptions | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Correct tool, overlapping descriptions | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Correct tool, overlapping, same argument name | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] The degradation did not reproduce. Every request went to the right tool in every condition, most likely because the tool names themselves (calculator, weather, search) carry the signal that the descriptions lost. Overlap becomes a real risk with many tools whose names are also similar, which is common once several MCP servers are connected; measure selection on your own tool set rather than assuming either outcome. Model gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 60 requests, 10,900 input and 1,318 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch05_tool_selection (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.15 Exercises
text: - Add a currency_convert tool. Write a model-facing description and schema that make it clearly distinct from the calculator. - Create two intentionally overlapping tool descriptions. Rewrite them so that the selection boundary becomes clearer. - Design a structured result for a search tool that distinguishes no_results, timeout, and unauthorized. - Give an example of a capability that should be exposed as two smaller tools rather than one broad tool. Explain the control benefit. - Design a 20-task tool-selection benchmark for calculator, weather, search, and currency conversion. Which ambiguous tasks would you deliberately include?

title: Chapter 5, Tools: 5.16 Chapter 5 checklist
text: - A tool's executable capability and its model-facing description are different objects. - Tool use consists of selection plus correct invocation. - Tool descriptions and schemas shape model behavior. - A correct model decision can still encounter an execution failure. - Tool errors should return useful structured observations rather than disappear. - Expanding the action space also expands the risk surface.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.1 The model can only decide from what it can see
text: Chapter 5 expanded the agent's action space. But choosing a useful action depends on the information visible when the choice is made. Imagine an agent deciding whether a customer is eligible for a refund. Somewhere in the system is the rule: Refunds are allowed within 30 days of purchase. If that fact is not in the model's current context, the model cannot reliably use it. The information may exist in a database, document store, memory system, or earlier conversation, but existence is not visibility. First principle Available information ≠ model-visible information.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.2 What is context?
text: For this book, context means the information presented to the model for the current decision. Context = Instructions + Current task + Current state + Retrieved knowledge + Tool results + Selected memory + Other relevant evidence This is conceptual composition, not literal string concatenation. Different model APIs represent these components differently. The engineering problem is the same: decide what enters the model-visible information state. Context is therefore broader than a prompt. Prompt engineering asks how to express instructions and information. Context engineering asks what information should be assembled, selected, ordered, transformed, and supplied at each step of a system.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.3 More context sounds safer
text: If missing information is dangerous, an obvious strategy is to include everything. This can fail for practical and reasoning reasons. More input consumes tokens, increases latency and cost, may exceed a context limit, can expose irrelevant or sensitive information, and can bury the fact that matters among distractors. The important claim is not that long context is always bad. The claim is that context has an information-selection problem. Quantity and relevance are different variables. Experiment 11 — Context quantity. Create a deterministic toy decision rule. The task is: Question: Can order #17 be refunded? Relevant facts: Purchase age: 12 days Refund window: 30 days Now add distractors: Customer tier: Gold Preferred language: English Last login: Tuesday Shipping method: Express Newsletter: subscribed Warehouse: North ... The primitive experiment compares three contexts: Context | Contains required facts? | Distractors Minimal relevant | Yes | 0 Relevant + noise | Yes | Many Large but incomplete | No — refund window omitted | Many The measurement at the heart of the experiment is required-fact coverage, a one-line function in the kernel: The full experiment builds the three contexts and applies a deterministic refund rule that can only use the facts it is given: Output: minimal relevant coverage=1.0 fields=2 distractors=0 -> refund relevant + noise coverage=1.0 fields=8 distractors=6 -> refund large but incomplete coverage=0.5 fields=7 distractors=6 -> cannot decide The largest context is not the best one, and the third context is large yet useless for this decision. Because the rule is deterministic, the experiment does not pretend to measure a live model's susceptibility to distraction: the noisy context still yields the right answer here. It exposes the variables a live benchmark must control: required-fact coverage, context size, and distractor count. Engineering lesson Context size is not a proxy for context quality.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.4 Context quality starts with sufficiency
text: Before optimizing relevance, ask whether the selected context contains the information required to solve the task. Sufficient context: contains the facts required for the decision Insufficient context: omits at least one required fact A tiny context that omits a critical constraint is not efficient; it is defective. This gives context engineering two competing pressures: Include enough ↕ Exclude noise The goal is not minimality for its own sake. It is sufficient relevant information with controlled resource use.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.5 Selection is a policy
text: Suppose the system has ten candidate facts but can show only three. Something must decide which three. Figure: A selection policy decides which available facts become model-visible context. That selection policy might be handcrafted, retrieval-based, recency-based, priority-based, model-driven, or a combination. Whatever mechanism we use, it becomes part of the agent's behavior. Causal chain Available information → Context selection → Model-visible information → Decision Experiment 12 — Context selection. Give each candidate fact a simple relevance score for the refund task and keep the top two. The selection policy is a sort and a slice: The experiment runs the same policy twice: once with sensible scores, and once with a deliberately corrupted ranking that scores the customer tier above the refund window. Output: GOOD RANKING purchase_age_days=12 score 1.0 refund_window_days=30 score 1.0 required-fact coverage: 2/2 CORRUPTED RANKING purchase_age_days=12 score 1.0 customer_tier=Gold score 0.9 required-fact coverage: 1/2 With good scores we halved the context while preserving task sufficiency. With corrupted scores, top-2 selection removes the refund rule. The context is just as small and apparently well ranked, but it is now insufficient. Failure mode A context selector can fail before the model ever reasons.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.6 Selection errors and reasoning errors are different
text: Suppose the final answer is wrong. There are at least two distinct explanations: Figure: A wrong answer can come from a context failure or from a reasoning failure. If we do not record the context supplied to the model, these failures can look identical from the final answer alone. This is another reason observability matters in agentic systems.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.7 Ordering is part of context engineering
text: Selection determines what is present. Ordering determines where it appears and what surrounds it. Version A [task] [critical policy] [customer facts] [irrelevant history] Version B [irrelevant history] [customer facts] [critical policy] [task] The two contexts contain the same facts but are not necessarily equivalent inputs to a model. Position effects have been measured: Liu et al. (2024) found that models used information placed in the middle of a long context less reliably than information near its beginning or end. Test ordering for your model and task rather than assuming it has no effect. The broader principle is that context is an engineered representation, not merely a bag of text.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.8 Context has a budget
text: Every model call has finite resources. Even when a model supports a very large context window, consuming that window has consequences. Context budget = instructions + state + retrieved evidence + memory + tool observations + room for model output Different components compete for the same budget. Keeping every old tool result may crowd out new evidence. Including entire documents may leave less room for multiple retrieved sources. Long histories may increase cost on every subsequent step. Context engineering is therefore partly resource allocation.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.9 Context can contain conflicting evidence
text: The challenge is not only irrelevant information. Two relevant facts can disagree. Policy A: Refund window = 30 days effective: 2025 Policy B: Refund window = 14 days effective: 2026 A selector based only on semantic similarity may retrieve both. The system then needs provenance, dates, authority, or other metadata to decide which evidence should govern. This prepares the ground for Chapter 7: retrieval is not merely finding similar text. It is selecting evidence appropriate to the task.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.10 Context is also a security boundary
text: Anything placed into context can influence the model's next decision. That makes context assembly a trust problem as well as a relevance problem. Figure: Trusted instructions, untrusted retrieved text and tool observations all end up in the same model context. The model may see all three, but they should not automatically carry equal authority. We will return to this in Chapter 26 when we examine prompt injection. For now, remember that context engineering decides not only what the model knows, but what potentially influences it.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.11 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Required-fact coverage | Did selected context include necessary information? Context size | How many tokens/items were supplied? Distractor count | How much irrelevant material was included? Task success | Did the model answer/act correctly? Latency | What did context assembly + inference cost in time? Cost | What inference/retrieval resources were consumed? For live models, vary one factor at a time where possible: keep the task fixed while increasing distractors; keep the facts fixed while changing ordering; keep the budget fixed while changing the selection policy.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.12 More context $\neq$ better context
text: We can now state the chapter's main principle precisely. Chapter principle More context ≠ better context. Better context contains the information needed for the current decision while controlling noise, cost, risk, and omission. This does not imply that short prompts are superior. Sometimes the task genuinely requires a large body of evidence. The engineering objective is relevance and sufficiency, not brevity.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.13 The context pipeline
text: Figure: The context pipeline: available information is gathered, filtered, ranked, budgeted, and formatted before it becomes model-visible context. The remaining chapters in Part II will progressively fill in this pipeline. Retrieval determines candidate evidence. Memory determines what past information is available. Compression changes representation when context grows. MCP standardizes how external tools, resources, and prompts are offered to an application.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.14 Bridge to Chapter 7
text: So far our candidate facts were already available in a Python list. Real systems may contain millions of documents, records, chunks, or knowledge objects. Before selecting the best evidence, we first need a way to find plausible candidates. How do we retrieve the right information from a large knowledge source? That leads to retrieval and RAG.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.15 Exercises
text: - Create a task requiring exactly three facts. Construct one context that is large but insufficient and another that is small but sufficient. - Add a token cost to every candidate fact in Experiment 12. Select the highest-value context under a fixed budget. - Give an example where recency is more important than semantic similarity for context selection. - Design metadata for conflicting policy documents so the system can prefer the authoritative current version. - Define a live-model experiment that measures task accuracy as distractor count increases while required facts remain constant.

title: Chapter 6, Context Engineering: 6.16 Chapter 6 checklist
text: - Information can exist in the system without being visible to the model. - Context engineering is broader than prompt wording. - Context must be sufficient before it can be considered efficient. - Selection policies can cause failures independently of model reasoning. - Ordering, provenance, trust, and budget are part of context design. - More context is not necessarily better context.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.1 Context selection begins before the context exists
text: Chapter 6 assumed that candidate facts were already sitting in a Python list. Real systems rarely have that luxury. The relevant fact may be one paragraph among thousands of documents. Suppose the user asks: What is the current refund window? Our knowledge source contains: doc_1: "Shipping usually takes 3–5 days." doc_2: "Refunds are accepted within 30 days." effective: 2025 doc_3: "Refunds are accepted within 14 days." effective: 2026 doc_4: "Gold customers receive free delivery." The first problem is not generation. It is finding plausible evidence. Only after candidate evidence is retrieved can context selection and answer generation begin.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.2 Retrieval is a candidate-generation problem
text: A retriever takes a query and returns a small set of items from a larger collection. Figure: A retriever turns a query into a small set of candidate documents. The retriever does not need to produce the final answer. Its job is to place useful evidence inside a candidate set small enough for later processing. Key distinction Retrieval asks: What evidence should we consider? Generation asks: What answer follows from that evidence?

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.3 The smallest vector retriever
text: Production retrieval systems may use embeddings, lexical search, hybrid search, learned rerankers, metadata filters, or domain-specific indexes. To expose the mechanism, we begin with a tiny bag-of-words vector representation, kept in the kernel so later experiments can reuse it. Tokenization matters more than it looks. Splitting on spaces alone would leave "days." and "refunds" as tokens, so the query words refund and days would match nothing at all. The crude plural rule is a stand-in for real stemming. Each text becomes a vector of counts over the query's terms, and cosine similarity compares directions rather than raw counts. This is intentionally crude. It is not presented as a state-of-the-art retrieval method. It lets us inspect every number and understand the pipeline before replacing the representation with embeddings. Experiment 13 — Retrieval. The deterministic example retrieves: QUERY TERMS: ['refund', 'day'] 1.00 Refunds are accepted within 30 days. 0.71 Shipping usually takes 3 to 5 days. 0.00 Gold customers receive free delivery. RETRIEVED: Refunds are accepted within 30 days. The shipping document shares one term (day) and scores in between; it would be the second candidate if we asked for two. The experiment establishes the retrieval interface: retrieve(query, documents, k) -> ranked candidates Later we can swap the representation and ranking method without changing that conceptual contract.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.4 From word counts to embeddings and chunks
text: Bag-of-words vectors only match shared words: refund and money back score zero. A dense embedding model maps a text to a vector of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers, trained so that texts with similar meaning land close together. Retrieval then becomes nearest-neighbour search over those vectors, usually through an approximate index once the collection is large. The interface does not change: query in, ranked candidates out. Lexical scoring such as BM25 remains strong for exact identifiers, names, and codes, which is why many systems combine the two (hybrid retrieval). Real documents are also too long to embed and retrieve whole. They are split into chunks, such as paragraphs or sections of a few hundred tokens, and each chunk is embedded separately. Chunk size is a design variable: small chunks give precise matches but can separate a rule from its exceptions; large chunks keep context but dilute the vector and consume more of the context budget. Each chunk should carry its metadata (source, section, effective date) because, as the next experiment shows, metadata often decides which retrieved chunk should govern.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.5 Retrieval quality has its own metrics
text: Before asking whether the model answered correctly, ask whether the retriever supplied the evidence needed to answer. Metric | Question Hit rate@k | Was at least one relevant item in the top k? Recall@k | What fraction of all relevant items appeared in the top k? Precision@k | What fraction of the top k was relevant? Rank (MRR) | How high did the first useful item appear? When an answer needs several pieces of evidence, Recall@k = 1 is the condition that all of them were retrieved. These metrics diagnose a different component from answer accuracy. If the correct document never enters the candidate set, blaming the generator is usually misplaced.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.6 RAG adds generation after retrieval
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation—RAG—uses retrieved evidence as part of the context supplied to a generative model. Figure: Retrieval-augmented generation adds context building and generation after retrieval. RAG is therefore not a database product or a particular vector algorithm. It is an architecture that couples retrieval to generation. Experiment 14 — The smallest RAG pipeline. Now make the knowledge source more realistic by including an obsolete policy and a current policy. The two texts differ only in the number, so a similarity retriever scores them identically. Taking the top-ranked candidate is then an accident of document order; metadata tells us which policy is current. The generator is a PolicyModel stand-in that quotes the number of days in the evidence it receives. It cannot invent anything, which isolates the question this experiment asks: which evidence reached the generator? Output: CANDIDATES: 2 (equal similarity) Naive: take the top-ranked candidate ANSWER: 30 days SOURCE: policy effective 2025 Metadata: take the newest effective policy ANSWER: 14 days SOURCE: policy effective 2026 Both answers are faithful to their evidence. The naive one is still wrong, and no amount of generator quality would fix it. Engineering lesson Retrieval provides evidence; metadata and selection determine which evidence should govern; generation turns selected evidence into an answer.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.7 Retrieval $\neq$ truth
text: A retrieved document can be relevant and still be wrong, obsolete, untrusted, incomplete, or malicious. Relevant? yes Current? no Authoritative? unknown True? not established Safe to follow? not established Similarity answers a narrow question: does this item resemble the query in the representation used by the retriever? It does not establish truth. Chapter principle Retrieval ≠ truth.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.8 Similarity $\neq$ relevance
text: Even before truth, semantic similarity can differ from task relevance. Consider: Query: "What is the current refund window?" Candidate A: "Refund window history: the refund window was 30 days when the refund window was introduced in 2025." Candidate B: "Current policy: claims must be made within 14 days." Candidate A repeats refund window and wins on word overlap; an embedding model may also place it close to the query because it is about the same topic. Candidate B shares only current with the query, yet it is the one that answers it. This motivates a second ranking stage.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.9 Reranking separates recall from precision
text: Figure: A fast retriever secures recall; a more expensive reranker improves precision. The first stage tries not to miss useful evidence. The second stage spends more computation deciding which candidates are most useful for the current task. Experiment 15 — Reranking. Start with a candidate set where a broadly related historical document appears above the current policy. A task-aware reranker prefers explicit current policy. Then break the pipeline by removing current before reranking. Output: BEFORE: 1. history 2. current 3. shipping AFTER: 1. current 2. history 3. shipping ZERO RECALL, AFTER: 1. history 2. shipping The keyword rules stand in for a learned reranker such as a cross-encoder, which reads query and candidate together. Whatever the scorer, no reranker can promote evidence that is absent from its candidate set. Failure boundary Reranking can improve ordering inside the candidate set. It cannot repair zero recall.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.10 Retrieval failure and generation failure
