text: Suppose the final answer says “30 days.” We should not immediately conclude that the language model hallucinated. Evidence state | Generator behavior | Failure Current policy absent | Uses retrieved old policy | Retrieval failure Current + old present | Chooses old without reason | Selection/reasoning failure Current selected | Invents 30 anyway | Generation/faithfulness failure Current selected | Answers 14 with source | Success A useful RAG evaluation therefore decomposes the pipeline instead of reporting one final accuracy number.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.11 Grounding and citation support
text: A generated answer can be fluent and still outrun its evidence. Grounding asks whether claims in the answer are supported by the supplied evidence. Evidence: "Refunds are accepted within 14 days." Grounded: "The refund window is 14 days." Unsupported extension: "The refund window is 14 days and Gold customers receive an extra 7 days." The second answer may sound plausible, but the added claim is not supported by the evidence shown. Citation presence alone is not enough; the cited source must actually support the claim.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.12 RAG is context engineering with a search stage
text: Chapter 6 gave us the context pipeline. Retrieval inserts a candidate-generation stage at its front. Figure: Retrieval-augmented generation as context engineering with a search stage at the front. This is why RAG belongs inside Agentic Engineering even when no autonomous loop is involved. Agents repeatedly face the same question: what evidence should be visible before the next decision?

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.13 Retrieval methods are interchangeable components
text: The toy bag-of-words retriever is deliberately replaceable. Method | Useful property | Typical limitation Keyword / lexical | Exact terms, transparent | Vocabulary mismatch Embeddings | Semantic similarity | Similarity may not equal task relevance Hybrid | Combines lexical + semantic | More tuning/complexity Metadata filters | Authority, date, tenant, type | Depends on good metadata Reranker | Task-aware ordering | Extra latency/cost; needs candidates The engineering question is not “Which vector database should I use?” It is “Which retrieval pipeline produces sufficient evidence for this task under our latency, cost, and trust constraints?”

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.14 What should we measure?
text: Layer | Measures Retrieval | Recall@k, precision@k, rank, required-evidence coverage Reranking | Ranking quality, top-n relevance, added latency/cost Generation | Task accuracy, groundedness, citation support System | End-to-end success, latency, cost, failure attribution The crucial practice is to retain layer-specific metrics. An end-to-end score tells us whether the system works. Component metrics tell us what to fix.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.15 Two inequalities to remember
text: Retrieval quality ≠ Answer quality A good retriever can feed a poor generator; a strong generator cannot reliably use evidence it never receives. Similarity ≠ Relevance Semantic closeness is evidence for candidate selection, not proof that a document is the right authority for the task.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.16 Bridge to Chapter 8
text: Retrieval has so far searched an external knowledge source. But agents also accumulate information through their own interactions. Some observations matter only for the current run. Others should persist across sessions. Some repeated experiences should become reusable procedures. What should an agent remember, and why? That is the problem of memory.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.17 Live run: Stale and current evidence
text: Ten policy questions each retrieve two documents: a superseded value and the current one. A small model answers from the documents with no metadata, with effective dates and a status marker, and with the stale document filtered out. Each condition runs twice per question. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Current value only, no metadata | 7/20 | 0.35 | [0.18, 0.57] Current value only, metadata | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Current value only, current only | 20/20 | 1.00 | [0.84, 1.00] Without metadata, the model answered with only the current value in about a third of the runs; otherwise it gave the stale value or both. Effective dates and a status marker fixed every case, as did filtering. Retrieval that returns both versions without saying which is current hands the model a decision it cannot make reliably. Model gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 60 requests, 3,852 input and 1,014 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch07_stale_evidence (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.18 Exercises
text: - Build a five-document collection where lexical overlap causes the wrong document to rank first. Add one metadata field that fixes the selection. - Construct a case with Recall@1 = 0 but Recall@3 = 1. Explain what a reranker can and cannot do. - Write one grounded answer and one unsupported answer from the same evidence passage. Mark the unsupported claim. - Design a retrieval benchmark where the answer requires two different documents. Which metric captures whether both were retrieved? - Compare a keyword, embedding, and hybrid retrieval design for a domain containing product codes and natural-language descriptions. What failure do you expect from each?

title: Chapter 7, Retrieval and RAG: 7.19 Chapter 7 checklist
text: - Retrieval generates candidate evidence; it does not generate the final answer. - RAG couples retrieval, context construction, and generation. - Similarity does not establish relevance, authority, currency, or truth. - Reranking cannot recover a relevant item absent from the candidate set. - Retrieval failures and generation failures should be measured separately. - Citations should support claims, not merely accompany them.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.1 State disappears unless we preserve it
text: Our Chapter 3 agent already had a primitive kind of memory: the message list. A tool returned 84, we appended 84 to the state, and the next decision could use it. But when the run ends, that list can disappear. Start a new run and the agent may know nothing about the previous one. Run 1: User: "I prefer concise answers." Agent: ... Run 2: User: "Explain RAG." Agent: ??? If the preference should matter later, the system needs persistence beyond the current context. That sounds like a storage problem. It is actually a larger decision problem.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.2 Storing everything is not remembering well
text: A naive memory system writes every message, every tool result, every failed attempt, and every temporary fact to a database. Now the database contains history. But the agent still needs answers to two questions: WRITE: Which experiences deserve to persist? READ: Which persisted items deserve to influence this decision? Core model Memory system = Write policy + Store + Retrieval policy The store matters, but it sits between two policies. A perfect database with poor write and retrieval policies produces poor memory behavior.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.3 Four useful kinds of memory
text: The terminology varies across systems, but four distinctions are useful for engineering. Type | Question it answers | Example Working | What matters during this run? | Current intermediate result = 84 Episodic | What happened before? | Yesterday's deployment failed after step 4 Semantic | What durable fact do we know? | User prefers concise answers Procedural | How should this kind of task be done? | Inspect error → edit smallest unit → rerun tests These are functional categories, not claims that software memory exactly reproduces human cognition. They help us reason about different persistence and retrieval needs. Experiment 16 — Working memory. Working memory is the simplest: preserve information needed across steps of the current task. The experiment records the first result, uses it for the second step, and then breaks working memory by replacing the state instead of accumulating it. Output: 84 FINAL: 90 12*7 still available? False Without the 84, the second operation lacks its input. Working memory therefore supports continuity inside a trajectory. After the replacement, the earlier observation is gone: if a later step still needs it, the system has forgotten it even though the run has not ended. Engineering lesson Working memory is task state selected for continued use, not necessarily the entire interaction history.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.4 Episodic memory stores events
text: An episodic memory records something that happened in a particular interaction or run. "type": "episode", "time": "2026-10-08T08:00", "task": "deploy service", "event": "health check failed after deployment", "outcome": "rolled back" The time and event matter because the memory is about an occurrence. Later, an agent facing another deployment might retrieve similar past failures.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.5 Semantic memory stores durable facts
text: A semantic memory abstracts away from a particular event and represents something intended to remain useful. "type": "fact", "subject": "user", "predicate": "response_preference", "value": "concise" The distinction is useful because retrieval can differ. “What happened during the last deployment?” calls for an episode. “What response style does this user prefer?” calls for a durable fact. Experiment 17 — Episodic and semantic memory. The kernel store is deliberately small. Every record carries a type and a source, and retrieval can filter by type. What to write is not the store's decision; that belongs to a write policy outside it. Store one session event and one durable preference. On a later run, a request for an explanation retrieves semantic records, because they shape how to answer; a question about the previous session retrieves episode records. Then break the write policy: a naive policy persists the temporary instruction "Use pirate language for this one joke." as if it were durable. A stricter policy refuses requests that announce their own short lifetime. Output: NAIVE write policy episode User asked for a Python example of RAG. semantic User prefers concise explanations. semantic Use pirate language for this one joke. DURABLE-ONLY write policy episode User asked for a Python example of RAG. semantic User prefers concise explanations. Under the naive policy, every future explanation request now retrieves the pirate instruction alongside the real preference. Future answers may be distorted by information that should have expired. The keyword rule is crude, and a model-assisted classifier could replace it, but the point stands: the write policy, not the store, decided what the future will see. Failure mode Persistence can turn a temporary observation into a long-lived error.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.6 The write policy is part of reasoning
text: What should be remembered? Possible criteria include: Signal | Example Explicit durability | “Remember that my project uses Python 3.12.” Repeated observation | Same preference appears across interactions Future utility | Fact is likely to improve later decisions Outcome significance | A costly failure should inform similar future tasks Trust / provenance | Source is sufficiently reliable to persist Expiry | Information has a known useful lifetime The policy can be deterministic, model-assisted, or hybrid. But it should be explicit. Otherwise “memory” quietly becomes uncontrolled data accumulation.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.7 Retrieval policy is context engineering
text: Once information is stored, recalling it is the same context-selection problem we met in Chapters 6 and 7. Figure: Recalling memory is a context-selection problem. This yields a useful relationship: Memory retrieval is context engineering over persisted state. A memory can exist without being recalled. A recalled memory can influence the model even if it is irrelevant or stale.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.8 Procedural memory stores how
text: Facts tell an agent something about the world. Procedures tell it how to approach a class of tasks. When a unit test fails: 1. Read the failing assertion. 2. Identify the smallest responsible function. 3. Make the smallest plausible edit. 4. Run the relevant test again. 5. Stop when tests pass. This procedure could be represented as instructions, a skill, a workflow template, code, or a structured policy. The representation matters less than its function: past experience changes future behavior by supplying a reusable method. Experiment 18 — Procedural memory. Give the agent two ways to approach a failing test. Without a stored procedure it chooses a broad rewrite. With a good procedure in context, it first inspects the failure and edits the smallest unit. Then break it by storing a bad procedure: "When any test fails, delete the test." The model is a PolicyModel stand-in that follows whatever procedure it is shown, which is exactly the property that makes procedural memory powerful and dangerous. Output: NO PROCEDURE -> rewrite_module refunds.py GOOD PROCEDURE -> inspect_then_edit refund_window() BAD PROCEDURE -> delete_test test_refund.py The bad procedure is retrieved by the same query and injected by the same code as the good one. The memory system can now make future behavior consistently worse. Persistence amplifies both good and bad abstractions. Engineering lesson Procedural memory turns past learning into future control policy. It therefore deserves stronger validation than an ordinary transient observation.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.9 Memory has provenance
text: A useful memory record should often carry more than content. "content": "Refund window is 14 days", "type": "semantic", "source": "policy_2026", "created_at": "...", "valid_until": "...", "confidence": "...", "trust": "authoritative" The exact fields depend on the domain. The principle is that persistent information should remain inspectable: where did it come from, when was it learned, and when should it stop influencing decisions?

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.10 Memory can conflict
text: Persistent systems eventually accumulate contradictions. Memory A: "User prefers detailed explanations." Memory B: "User prefers concise explanations." The correct response is not necessarily to concatenate both into context. The system needs a conflict policy: recency, explicit user correction, source authority, scope, confidence, or human review. This is another reason memory is a policy problem rather than a storage problem.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.11 Forgetting is a feature
text: A system that never forgets accumulates stale state, privacy exposure, retrieval noise, and contradictory facts. Good memory system: write retrieve update expire supersede delete Some memories should decay. Some should be replaced by newer facts. Some should be scoped to a project or session. Some should never have been written in the first place. Design principle Useful memory requires selective forgetting as well as selective remembering.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.12 Memory is also a security boundary
text: Persistence increases the lifetime of an input. If untrusted content can write directly into durable memory, one malicious interaction can influence many future decisions. Figure: A write policy decides whether untrusted input may persist into future contexts. Chapter 26 will examine memory poisoning directly. For now, the important architectural fact is that the write policy is a security boundary.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.13 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Write precision | Of the items we persisted, what fraction deserved to persist? Write recall | Of the items worth remembering, what fraction did we persist? Retrieval relevance | Were recalled memories useful to the current task? Staleness rate | How often did expired/superseded memories influence decisions? Task lift | Did memory improve downstream success? Negative transfer | How often did memory make performance worse? Storage size is an operational metric, not a sufficient quality metric. A large memory can be useless; a tiny memory can contain exactly what future decisions need.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.14 The complete memory pipeline
text: Figure: The complete memory pipeline: a write policy decides what persists, and a retrieval policy decides what reaches the current context. Chapter principle Memory = Write policy + Store + Retrieval policy

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.15 Memory is not the same as RAG
text: The mechanisms overlap. Both may retrieve text or structured records into context. Their purpose differs. RAG / knowledge retrieval | Memory Searches an external knowledge source | Preserves information from prior state/experience Evidence may pre-exist the agent | Information often arises through interaction Question: what knowledge is relevant? | Question: what past state/experience should matter now? May be authoritative documentation | May include preferences, episodes, learned procedures In production, the same vector store could technically hold both. The conceptual distinction still matters because write, trust, retention, and update policies differ.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.16 Bridge to Chapter 9
text: Memory solves persistence, but persistence creates a new problem: accumulated state grows. If we continually place working history, retrieved knowledge, tool results, and memories into context, the context eventually becomes expensive and noisy. How do we make context smaller without forgetting what matters? That is the problem of context compression.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.17 Exercises
text: - Classify these as working, episodic, semantic, or procedural memory: an intermediate calculation; last week's failed deployment; a user's stable language preference; a debugging checklist. - Write a rule that prevents one-off stylistic requests from becoming durable semantic memory. - Design a memory record that can be superseded by a newer value while preserving provenance. - Create two conflicting memories and define a deterministic conflict-resolution policy. - Design a benchmark that measures both positive transfer and negative transfer from procedural memory.

title: Chapter 8, Memory: 8.18 Chapter 8 checklist
text: - Working memory preserves task state inside a trajectory. - Episodic memory records events; semantic memory records durable facts; procedural memory records reusable methods. - Persistence requires an explicit write policy. - Recall is context selection over persisted state. - Forgetting, expiry, and supersession are useful memory operations. - Memory write policy is also a security boundary.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.1 Context grows
text: An agent loop accumulates state. Tools return observations. Retrieval adds evidence. Memory contributes prior facts. A long-running agent can therefore produce more potentially useful information than we want to place into every model call. Goal + instructions + 20 prior messages + 12 tool observations + 5 retrieved documents + 4 memories + current plan + permissions + budget = growing context One response is simply to keep everything until the model's context limit forces us to stop. That treats compression as an emergency. A better approach is to treat context as a managed resource from the beginning.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.2 Context compression is usually lossy
text: Some compression is lossless: removing an exact duplicate, or replacing a long document with a pointer that can be dereferenced later, loses nothing. But the compression that matters for agents usually makes a representation smaller by dropping something: wording, detail, examples, chronology, provenance, or uncertainty. Figure: Compression produces a smaller representation of the original information. The engineering question is not whether information is lost. It is whether the lost information matters to future decisions. Core idea Good compression removes expendable detail while preserving task-relevant state, constraints, evidence, and uncertainty.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.3 Summarization is one compression operator
text: Consider a long interaction: User wants a report. It must be under 500 words. The audience is technical. The user asks several exploratory questions. Two search calls fail. One search succeeds. The final report must cite the successful source. Sending email requires approval. A useful working summary might be: TASK: Write technical report, <=500 words. EVIDENCE: Use successful source S3. CONSTRAINT: Email send requires approval. The failed searches may be irrelevant to the final writing decision. The 500-word limit and approval constraint are not. Experiment 19 — Compress working context. Represent the context as structured facts so we can see exactly what survives. A simple compressor retains fields declared critical to the next phase: The experiment runs a good keep list and a broken one that omits the approval constraint. A harness rule then asks whether the agent may send without approval; like many real checks, it treats a missing constraint as no constraint. Output: GOOD compressor: 137 of 194 characters (71%) "task": "write technical report", "word_limit": 500, "audience": "technical", "successful_source": "S3", "send_requires_approval": true may send without approval: False BROKEN compressor: 105 of 194 characters (54%) "task": "write technical report", "word_limit": 500, "audience": "technical", "successful_source": "S3" may send without approval: True The broken compressor achieves a better ratio, and the agent may now attempt an unauthorized send. Nothing in the compressed state looks wrong; the constraint is simply absent. Failure mode A shorter context can be operationally worse if compression deletes a constraint.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.4 Compression quality is downstream quality
text: A summary can look excellent to a human reader and still be poor agent state. The correct evaluation is not “Does this sound like a good summary?” but “Can downstream decisions still be made correctly?” Figure: Compression quality is judged by whether the next task can still succeed. This shifts evaluation from linguistic similarity toward retained utility.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.5 What must survive?
text: Information class | Example | Usually preserve when relevant? Goal | Prepare investment memo | Yes Hard constraint | Maximum 500 words | Yes Permission | Approval required before send | Yes Current state | Research complete | Yes Key evidence | Source S3 supports claim | Yes Uncertainty | Revenue figure unverified | Yes Transient chatter | “Thanks!” | Usually no Superseded attempt | Old failed query | Depends There is no universal keep list. The preservation policy depends on the next decisions the system expects to make.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.6 Preserve provenance when claims matter
text: Compression often replaces several evidence items with a statement. If the source relationship disappears, later generation may retain the claim but lose the ability to verify or cite it. Poor: "Refund window is 14 days." Better: "Refund window is 14 days [source: policy_2026]." For consequential claims, provenance can be part of the information that must survive compression.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.7 Preserve uncertainty
text: Compression can accidentally turn uncertainty into certainty. Original: "Source A says 14 days. Source B says 30 days. A appears newer, but authority is unverified." Bad summary: "Refund window is 14 days." The shorter statement removed the unresolved conflict. This is not merely information loss; it changes the epistemic state of the system. Design principle Do not compress uncertainty into false certainty.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.8 Compression and memory are related but different
text: Compression changes representation. Memory changes persistence. They often interact. Operation | Primary question Context compression | How can active information be represented more compactly? Memory write | What should persist beyond the current context/run? Memory retrieval | What persisted information should return now? A compressed working summary may later be written to memory. A retrieved memory may be compressed before entering context. But the operations solve different problems.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.9 Consolidation turns many experiences into one abstraction
text: Suppose an agent observes the same preference across several sessions: Episode 1: user asks for concise answer. Episode 2: user asks to shorten response. Episode 3: user chooses concise version. Instead of retrieving all three episodes forever, the system may derive a durable semantic memory: Semantic memory: "User prefers concise responses." This is memory consolidation: repeated or related experiences are transformed into a more durable abstraction. Experiment 20 — Memory consolidation. The experiment compares two consolidators on a consistent episode set and on a conflicting one. The blind consolidator always emits the concise preference. The guarded one requires at least two agreeing episodes and refuses to write a fact when the evidence conflicts. Output: CONSISTENT blind: User prefers concise responses. guarded: User prefers concise responses. CONFLICTING blind: User prefers concise responses. guarded: No fact: conflicting episodes 'concise': 1, 'detailed': 1 On consistent evidence the two agree, and three event records become one reusable fact. On conflicting evidence the blind consolidator has erased the contradiction. Consolidation needs thresholds, scope, provenance, and conflict handling; the keyword classifier here is a stand-in for whatever (possibly model-based) judgment a real system uses. Engineering lesson Consolidation is abstraction, not mere summarization.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.10 Summarization vs consolidation
text: Summarization / compression | Consolidation Makes active information smaller | Creates a durable abstraction from experiences Often scoped to current task/run | Often intended for future runs Goal: preserve next-step utility | Goal: extract reusable knowledge May discard transient details | May replace many episodes with a fact/skill Both are lossy transformations. Both therefore need downstream evaluation.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.11 Hierarchical compression
text: Long-running systems need not choose between raw history and one giant summary. They can maintain layers. Figure: Hierarchical compression keeps several layers instead of one summary. Recent events remain detailed while older material becomes increasingly abstract. If necessary, the system can retain pointers back to original evidence rather than forcing every detail into active context.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.12 Compression can be reversible or irreversible
text: If a summary replaces raw data permanently, omitted information may be unrecoverable. If the summary retains references to archived originals, the active representation is compressed while the underlying evidence remains accessible. Figure: Irreversible compression deletes the raw events; recoverable compression archives them and keeps references. For high-value evidence, recoverable compression is often easier to audit.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.13 Context compression is also control
text: What survives compression influences what the model can consider later. A compressor therefore shapes future behavior just as a retriever or memory policy does. Figure: What survives compression shapes the next decision. This means compression belongs in the agent's harness, not merely in token optimization.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.14 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Compression ratio | How much smaller is the representation? Critical-fact retention | Were required facts/constraints preserved? Provenance retention | Can important claims still be traced? Uncertainty retention | Were unresolved conflicts preserved? Downstream success | Can later tasks still be completed correctly? Cost/latency reduction | Did compression actually save resources? A high compression ratio is not success if downstream task quality collapses. Resource savings and retained utility must be reported together.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.15 The context lifecycle
text: Figure: The context lifecycle: working context is compressed into compact state, and selected items persist into memory and are consolidated into durable facts or skills. Chapter principle Compression is successful when it reduces representation cost while preserving the information required for future decisions.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.16 Bridge to Chapter 10
text: Part II has now given our agent tools, engineered context, retrieval, memory, and compression. But every capability has so far been integrated through our own local Python interfaces. As ecosystems grow, custom integration becomes expensive. Agents need a standard way to discover and invoke external capabilities and resources. Can capabilities be exposed through a common protocol? That leads to MCP.

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.17 Exercises
text: - Compress a ten-item task state into five items while preserving the goal, one permission, one uncertainty, and one evidence source. - Construct a summary that sounds correct but loses provenance. Modify it so the claim remains traceable. - Create three contradictory episodes and design a rule for when they may be consolidated into a semantic memory. - Compare irreversible compression with archive-plus-summary for a regulated workflow. Which information would you refuse to delete? - Design an experiment measuring compression ratio against downstream task accuracy. What would count as a Pareto improvement?

title: Chapter 9, Context Compression: 9.18 Chapter 9 checklist
text: - Compression is a lossy transformation and should be evaluated by downstream utility. - Critical constraints, permissions, provenance, and uncertainty may need explicit preservation. - Shorter context is not automatically better context. - Compression and memory persistence solve different problems. - Consolidation creates reusable abstractions from multiple experiences. - Recoverable compression can preserve access to original evidence.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.1 We already built the idea
text: Chapter 5 used a local tool registry. The model saw a capability description, proposed a call, trusted software validated the proposal, executed the function, and returned an observation. MCP does not replace that architecture. It standardizes important parts of the boundary. Figure: MCP standardizes the boundary that Chapter 5 built with a custom registry. The important continuity is that the model still proposes actions and software still executes them.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.2 The integration problem
text: Without a common protocol, every application may invent its own representation for tool discovery, schemas, invocation, results, resources, and errors. One agent may call a database through a bespoke Python wrapper, another may integrate the same database through a different JSON contract, and a third may require framework-specific adapters. With M applications and N services, that tends towards M × N integrations. Figure: Without a shared protocol, every agent needs its own adapter for the same service. A protocol moves some of this integration complexity behind a shared contract: each application implements the client side once, and each service implements the server side once. Figure: With a protocol, every agent uses one common client contract to reach the server and its service.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.3 MCP is a protocol, not an agent
text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to external capabilities and context. It names three roles. The host is the AI application the user works with, such as a chat client, an IDE, or an agent harness. Inside the host, an MCP client maintains a connection to exactly one MCP server; a host that uses five servers runs five clients. A server is a program that exposes capabilities, often a thin wrapper around an existing system such as a file store, a database, or a ticketing API. The protocol defines how these parties exchange messages. It does not decide the user goal, plan a solution, choose whether a tool should be used, or decide whether a particular action should happen now. Question | Owned by What capabilities exist? | Server implementation Message format, lifecycle, discovery, invocation | The protocol May this client use this server at all? | Transport-level authorization and deployment What does the model see? | Host context construction Which capability should be used? | Model, within host control Is this specific action allowed now? | Host policy, human approval What actually executes? | Server implementation When should the agent stop? | Agent harness

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.4 What the protocol actually defines (part 1 of 2)
text: MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. There are three kinds: a request carries an id and a method and expects a response; a response carries the same id and either a result or an error; a notification has a method but no id and expects no reply. Lifecycle. A session begins with an initialize request. The client states the protocol revision it speaks and the optional features it supports; the server answers with the revision it will use and its own capabilities. The client then sends an initialized notification, and only then does normal traffic begin. client -> server "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": "elicitation": , "clientInfo": "name": "book-client", "version": "1.0" server -> client "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": "tools": "listChanged": true, "resources": , "serverInfo": "name": "calc-server", "version": "1.0" client -> server "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized" This exchange is capability negotiation: neither side may use a feature the other did not declare. Protocol revisions are named by date. The examples in this chapter use the 2025-06-18 revision; later revisions exist, so check the current specification before building against it. Server features. A server can offer three kinds of primitive, distinguished by who is meant to control them: Primitive | Controlled by | Purpose and methods Tools | The model | Functions the model may propose to call: tools/list, tools/call Resources | The application | Read-only context identified by URI, such as files or records: resources/list, resources/read Prompts | The user | Reusable prompt templates, often surfaced as commands: prompts/list, prompts/get Client features. The traffic is not one-way. A client may offer roots (the filesystem locations a server may operate within), sampling (the server asks the host's model for a completion, so the server needs no model credentials of its own), and elicitation (the server asks the user, through the host, for structured input). Each is opt-in through capability negotiation and each keeps the host, and ideally the user, in the loop.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.4 What the protocol actually defines (part 2 of 2)
text: Transports. The same messages can travel over two standard transports. With stdio, the host launches the server as a local subprocess and they exchange newline-delimited JSON over standard input and output. With Streamable HTTP, the server exposes one HTTP endpoint; the client POSTs each message and the server replies with a JSON body or a stream of server-sent events. Many MCP servers are therefore local processes, not remote services.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.5 Discovery before invocation (part 1 of 2)
text: A custom application can hard-code every tool description. MCP lets the client discover them at run time. For tools, two methods do the work. "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list" "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "result": "tools": [ "name": "calculator", "description": "Evaluate basic arithmetic such as 18*7.", "inputSchema": "type": "object", "properties": "expression": "type": "string", "required": ["expression"]] The host decides which of these definitions to show the model, usually by translating them into its model provider's tool-calling format. When the model proposes a call, the client sends it: "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call", "params": "name": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "18*7" "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "result": "content": ["type": "text", "text": "126"], "isError": false A tool result is a CallToolResult: a list of content blocks (text, images, audio, embedded resources, or links to resources) plus an isError flag. A tool may also declare an outputSchema and return machine-readable structuredContent alongside the content. Large result lists are paginated with a cursor, and a server that declared listChanged can send notifications/tools/list_changed when its tool set changes. Experiment 21 — A minimal MCP-shaped calculator. To see the contract without hiding it inside a library, the experiment simulates both sides of the exchange in one process. It is not the MCP SDK and it uses no transport: send serializes each request to JSON text, as stdio or HTTP would carry it, and passes it straight to the server's handle function. The calculator is the kernel's AST-based evaluator from Chapter 5, so no eval is involved. Output: SERVER: calc-server | version: 2025-06-18 | capabilities: ['tools'] TOOL: calculator | requires: ['expression'] CALL: calculator "expression": "18*7" content: ["type": "text", "text": "126"] isError: false CALL: calculator "expression": "delete all invoices" content: ["type": "text", "text": "invalid arithmetic expression"] isError: true CALL: delete_invoice "id": 7 protocol error: "code": -32602, "message": "Unknown tool: delete_invoice"

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.5 Discovery before invocation (part 2 of 2)
text: The arithmetic is deliberately uninteresting. The experiment makes three boundaries visible. Discovery and invocation go through messages, not through direct knowledge of a Python function. A tool that runs and fails returns a normal result with isError: true. A request the protocol cannot honor, such as calling a tool the server never listed, returns a JSON-RPC error instead. A real implementation would use an official SDK (for example the mcp package for Python), which handles framing, the lifecycle, transports, and pagination; the repository deliberately does not depend on one.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.6 The model does not speak directly to the server
text: It is easy to draw an architecture that suggests a language model independently connects to arbitrary MCP servers. A more useful engineering picture keeps the host application in the control path. Figure: The host application stays in the control path: it builds context, exposes capabilities, validates decisions, and owns the MCP client that talks to servers. The host determines which server capabilities become model-visible and what policy surrounds their use. Some model providers can also connect to remote MCP servers on the application's behalf; then the provider's platform plays the client role, and the same questions about exposure and policy move into its configuration. Either way, probabilistic proposals remain inside deterministic control boundaries.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.7 MCP does not eliminate validation
text: A standardized schema improves interoperability. It does not make every proposed invocation semantically valid or authorized. Model proposes: calculator(expression="delete all invoices") The argument satisfies the string schema while still being meaningless for the capability; in Experiment 21 it passes the protocol and fails in the tool. The distinctions from Chapter 2 survive protocol standardization: Parseable ≠ Valid ≠ Authorized Protocols define communication contracts. Application policy still decides what may happen.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.8 Deliberately break discovery
text: Suppose the server exposes a vague description: "name": "do_math", "description": "Do useful things with numbers." The protocol exchange can be perfectly valid while the model-facing affordance is poor. MCP standardizes how the description is delivered; it cannot guarantee that the description itself is well designed. Engineering lesson Interoperability does not remove tool-interface design.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.9 Deliberately break execution
text: Now let discovery and selection succeed but make the underlying capability fail: Figure: Discovery and selection succeed, but execution fails. Again, protocol success and task success are different. MCP separates two kinds of failure. A tool that ran and failed reports it inside a normal result, so the host can show the error to the model and let it adjust: "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "result": "content": ["type": "text", "text": "upstream service timed out"], "isError": true A request that could not be processed at all (unknown tool, malformed arguments, unknown method) gets a JSON-RPC error, which the client handles: "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "error": "code": -32602, "message": "Unknown tool: delete_invoice" If the server never answers, the client's own timeout fires, and it can send a notifications/cancelled message for the outstanding request. None of this decides whether the agent should retry, fall back, ask the user, or stop. That remains a recovery policy in the harness.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.10 Deliberately break authorization
text: The most important misconception is that discoverability implies permission. Imagine a server exposes both read_invoice and delete_invoice. Discovered capability ≠ authorized capability The host may expose only read_invoice to the model, require human approval for delete_invoice, or refuse deletion entirely. MCP does say something about authorization, at a different level. For HTTP transports the specification defines an optional authorization framework built on OAuth 2.1: the MCP server acts as an OAuth resource server, and the client obtains an access token, with scopes, from an authorization server. Local stdio servers typically take credentials from their environment instead. That answers "may this client use this server, with these scopes?" It does not answer "should the agent delete invoice 7 right now?" The specification's security principles call for explicit user consent before tools are invoked, and tools may carry annotations such as readOnlyHint and destructiveHint; but annotations are hints a host must not trust from an untrusted server, and enforcing consent is the host's job. Capability and permission remain separate concepts. This distinction becomes central in Chapter 25: Capability ≠ Permission

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.11 Standardization changes coupling
text: Without a protocol, the agent application is coupled to each custom integration. With a protocol, it can depend more heavily on a shared client contract while servers adapt their own systems behind that contract. Before: agent ↔ service-specific integration After: agent ↔ protocol client ↔ server ↔ service This does not remove all coupling. Tool names, descriptions, schemas, semantics, authentication, server behavior, protocol revisions, and application policy still matter. It changes where coupling lives.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.12 Tools are only part of the broader context problem
text: MCP is often introduced through tools because tool invocation is easy to demonstrate. But resources and prompts are the protocol's other two server primitives, and they are pure context: a resource is information the application may place in front of the model, and a prompt is a template the user may choose. This connects directly to the previous chapters. Information arriving through MCP must still be selected, represented, trusted, and placed into model context appropriately. Figure: Information arriving through MCP is still selected and controlled by the host.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.13 Protocol boundaries create trust boundaries
text: A server provides descriptions, content, results, and errors that influence future model decisions. Tool descriptions themselves enter the model's context, so a server can steer the model before any tool is called. An external server is therefore not merely a convenience integration; it is another trust boundary. Risk | Engineering response Unexpected capability | Allowlist / capability filtering Tool-definition poisoning (instructions hidden in a description) | Review descriptions as untrusted input; show users what the model will see Definition changed after approval ("rug pull") | Pin or hash approved definitions; re-approve when tools/list changes Name collision across servers | Namespace tools by server; resolve names explicitly in the host Malformed result | Validate server output Sensitive operation | Permission and approval policy Untrusted returned content | Treat as data, not automatically as instruction Credential misuse | Scope tokens per server; never pass a client's token through to another service Server failure | Timeout, fallback, recovery policy

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.14 MCP vs function calling
text: These concepts operate at different layers. Model-provider function or tool calling gives a model a structured way to propose an invocation. MCP provides a standardized integration protocol through which an application can discover and invoke external capabilities. They are used together: a host typically converts tools/list results into the provider's tool format, and converts the model's tool call into a tools/call request. Figure: Provider tool calling and MCP solve different problems. One helps structure the model/application boundary. The other helps structure the application/external-system boundary.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.15 MCP vs agents
text: A calculator exposed through MCP is still a calculator. A file server exposed through MCP is still a capability provider. Neither becomes autonomous merely because it uses a protocol designed for AI applications. MCP server + no agent loop = standardized capability access Agent loop + no MCP = still an agent Agent loop + MCP = agent using standardized capabilities Chapter principle MCP standardizes capability access. It does not create agency.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.16 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Discovery correctness | Did the client receive the intended capability set? Selection accuracy | Did the model choose the right exposed capability? Schema-valid calls | Were proposed arguments structurally valid? Execution success | Did the capability complete without isError? Protocol errors | How many requests failed at the JSON-RPC level? Policy violations | Were disallowed capabilities/actions blocked? Integration overhead | What latency/cost does the boundary add? As before, component metrics matter. A protocol-level success does not imply end-to-end agent success.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.17 From local registry to protocol
text: Figure: From a local tool registry to discovery and execution over a protocol. The abstraction did not change. The integration boundary did.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.18 Part II synthesis
text: Part II began with a nearly powerless agent and progressively engineered what it can do and what it can know. Chapter 5 Tools What can the agent do? Chapter 6 Context Engineering What should it see now? Chapter 7 Retrieval and RAG How does it find external evidence? Chapter 8 Memory What should persist from the past? Chapter 9 Context Compression How do we preserve what matters as state grows? Chapter 10 MCP How can external capabilities be exposed through a common interface? Together these chapters produce the second layer of Agentic Engineering: capability and information are not simply given to a model. They are exposed, selected, constrained, persisted, transformed, and governed by the surrounding system.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.19 Part III: making agents think and work
text: Our agent now has capabilities and information. The next question is how control should be organized when solving harder tasks. Should it alternate reasoning and action? Plan first? Critique itself? Search several possibilities? Route tasks? Run work in parallel? Part III treats each of these not as magic intelligence upgrades but as reasoning architectures whose benefits must be measured against their cost. We begin with ReAct: interleaving decisions with observations from the world.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.20 Exercises
text: - Add a second tool (for example a unit converter) to the server in Experiment 21. What must change in the client, and what must not? - Add a delete_file tool to the server but prevent it from becoming model-visible. Which layer owns that decision? - Make a tool description deliberately ambiguous, then improve it without changing the underlying capability. - Extend Experiment 21 so one call returns isError: true with a timeout message, and define three agent policies for it: retry, fallback, and stop. Which policy suits a JSON-RPC error instead? - Make the server change the calculator's description after the client has listed it. How should the host detect the change, and what should it do? - Draw the boundaries among provider-native tool calling, the host application, an MCP client, an MCP server, and the underlying service.

title: Chapter 10, Model Context Protocol (MCP): 10.21 Chapter 10 checklist
text: - MCP standardizes an integration boundary; it is not itself an agent. - MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 with an initialize handshake, capability negotiation, and stdio or Streamable HTTP transports. - Servers offer tools, resources, and prompts; clients may offer roots, sampling, and elicitation. - A failed tool returns isError: true; an unprocessable request returns a JSON-RPC error. - Protocol authorization governs access to a server; per-action permission remains host policy. - Tool definitions are untrusted input: they can be poisoned, changed, or collide across servers.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.1 From abilities to reasoning architectures
text: Part II gave our agent capabilities: tools, context, retrieval, memory, compression, and a standardized way to expose external capabilities. Part III asks a different question: how should those capabilities be orchestrated while solving a task? The simplest approach is one shot: Figure: One-shot use of a model: the goal goes in and an answer comes out, with no intermediate feedback. But many tasks reveal useful information only after an action. Search returns evidence. A calculator returns a number. A test run returns an error. A database query returns state. If the model can observe that result, it can revise what it does next.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.2 The ReAct pattern
text: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) prompts a language model to interleave three kinds of step: a free-text reasoning trace ("Thought"), an action, and the observation that the action returns. The paper compared it with an Act-only baseline that keeps the actions and observations but drops the thoughts; the thoughts helped, most clearly on multi-step household tasks in ALFWorld. In ReAct the thoughts are ordinary generated text in the context window, visible to the harness, not a hidden channel. This chapter isolates the part of ReAct that the harness controls: the action–observation feedback loop. Thought traces remain a useful prompting technique, but the loop does not depend on them. With modern tool-calling APIs and reasoning models, much of a model's reasoning may happen in a channel the application never sees, so we do not make reasoning text part of the system interface. Figure: The ReAct loop: decide an action, act, observe the result, and feed it back into the next decision. Operational definition A ReAct-style loop is a feedback pattern in which the agent alternates decisions and actions, using each new observation to condition the next decision. This definition focuses on what the system needs to execute and evaluate: selected actions, arguments, observations, and termination. Reasoning text, where it exists, is optional evidence rather than a required interface.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.3 We already built most of it
text: The reusable agent loop from Chapter 3 already contains the mechanical structure. Each iteration appends two messages: the model's own decision, and then the observation that executing it produced. What changes in this chapter is the experimental question. We are no longer merely demonstrating a loop. We are asking whether feedback from intermediate actions creates measurable value. Experiment 22 — ReAct as feedback control. Consider a task whose second action depends on the first observation: Goal: Find the current value of X, then calculate X * 1.15. A one-shot system must either know X already or guess it. A ReAct-style system can first obtain X and then calculate using the observed value. The experiment runs both, plus a deliberately broken loop. The decisions come from deterministic stand-in models rather than an LLM: ScriptedModel returns a fixed answer, and PolicyModel chooses its next decision from the observations it can see. Output: == One-shot: no tools, so X must be guessed (here X = 100) == STEP 1 DONE: 115.0 == ReAct: each observation is appended to the messages == STEP 1 ACTION: lookup('key': 'X') OBSERVATION: 80 STEP 2 ACTION: calculator('expression': '80 * 1.15') OBSERVATION: 92.0 STEP 3 DONE: 92.0 == BREAK: the lookup runs but its result is never fed back == STEP 1 ACTION: lookup('key': 'X') OBSERVATION: 80 STEP 2 ACTION: lookup('key': 'X') OBSERVATION: 80 STEP 3 ACTION: lookup('key': 'X') OBSERVATION: 80 STEP 4 ACTION: lookup('key': 'X') OBSERVATION: 80 STOPPED: step limit after 4 model calls The one-shot stand-in has no tool, so it can only guess: it assumes X = 100 and answers 115.0. The ReAct loop answers 92.0 because the environment supplied information after step 1 that was unavailable before the action. The key event is not that the model "thought more."

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.4 What the loop must feed back
text: Two appends make the loop work: the model's own decision, so that it can see what it already tried, and the observation that decision produced. The model receives the updated state on every iteration. Its next decision can therefore depend on the consequence of its previous action. Provider chat APIs add one more requirement: a tool result message must carry the identifier of the tool call it answers, and must follow the assistant message that made that call.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.5 Feedback is the source of value
text: If an action cannot reveal anything that changes the next decision, an iterative ReAct loop may add little. Figure: Useful feedback changes the next decision; weak feedback leaves the decision path unchanged. This suggests a practical test: before adding an iterative reasoning architecture, ask what new information each action is expected to reveal.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.6 Deliberately remove the observation
text: The third run in Experiment 22 breaks the loop by executing the lookup but not returning its result to the model. The environment knows that X = 80. The next model call does not. The lookup executed four times, and the run ended only because the step limit stopped it. Failure mode Action without observation is not useful feedback.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.7 Deliberately ignore the observation
text: A subtler failure occurs when the result is visible but the next decision does not actually use it. OBSERVATION: X = 80 NEXT ACTION: calculator("100 * 1.15") The loop is structurally correct but behaviorally defective. This is why trajectory evaluation matters: the final answer alone does not tell us whether the agent used observations appropriately.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.8 ReAct is not synonymous with chain-of-thought
text: ReAct's thought traces are a prompting device; the feedback loop does not depend on them. An implementation does not need to read a model's reasoning text, visible or hidden, in order to use iterative action and observation. Observable decision: "action": "calculator", "arguments": "expression": "80 * 1.15", "done": false This is enough for the harness to execute, trace, validate, and evaluate the trajectory. Design principle Engineer around observable decisions and state transitions. Do not make hidden reasoning text a required system interface.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.9 ReAct can waste work
text: Feedback loops create adaptability, but every loop iteration consumes resources. A poorly controlled agent can repeatedly search for information it already has. search("refund policy") search("refund policy") search("refund policy") search("refund policy") ... This is the same local-success/global-failure pattern from Chapter 3: every search may execute correctly while the trajectory makes no progress.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.10 No-progress detection
text: A simple harness can detect repeated actions or repeated observations. Added to the broken run of Experiment 22, this detector would stop at step 3 instead of waiting for the step limit. Production systems need more nuanced definitions of progress, but the principle is general: iterative reasoning should earn each additional step.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.11 One-shot vs ReAct is an empirical question
text: ReAct should not be treated as automatically superior to a single model call. Compare them on task classes. Task | One-shot expectation | ReAct expectation Static factual task with sufficient context | Strong baseline | May add overhead Task requiring external lookup | Cannot use unseen result | Can incorporate observation Multi-step tool task | May predict plan/results | Can adapt after each step Simple deterministic calculation | Adequate, or call the calculator directly | Likely overhead The architecture should win because the task contains useful feedback, not because iterative agents are fashionable.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.12 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Task success | Did the system solve the task? Model calls | How many decisions were requested? Tool calls | How much external work was performed? Observation use | Did later actions depend correctly on returned evidence? Repeated actions | Did the loop make progress? Tokens / cost | What did iteration consume? Latency | How much wall time did the loop add? For stochastic models, repeated trials and variance matter. A reasoning architecture that improves mean success but creates extreme cost or unstable trajectories may not be the better system.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.13 The Part III experimental rule
text: This chapter introduces a discipline that will govern the rest of Part III. Reasoning architectures are hypotheses Planning, reflection, search, routing, and parallelism should each be tested against a simpler baseline. More reasoning is not assumed to mean better answers. For each pattern we will ask three questions: 1. What new capability does the pattern provide? 2. On which task class should that capability help? 3. What additional cost or failure mode does it introduce?

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.14 ReAct as control
text: Viewed from control theory, the important structure is feedback: Figure: ReAct viewed as feedback control: observations from the environment return to the controller. The model participates in the controller. The harness defines the action interface, executes the action, captures the observation, updates state, and enforces stopping conditions. This makes ReAct an agentic control architecture rather than merely a prompting trick.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.15 When not to use it
text: Prefer a simpler architecture when the required path is known, intermediate observations cannot change the path, the task is cheap to solve directly, or iteration creates unacceptable latency/risk. Chapter 4's least-autonomy principle therefore applies inside reasoning architectures too: Use the least iterative control necessary A loop is justified when feedback has enough value to pay for another decision.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.16 Bridge to Chapter 12
text: ReAct is primarily reactive: decide, act, observe, and decide again. But some tasks benefit from considering a sequence of future steps before executing the first one. Should an agent plan before it acts? That leads to planning—and to a new question: when does a plan help, and when does reality make the plan obsolete?

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.17 Exercises
text: - Construct a task where the second action cannot be chosen correctly until the first tool returns an observation. - Add the no-progress detector to the broken run of Experiment 22. At which step does it stop, and what should the harness report to the user? - Create a task where ReAct adds model calls but no useful new information. Which architecture should win? - Design a no-progress detector that catches repeated tool calls without stopping legitimate repeated polling too early. - Define a benchmark comparing one-shot and ReAct behavior on 10 static tasks and 10 feedback-dependent tasks.

title: Chapter 11, ReAct: 11.18 Chapter 11 checklist
text: - ReAct alternates decisions, actions, and observations. - Its value comes from new feedback that can change later decisions. - The harness needs observable actions, observations, and state transitions; reasoning text, whether ReAct thoughts or hidden reasoning, is optional rather than an interface. - A structurally valid loop can still ignore evidence or fail to make progress. - Iterative reasoning adds model calls, cost, latency, and possible failure trajectories. - Reasoning architectures should be tested against simpler baselines.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.1 Reacting one step at a time
text: Chapter 11's ReAct agent chooses the next action after observing the current state. This is powerful when new information arrives continually. But purely local decisions can miss dependencies that are visible from the start. Goal: Prepare a short comparison of products A and B. Possible local behavior: search A write about A search B discover comparison requires same-year data search A again rewrite A compare Nothing here is necessarily wrong. The agent simply committed to work before considering the structure of the whole task.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.2 Planning introduces an intermediate representation
text: A planner converts a goal into an intended sequence or dependency structure before execution. Figure: A planner turns the goal into an explicit plan of ordered steps before execution begins. The plan is not the work itself. It is a representation of expected future work. Key distinction Planning decides an intended path. Execution discovers whether that path actually works.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.3 Why plan?
text: Potential benefit | Mechanism Dependency awareness | Identify which steps require outputs from earlier steps Coverage | Represent major subtasks before execution begins Resource allocation | Decide which tools or specialists are needed Parallelization | Identify independent work that can run concurrently Progress tracking | Compare completed work with intended work Reduced myopia | Avoid repeatedly optimizing only the immediate next step These benefits are hypotheses. Planning also consumes model calls and can anchor execution to incorrect assumptions. Experiment 23 — Planning. Use a task with an explicit dependency: Goal: Find the price of 3 units of product A, find the price of 2 units of product B, then compute the total. The plan below is written by hand, standing in for a planner's output. Each step names a tool, its arguments, and where to store the result. The executor fills placeholders such as A from the state built by earlier steps. The same file also runs a second plan, discussed in the next section. Output: plan: valid, executing lookup_price('product': 'A') -> A = 10 lookup_price('product': 'B') -> B = 7 calculator('expression': '3*10 + 2*7') -> total = 44 total = 44 bad plan: rejected before execution: ["step 3: no tool 'currency_converter'"] The plan makes the dependency explicit: the calculator step cannot even be formatted until both prices are in the state. The important contribution is coordination, not extra prose about reasoning.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.4 A plan can be wrong before execution starts
text: Now give the planner an unavailable capability: 1. lookup A 2. lookup B 3. call currency_converter 4. calculate total But the agent has no currency converter and all prices already share a currency. The plan contains unnecessary or impossible work. This is the second plan in Experiment 23; it is rejected before any step runs. Failure mode Planning can move errors earlier without removing them. A plan should therefore be validated against available capabilities, permissions, budgets, and known constraints before execution.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.5 Plan validation
text: Experiment 23 checks only that each tool exists. Permissions and budgets follow the same shape: collect every problem and return it, rather than relying on assert, which Python removes when run with -O. Validation cannot prove the plan will succeed. It can reject plans that are already inconsistent with the system's known boundaries.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.6 Plans encode assumptions
text:
Every future step assumes something about the state that will exist when that step executes. Plan: 1. Download report. 2. Parse PDF. 3. Extract revenue. Hidden assumptions:
- report exists
- download succeeds
- file is a PDF
- PDF is readable
- revenue is present Execution tests those assumptions against reality. This leads to the chapter's central principle: Chapter principle A plan is a hypothesis about the future.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.7 Plan-and-execute (part 1 of 2)
text: A plan-and-execute architecture separates the planning decision from the execution loop. Figure: Plan-and-execute separates the planning decision from the execution loop. This separation can make behavior easier to inspect. It also creates a new failure mode: the executor may continue obeying a plan after the world has changed. Experiment 24 — Plan, execute, replan. Consider a travel-like toy task with two routes: Goal: Reach destination D. Initial state: Route A is shortest. Route B is longer. Plan: 1. take Route A 2. continue to D After the first decision, the environment reports: OBSERVATION: Route A is blocked. We can now compare three architectures. Architecture A — Purely reactive. The reactive agent sees the blockage and chooses Route B. It pays no up-front planning cost but reasons locally at every step. Architecture B — Fixed plan-first. If the executor obeys the original plan, it fails when the assumption behind the plan becomes false. With retries, it keeps attempting Route A until its action budget runs out. Failure mode Plan obedience can become a control defect when observations invalidate plan assumptions. Architecture C — Plan + replan. The initial plan supplies global structure. Feedback tests the plan. Replanning occurs only when the observed state makes the current plan unsuitable. Figure: Replanning: an observation invalidates the initial route, and a new plan is made from what is now known. Experiment 24 runs all three controllers against the same environment. Route A is blocked in the world, but none of the controllers knows that at the start. Each controller gets at most four actions. Output: reactive: success=True plans=0 actions=3 wasted=1 take A -> Route A is blocked take B -> on Route B continue D -> arrived at D plan-first: success=False plans=1 actions=4 wasted=4 take A -> Route A is blocked take A -> Route A is blocked take A -> Route A is blocked take A -> Route A is blocked plan+replan: success=True plans=2 actions=3 wasted=1 take A -> Route A is blocked take B -> on Route B continue D -> arrived at D

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.7 Plan-and-execute (part 2 of 2)
text: Plan-first spends its whole action budget on the blocked route. Reactive and plan-plus-replan both recover after one wasted action. In this toy, the reactive controller does as well as plan-plus-replan: the plan contains only one real decision, so global structure buys nothing. Planning earns its cost when a task has dependencies that local decisions would discover too late, as in Experiment 23.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.8 Replanning should have a trigger
text: Replanning after every step collapses toward reactive reasoning with extra overhead. Never replanning makes the plan brittle. A useful architecture defines explicit triggers. Trigger | Example Failed action | API/tool step could not complete Invalidated assumption | Required file does not exist New constraint | Budget reduced during execution Goal change | User modifies requested output No progress | Repeated actions do not advance state Materially better path | New evidence makes another route preferable The trigger itself can be deterministic, model-assisted, or hybrid.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.9 Plan granularity
text: Plans can be too coarse or too detailed. Too coarse: 1. Solve the problem. Too detailed: 1. Open search. 2. Type first word. 3. Type second word. 4. Press enter. ... Useful: 1. Gather evidence. 2. Verify evidence. 3. Calculate result. 4. Produce answer. Good granularity exposes meaningful dependencies without precommitting to every low-level action.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.10 Plans can be partial
text: An agent does not always need a complete path to the goal. It can plan only until the next major uncertainty. Plan until uncertainty: 1. retrieve candidate policies 2. identify current authoritative policy STOP PLANNING HERE 3. decide next phase using what was found Partial planning combines global structure where the environment is predictable with reactive control where uncertainty is high.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.11 Planning and the least-autonomy principle
text: Planning is another place to allocate control deliberately. Deterministic dependencies need not be rediscovered by a model. Figure: Known dependencies are fixed in code; only uncertain choices are left to the model. A hybrid planner can encode stable structure in software while delegating uncertain subtask selection to the model.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.12 How should we compare the three architectures?
text: Metric | Reactive | Plan-first | Plan + replan Task success | yes | no | yes Plans made | 0 | 1 | 2 Actions | 3 | 4 (budget) | 3 Wasted actions | 1 | 4 | 1 Decision cost | One decision per step | One plan up front | One plan, plus one per trigger Recovery after change | Immediate, local | None | At the trigger The first four rows are Experiment 24's results; the last two describe what to expect and measure on real tasks, together with tokens, cost, and latency. The most revealing benchmark contains both stable tasks and tasks where an assumption is deliberately invalidated during execution.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.13 Planning quality $\neq$ execution quality
text: A perfect plan can fail because a tool fails. A mediocre plan can succeed because the executor adapts. We therefore need separate measurements. Plan quality: coverage valid dependencies feasibility estimated efficiency Execution quality: step success observation use recovery final task success Key distinction Planning quality ≠ execution quality.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.14 More planning $\neq$ better performance
text: A trivial task does not need a ten-step plan. A volatile environment may invalidate detailed plans quickly. A highly constrained workflow may already encode the optimal sequence. Part III principle Reasoning effort must earn its cost. Planning should be evaluated by the improvement it creates in task performance, coordination, or resource use—not by the sophistication of the generated plan.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.15 Bridge to Chapter 13
text: Planning asks whether we should think about future actions before executing them. But agents can also inspect what they have already produced. Suppose an agent completes a draft. Should it immediately return the result, or should it critique the draft and attempt an improvement? Does letting an agent criticize itself actually improve its answers? That is the question of Chapter 13: Reflection.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.16 Exercises
text: - Take a task with three dependent subtasks. Draw its dependency graph before writing a linear plan. - Extend validate in Experiment 23 so that it also rejects a plan whose estimated cost exceeds a remaining budget. Give each tool an estimated cost. - Design a task where a detailed plan becomes obsolete after the first observation. What replanning trigger should fire? - Give an example where partial planning is preferable to a complete plan. - Design a benchmark with 10 stable and 10 dynamically disrupted tasks comparing reactive, plan-first, and plan-plus-replan architectures.

title: Chapter 12, Planning: 12.17 Chapter 12 checklist
text: - Planning creates an intermediate representation of intended future work. - Plans can expose dependencies, coverage, and opportunities for coordination. - A plan should be validated against known capabilities and constraints. - Execution tests the assumptions embedded in a plan. - Replanning needs an explicit trigger; always replanning can waste resources. - Planning quality and execution quality should be measured separately. - More planning is not automatically better performance.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.1 The appealing idea
text: Suppose a model produces a draft answer. Instead of returning it immediately, we ask a model to inspect the draft for defects and then produce a revision. Figure: The reflection idea: a draft is critiqued and then revised before it is returned. This pattern is often called reflection, self-critique, critique-and-revise, or iterative refinement. Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) applies it to a single answer. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) stores verbal reflections on failed attempts, usually prompted by environment feedback such as failing tests, and uses them in the next attempt. The intuition is attractive: a second pass may notice something the first pass missed. But a second model call is not automatically a second source of truth. Huang et al. (2024) found that when models revise their reasoning answers without external feedback, accuracy often fails to improve and sometimes drops.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.2 Reflection creates another decision-maker
text: A critic can detect an error. It can also invent one. Draft: correct Critic: "This is wrong because..." Revision: now incorrect First principle Reflection adds another probabilistic component. Its errors must be measured just like the errors of the original generator.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.3 The smallest reflection loop
text: The architecture is simple. The evaluation is not. We need to compare the revision with the original draft rather than assuming revision implies improvement. Experiment 25 — Reflection. Use a task with an objective check: Task: Calculate 17 * 6. Script the initial draft incorrectly. The critic identifies the defect, and the revision applies the correction: DRAFT: 17 * 6 = 96 CRITIQUE: The multiplication is incorrect. 17 * 6 = 102. REVISION: 17 * 6 = 102 In this case reflection helps. But the interesting experiment begins when the initial draft is already correct, or when the critic is wrong. The experiment therefore runs two scripted critics, a good one and a bad one, against a wrong draft (96) and a correct draft (102). It uses two revision policies: always applies every critique, while verified applies a critique only when a calculator confirms the proposed value. Output: draft critic policy revision outcome 96 good always 102 improvement 102 good always 102 preserved 96 bad always 112 no useful repair 102 bad always 112 REGRESSION always: improvements=1 regressions=1 96 good verified 102 improvement 102 good verified 102 preserved 96 bad verified 96 no useful repair 102 bad verified 102 preserved verified: improvements=1 regressions=0 With the always policy, the bad critic turns the correct draft into 112: a regression. The verified policy keeps the improvement and removes the regression, because the calculator rejects the invented defect. It cannot rescue the wrong draft when the only critique on offer is also wrong.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.4 Deliberately use a bad critic
text: DRAFT: 17 * 6 = 102 BAD CRITIQUE: The answer should be 112. REVISION: 17 * 6 = 112 The architecture performed exactly as designed: draft, critique, revise. The result became worse. Failure mode A revision loop can convert a correct answer into an incorrect one. This is the core reason reflection must be evaluated as a transformation, not treated as a virtue.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.5 Improvement is a delta
text: For tasks with an evaluator, define quality before and after reflection. Then reflection outcomes fall into four useful categories. Draft | Revision | Outcome Wrong | Correct | Improvement Wrong | Still wrong | No useful repair Correct | Still correct | Preserved Correct | Wrong | Regression Experiment 25's output contains all four outcomes. A benchmark should report regressions explicitly. Average final accuracy can hide how often reflection damages already-correct outputs.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.6 The critic needs evidence
text: Criticism is most useful when it can compare the draft against something beyond its own unsupported opinion. Critic signal | Example Executable test | Does the code pass? Ground truth | Does the numeric answer equal 102? Retrieved evidence | Is the claim supported by the source? Schema / rule | Does output satisfy required constraints? Independent model judgment | Does another model detect a defect? The signals differ in reliability. An executable unit test is not equivalent to an unconstrained model saying "I think this could be better."

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.7 Critique $\neq$ verification
text: A critique may provide a hypothesis about a defect. Verification establishes whether the defect actually exists using an appropriate check. Figure: A critique proposes a possible defect; verification checks it. Key distinction Critique proposes defects. Verification tests them.
