title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.8 Conditional reflection
text: If reflection can regress correct outputs, do not necessarily revise every answer. This architecture introduces two gates: whether reflection is worth invoking, and whether the critique is credible enough to justify a change. The verified_revise function in Experiment 25 is the second gate, with a calculator deciding whether the critique is supported.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.9 When should reflection trigger?
text: Trigger | Example Low confidence / uncertainty | Evidence conflicts Failed deterministic check | Unit test fails High-risk output | Financial action requires review Constraint violation | Answer exceeds required format Novel or difficult task | No known deterministic path Evaluator disagreement | Two checks produce different conclusions The trigger can save cost on easy tasks and reduce unnecessary opportunities for regression.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.10 Separate generator and critic?
text: The same model can draft and critique. A different model or prompt can also be used. Neither design guarantees independence. Figure: Three ways to pair a generator with a critic; none guarantees independence on its own. The important variable is not merely whether model names differ. It is whether the evaluator brings useful information or error diversity to the decision.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.11 Repeated reflection can drift
text: Figure: Repeated critique rounds produce a chain of drafts that can drift. Repeated refinement may improve a difficult answer, but it can also introduce stylistic churn, unsupported changes, and escalating cost. The system needs a stopping rule. Control principle Reflection is a loop, so it needs the same budgets and stopping discipline as every other agent loop.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.12 Stopping reflection
text: Stop condition | Example Verifier passes | All tests pass No material critique | Critic finds no supported defect No improvement | Score fails to improve Iteration budget | Maximum two revisions Cost/time budget | Reflection budget exhausted Human escalation | High-risk disagreement remains A useful reflection architecture specifies the stopping policy before the loop begins.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.13 Reflection over actions, not only answers
text: An agent can reflect on a trajectory as well as a final response. Figure: Reflection over an observed trajectory rather than only the final answer. This begins to connect reflection with procedural memory and later self-improvement. But the same caution applies: a lesson derived from one episode may overgeneralize.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.14 Reflection has a cost profile
text: A draft-only system may require one model call. A critique-and-revise system may require three. Draft only: 1 model call Reflection: draft + critique + revision ≈ 3 model calls Actual token use depends on the implementation, but the direction is clear: reflection spends resources. The quality gain must justify them.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.15 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Draft score | How good was the original output? Revision score | How good was the revised output? Improvement rate | How often did reflection repair a defect? Regression rate | How often did reflection damage a correct output? Critic precision | When critic claimed a defect, how often was it real? Critic recall | How many real defects did critic detect? Calls / tokens / cost | What did reflection consume? Latency | How much time did the extra passes add? Critic precision is particularly important for conditional revision. A critic that flags everything may have high recall but cause unnecessary changes.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.16 Baselines matter
text: Reflection should be compared with alternatives that spend similar resources. Figure: Baselines that spend similar resources, compared with reflection. If three model calls are available, critique-and-revise is not the only way to spend them. Architecture evaluation should compare resource-equivalent alternatives where practical.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.17 More reasoning $\neq$ better answers
text: Part III principle More reasoning ≠ better answers. Additional reasoning is valuable only when it adds information, catches defects, improves search, or otherwise changes outcomes enough to justify its cost and risk. Reflection makes this principle unusually visible because the architecture can directly turn a correct output into an incorrect one.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.18 Reflection as feedback
text: Figure: Reflection as feedback: an evaluator critiques each draft, and the revision becomes the next draft. Like ReAct, reflection is a feedback architecture. The difference is what is being observed: ReAct typically incorporates consequences from the environment; reflection incorporates evaluation of the agent's own intermediate output. The line blurs in practice: Reflexion reflects on environment feedback, and the verified policy in Experiment 25 brings a tool into the critique.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.19 Bridge to Chapter 14
text: Reflection explores one alternative: revise the current candidate. But some tasks benefit from considering several candidate solutions before committing to one. When is it worth searching over multiple possible reasoning paths? That leads to tree reasoning and search.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.20 Live run: Intrinsic self-critique
text: A small model solves thirty multi-step word problems, then is asked to review its own answer with no external feedback: no calculator, no test, no reference. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Correct before review | 28/30 | 0.93 | [0.79, 0.98] Correct after review | 30/30 | 1.00 | [0.89, 1.00] Wrong to right (repaired) | 2/30 | 0.07 | [0.02, 0.21] Right to wrong (regressed) | 0/30 | 0.00 | [0.00, 0.11] The model was right first time on 28 problems. Review repaired both wrong answers and broke none. That is better than the reasoning results reported by Huang et al., but two repairs is thin evidence: the intervals are wide, and the problems are short arithmetic where errors are easy to spot on a second read. Run the same protocol on your own task before relying on unverified reflection, and keep counting regressions. Model gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 60 requests, 6,707 input and 5,506 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch13_self_critique (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.21 Exercises
text: - Create five arithmetic drafts: three wrong and two correct. Script a critic that catches some errors but invents one defect. Calculate improvement and regression rates. - Design a reflection trigger based on a deterministic validator rather than model confidence. - Give an example where critique should be verified with a tool before revision. - Compare three calls spent on draft-critique-revise with three independent candidate answers plus selection. What would you measure? - Design a stopping rule for code reflection where unit tests provide objective feedback.

title: Chapter 13, Reflection: 13.22 Chapter 13 checklist
text: - Reflection adds a critic and revision stage; it does not guarantee improvement. - A critic is a fallible component whose precision and recall can be measured. - Critique proposes a defect; verification tests whether the defect is real. - Reflection can regress already-correct outputs. - Conditional reflection can gate expensive or risky revision. - Reflection loops need budgets and stopping conditions. - Resource-equivalent baselines should be compared where practical.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.1 One path is a commitment
text: ReAct chooses a next action and continues. Planning proposes an intended path. Reflection revises a candidate. All three can still spend most of their computation on one evolving trajectory. Figure: A single trajectory commits to one path from start to answer. But some problems contain several plausible next moves. Choosing the first one may commit the system to a poor branch before enough evidence exists to distinguish alternatives.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.2 Search delays commitment
text: Figure: Search delays commitment by keeping several branches open before choosing one. A search architecture generates alternatives, evaluates them, and allocates more computation to promising candidates. The model can participate in generation, evaluation, or both. Operational definition Tree reasoning is search over intermediate candidate states or actions, guided by an evaluator and constrained by a budget. Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) applies this idea to language-model reasoning. The model proposes intermediate "thoughts" and rates them, and a breadth-first or depth-first search decides which ones to extend. Language Agent Tree Search (Zhou et al., 2024) applies Monte Carlo tree search to agent actions, using environment feedback as part of the evaluation.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.3 Four components
text: Component | Question State | What does a partial solution contain? Generator | What alternatives can be produced from this state? Evaluator | Which alternatives appear promising? Search policy | Which candidate should receive the next unit of computation? Without these four pieces, and a budget that bounds them, "think of several possibilities" is not yet an engineered search procedure.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.4 The smallest tree search (part 1 of 2)
text: Two details matter. The selected state is removed from the frontier; otherwise the loop re-expands the same state on every iteration. The goal test runs when a state is selected, so the search returns a verified solution rather than merely the best-scored state. This tiny loop already exposes the central engineering choices: branching factor, evaluator quality, selection policy, stopping rule, and resource budget. Experiment 26 — Tree reasoning. Use a transparent toy problem: transform 2 into 13 using exactly two operations. Available operations are +3, 2, and +9. Start: 2 Candidate first moves: A: 2 + 3 = 5 B: 2 * 2 = 4 C: 2 + 9 = 11 A greedy strategy that scores states only by immediate closeness to 13 prefers 11. But with one operation remaining, 11 cannot reach 13 using the available operations. From 11: 11 + 3 = 14 11 * 2 = 22 11 + 9 = 20 Another branch succeeds: 2 * 2 = 4 4 + 9 = 13 The example is intentionally simple: it shows why evaluating only the current state can differ from evaluating the future potential of a branch. The experiment runs beam search (Section ) with widths 1, 2, and 3 under two evaluators. closeness scores a state by its immediate distance to 13. lookahead scores it by the best closeness still reachable in the remaining steps. Output: first moves scored by closeness: 2 +3 = 5 score -8 2 *2 = 4 score -9 2 +9 = 11 score -2 closeness width 1: expansions=2 solution=None closeness width 2: expansions=3 solution=None closeness width 3: expansions=4 solution=2 *2 +9 = 13 lookahead width 1: expansions=2 solution=2 *2 +9 = 13 lookahead width 2: expansions=3 solution=2 *2 +9 = 13 lookahead width 3: expansions=4 solution=2 *2 +9 = 13

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.4 The smallest tree search (part 2 of 2)
text: With the closeness heuristic, widths 1 and 2 both fail: width 2 keeps 11 and 5 and still prunes 4. Only width 3 finds 2 × 2 + 9 = 13, and in this tree width 3 is exhaustive search. The look-ahead evaluator lets even width 1 succeed. It is not free: it quietly expands the rest of the tree for every candidate it scores, which is affordable only because this tree is tiny. Better evaluation often means spending computation inside the evaluator instead of the search.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.5 Breadth creates opportunity---and cost
text: If every state produces b alternatives and search explores depth d, the number of candidate nodes can grow rapidly. depth 0: 1 depth 1: b depth 2: b^2 depth 3: b^3 ... Not every implementation expands a complete tree, but branching makes resource growth a first-class design concern. Control principle Search requires a budget because possibility spaces can grow faster than useful evidence.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.6 Search needs pruning
text: Figure: Pruning a search: generate many candidates, score them, and expand only the best. Pruning concentrates computation. It also creates the risk of deleting the branch that would eventually have produced the best answer.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.7 Deliberately break the evaluator
text: Return to the toy problem. Suppose the evaluator rewards immediate numerical closeness to 13. score(5) = -8 score(4) = -9 score(11) = -2 # looks best If the search keeps only the top branch, it selects 11 and prunes 4—the branch that can actually reach the goal. Keeping the top two does not help either: 4 has the worst score, so it is still the branch that gets pruned. Failure mode A misleading evaluator can make search systematically worse by spending more computation on the wrong branches.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.8 Search quality depends on generation, evaluation, and allocation
text: More branches do not help if scoring cannot distinguish useful from useless candidates. Conversely, an excellent evaluator cannot recover a branch that was never generated. Figure: Useful search needs all three factors: candidate generation, evaluator discrimination and search allocation. This mirrors retrieval: recall and ranking are separate. Search must first produce viable alternatives, then identify which deserve further work.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.9 Evaluators come in different strengths
text: Evaluator | Example | Typical property Exact verifier | Does equation equal 13? | Strong when available Constraint check | Does candidate violate a rule? | Good for pruning Heuristic | Distance from target | Cheap but imperfect Simulation/tool | Run candidate and observe result | Grounded but costly Model judge | Rate candidate quality | Flexible but fallible The search policy should reflect evaluator reliability. Aggressive pruning is safer with strong verification than with a noisy heuristic.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.10 Best-of-N is search too
text: A tree is not required for search. Generate several complete candidates and select the best: Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) is a close relative: it samples several reasoning paths and takes a majority vote over their final answers instead of scoring them. Best-of-N searches at the answer level. Tree reasoning searches at intermediate states. Both trade additional computation for a chance to find a better candidate.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.11 Beam search
text: A simple compromise keeps a fixed number of promising partial candidates at each depth. The beam width controls exploration. Width 1 behaves like greedy search. Larger widths preserve more alternatives but consume more resources.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.12 Search can diversify deliberately
text: If all generated candidates are nearly identical, branching provides little value. Weak diversity: A: search web for X B: search web for X C: search web for X Useful diversity: A: retrieve primary source B: compute from raw data C: inspect independent reference Candidate diversity matters when different paths expose different evidence or failure modes.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.13 Search over actions vs search over reasoning artifacts
text: Search space | Candidate example Actions | Which tool should be called next? Plans | Which sequence of subtasks should be attempted? Answers | Which complete response is best? Code patches | Which modification should be tested? Evidence sets | Which combination of sources supports the claim? The same search abstraction can therefore appear in planning, coding agents, retrieval, and multi-agent systems.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.14 Search should exploit external feedback
text: A powerful search architecture can test candidates against the environment rather than asking a model to judge everything internally. Figure: Search driven by external feedback: each candidate patch is tested, and the pass or fail result informs the search decision. External feedback often supplies a stronger evaluation signal than unsupported self-scoring.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.15 Stopping search
text: Stop condition | Example Verified solution | All tests pass Search budget | 20 node expansions Depth limit | Maximum 5 steps Cost limit | $0.50 remaining Time limit | 30 seconds No improvement | Best score unchanged for 3 expansions Sufficient confidence | Candidate exceeds acceptance threshold Without stopping conditions, tree reasoning turns uncertainty into an unbounded compute request.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.16 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Task success | Did search find a correct/acceptable solution? Pass@N / success@N | Was a valid solution generated among N candidates? Selection accuracy | Did evaluator choose the best available candidate? Nodes expanded | How much search was performed? Branching / depth | How broad and deep was exploration? Pruning errors | Were promising branches discarded? Calls / tokens / cost | What resources did search consume? Latency | How long did exploration take? Final success alone cannot distinguish weak generation from weak evaluation. Instrument the search process.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.17 Compare against simpler baselines
text: Baseline A: single candidate Baseline B: reflection Baseline C: best-of-N Baseline D: tree search If best-of-3 achieves the same quality as a complex tree, the simpler architecture may be preferable. If a deterministic verifier can repair a single candidate, search may be unnecessary.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.18 Search is not free intelligence
text: Part III principle More search ≠ better answers. Search helps when useful alternatives exist, they can be generated, and an evaluator can discriminate among them. Search can amplify both competence and evaluator bias. A bad scoring function does not merely make one bad decision; it can steer an entire compute budget toward the wrong region of the solution space.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.19 A useful mental model
text: Figure: Search as a loop of generation, evaluation, and allocation under a compute budget. Tree reasoning is fundamentally resource allocation under uncertainty. The search policy decides where the next unit of computation is most likely to be useful.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.20 Bridge to Chapter 15
text: Search allocates computation among candidate paths within a task. But agentic systems also need to allocate whole tasks among models, tools, workflows, or specialists. Which path—or which model—should handle this task? That leads to routing.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.21 Exercises
text: - Modify the arithmetic tree so a greedy heuristic succeeds. Then change one operation so the same heuristic fails. - Experiment 26 counts expansions but not evaluator work. Count the states that the look-ahead evaluator visits, and compare the total with exhaustive search. - Design a search where an exact verifier is available only at terminal states. What heuristic would you use for partial states? - Give an example where best-of-N is preferable to tree search, and another where intermediate-state search is necessary. - Design an evaluator benchmark that separates candidate-generation recall from selection accuracy.

title: Chapter 14, Search and Tree Reasoning: 14.22 Chapter 14 checklist
text: - Search delays commitment by maintaining multiple candidate paths. - A search system needs a state, a generator, an evaluator, and a search policy, all bounded by a budget. - More candidates help only if viable alternatives are generated and can be evaluated. - Pruning saves resources but can discard the eventual best branch. - Best-of-N is a simple form of search; trees search intermediate states. - External verification can be stronger than model-only scoring. - Search should be compared with simpler, resource-aware baselines.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.1 Not every task should follow the same path
text: A system may have several ways to handle a request. Arithmetic can go to a calculator. Policy questions can go to retrieval. A document-generation request can enter a writing workflow. A difficult reasoning problem may justify a stronger model. Figure: A router sends each request to the capability best suited to handle it. Routing inserts a decision before execution: which path should receive this task?

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.2 Routing is a policy
text: A router maps observable task features and system state to a destination. The policy may be deterministic, model-based, learned from data, or hybrid. Whatever its implementation, the engineering contract is the same: choose a destination from an allowed set. Operational definition Routing is the controlled allocation of a task to one of several execution paths.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.3 Why route?
text: Reason | Example Specialization | Send arithmetic to calculator Quality | Escalate difficult task to stronger model Cost | Use cheaper model for easy requests Latency | Prefer fast path when quality is sufficient Risk | Route high-risk action to approval workflow Availability | Fallback when preferred service is unavailable Routing is therefore not merely classification. The destination changes the capabilities, resources, and risk profile of the system. Experiment 27 — Task routing. Start with three transparent task classes. The experiment scores three routers on five labeled tasks. rule_router is a minimal deterministic router. misroute sends everything to the writing workflow. SEMANTIC is a scripted stand-in for a model-based router. Each misroute is weighted by what it costs for that kind of task. Output: rules: 'Calculate 3 + 4' -> write (should be math) rules: accuracy 4/5, misroute cost 1 always-write: 'calculate 17 * 6' -> write (should be math) always-write: 'what is refund policy?' -> write (should be policy) always-write: 'Calculate 3 + 4' -> write (should be math) always-write: 'is the travel policy current?' -> write (should be policy) always-write: accuracy 1/5, misroute cost 12 semantic: 'what is refund policy?' -> write (should be policy) semantic: accuracy 4/5, misroute cost 5 The point is not that keyword routing is sophisticated. It exposes the boundary cleanly: routing chooses; the destination executes. The rule router fails on a capitalised request, because startswith is case-sensitive. The rule router and the semantic router have the same accuracy, but their errors cost 1 and 5, as the next sections explain.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.4 Deliberately misroute a task
text: Figure: A deliberate misroute: an arithmetic request sent to the writing workflow. The writing workflow may still produce an answer, but it has received a task for which another route is more reliable and efficient. The always-write run in Experiment 27 does this to every task and scores 1 of 5. Failure mode A valid downstream component can still be the wrong component for the task.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.5 Router accuracy is not enough
text: Suppose a router achieves 95% classification accuracy. That sounds strong, but the remaining 5% may contain the most expensive mistakes. Figure: Routing errors differ in cost: a low-cost misroute versus a high-cost one. Routing errors have asymmetric consequences. A useful evaluation therefore weights mistakes by downstream impact, not merely count. In Experiment 27, two routers with identical accuracy differ fivefold in misroute cost.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.6 A routing confusion matrix
text: Actual task | Routed to | Result Math | Calculator | Correct specialization Math | Writer | Possible quality/cost loss Policy | Retriever | Grounded path Policy | Writer | Possible unsupported answer High-risk action | Approval | Controlled High-risk action | Autonomous path | Potentially severe The same router accuracy can correspond to very different system risk depending on which cells contain the errors.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.7 Confidence and fallback
text: A router need not force a destination when evidence is weak. Fallback might ask for clarification, use a general-purpose route, invoke a stronger classifier, or require human review. Confidence itself must be calibrated before it is trusted as a probability.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.8 Deterministic rules and model routers
text: Router | Strength | Weakness Rules | Predictable, cheap, auditable | Brittle on semantic variation Small classifier | Fast, trainable | Needs labels and monitoring LLM router | Flexible semantic interpretation | Cost, latency, stochastic errors Hybrid | Rules for hard boundaries; model for ambiguity | More engineering complexity Stable safety boundaries are often better expressed deterministically. Semantic ambiguity is where a model router may add value.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.9 Routing can depend on system state
text: The same task may take a different route depending on budgets, availability, permissions, or deadlines. Order matters. The risk check comes first, so that an outage or a low budget can never send a high-risk task down an unreviewed path. Routing is therefore a control policy over both the task and the current operating state. Experiment 28 — Model routing. Now give the system two model classes. Assume, for the experiment, that easy tasks are handled adequately by FAST while difficult tasks need STRONG. call_model encodes that assumption: FAST answers hard tasks wrongly. Each task carries a difficulty label that only the oracle may read. The deployable router, choose_model, must predict difficulty from an observable feature; here it treats long expressions as hard. The cascade (Section ) tries FAST first and escalates when an exact verifier rejects the answer. Output: always fast solved 2/5 cost 5 always strong solved 5/5 cost 50 oracle solved 5/5 cost 32 length router solved 4/5 cost 23 cheap-first cascade solved 5/5 cost 35 Every strategy tries to preserve quality while avoiding the cost and latency of using the strongest model for every request. The following sections read this table row by row.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.10 The oracle baseline
text: For a controlled benchmark, imagine an oracle that already knows which model is sufficient for every task. Figure: The oracle baseline knows which model is sufficient for each task. The oracle is not deployable; it provides an upper-bound routing reference. In Experiment 28 it solves all five tasks for 32 units, against 50 for always-strong. The real router must infer task difficulty from observable features.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.11 Deliberately underestimate difficulty
text: Figure: Underestimated difficulty: the router sends a hard task to the fast model, which fails. In Experiment 28, 99 * 99 is short, so the length router predicts "easy" and FAST gets it wrong: 4 of 5 solved for 23 units. This error saves resources but loses task quality. The opposite error sends an easy task to STRONG: quality may remain high, but cost and latency increase. Asymmetric model-routing errors Under-routing risks quality. Over-routing risks resources.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.12 Escalation after failure
text: A router can make an initial cheap attempt and escalate only when a verifier detects failure. This changes the routing problem. Instead of predicting difficulty perfectly in advance, the system uses observed performance as feedback.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.13 Cascade routing
text: Figure: Cascade routing: try the cheap, fast option first and escalate to a stronger one only when verification fails. Cascades are attractive when verification is reliable and many tasks can be solved cheaply. They are dangerous when failure cannot be detected reliably. In Experiment 28 the cascade solves all five tasks for 35 units. That is more than the oracle, because every hard task pays for a failed FAST attempt first, but it needs no advance prediction of difficulty. It relies on an exact verifier, which arithmetic allows and most real tasks do not.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.14 The verifier becomes part of the router
text: In an escalation architecture, routing quality depends on both the first model and the verifier. Effective routing = initial allocation + failure detection + escalation policy A false pass returns a bad cheap answer. A false failure escalates unnecessarily. Once again, the evaluator is a critical component.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.15 Optimize the system, not the router
text: A router exists to improve end-to-end outcomes. Its own classification score is secondary. Figure: A router is judged by the end-to-end outcome, not by its own classification score. Key distinction Router accuracy ≠ system quality. The best router is the one that produces the best quality-cost-latency-risk trade-off for the whole system.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.16 A simple routing objective
text: Do not force all dimensions into a universal scalar. But a deployment policy can express constraints explicitly. maximize task success subject to: average cost <= budget p95 latency <= target high-risk tasks require approved route This framing is often more useful than “maximize router accuracy.” It connects routing directly to operational objectives.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.17 Route descriptions are interfaces
text: Model-based routers need clear descriptions of available destinations, just as tool-calling models need clear tool descriptions. calculator: Use for deterministic arithmetic. policy_retrieval: Use for questions requiring authoritative policy evidence. writer: Use for drafting or rewriting text. Overlapping or vague route descriptions create routing ambiguity. Interface design therefore affects router performance.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.18 Hierarchical routing
text: Large systems need not choose among dozens of destinations in one decision. Figure: Hierarchical routing: a first decision picks a category, and a second picks the destination within it. Hierarchies can simplify each decision but add extra routing stages and new failure points.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.19 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question End-to-end success | Did the chosen path solve the task? Route accuracy | Did router choose intended destination? Cost-weighted error | How expensive were misroutes? Risk-weighted error | How severe were unsafe misroutes? Escalation rate | How often did cheap path need stronger path? False pass / false fail | Did verifier make cascade mistakes? Cost | What did routing save or add? Latency | What delay did routing/escalation create? For model routing, also report quality by task difficulty. Average performance can hide systematic under-routing of the hardest tasks.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.20 Compare against simple baselines
text: Baseline A: always use one general route Baseline B: always use strongest model Baseline C: deterministic rules Candidate D: model router Candidate E: cheap-first cascade A router earns its complexity only if it improves the operating frontier. If "always strong" meets the budget and latency requirements, routing may be unnecessary. If deterministic rules solve the task classes reliably, a model router may add little.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.21 Routing as resource allocation under uncertainty
text: Search allocated compute among candidate paths. Routing allocates tasks among execution resources. Both make decisions before the final outcome is known. Figure: Routing as resource allocation: a policy maps the observed task and system state to an execution resource. Chapter principle Routing is resource allocation under uncertainty. Judge it by downstream outcomes, not by the sophistication of the router.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.22 Bridge to Chapter 16
text: Routing chooses one path from several alternatives. But sometimes several independent paths should run at the same time. When should an agent do several things in parallel? That leads to parallelism and fan-out/fan-in.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.23 Live run: A cheap-first cascade
text: Thirty word problems. Each model writes an arithmetic expression and the calculator computes its value. The cascade asks the small model twice and escalates to the larger model only when the two values disagree. Measure | Count | Rate | 95% interval Correct, small model only | 26/30 | 0.87 | [0.70, 0.95] Correct, large model only | 29/30 | 0.97 | [0.83, 0.99] Correct, cascade | 29/30 | 0.97 | [0.83, 0.99] Escalated to large model | 7/30 | 0.23 | [0.12, 0.41] Small samples agreed but were wrong | 0/30 | 0.00 | [0.00, 0.11] Small model's stated number matched its own expression | 3/60 | 0.05 | [0.02, 0.14] Large model's stated number matched its own expression | 1/30 | 0.03 | [0.01, 0.17] The cascade matched the larger model's accuracy while sending it under a quarter of the requests, and the agreement check never accepted a wrong answer here. The run also exposed a real failure: both models usually stated a final number that did not equal their own, correct, expression. The first version of this experiment trusted the stated number, so its check failed every time and everything escalated. Letting software do the arithmetic is what made the cheap path usable. Model gpt-5.4-nano-2026-03-17, gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17, run 2026-10-12, 90 requests, 9,264 input and 2,283 output tokens, provider default settings. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals. One recorded run, not a general property of the model. Reproduce with python -m live.ch15_cascade (requires OPENAI_API_KEY; makes paid requests); source and recorded results.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.24 Exercises
text: - Build a rule router for math, retrieval, and writing. Create five ambiguous tasks designed to break the rules. - Add a high-risk action class to Experiment 27 whose correct route is approval, and give its misroutes a large cost. How does the ranking of the routers change? - Make the verifier in Experiment 28 accept one wrong answer (a false pass). How do success and cost change for the cascade? - Define a routing policy as constrained optimization: maximize success subject to a cost and latency budget. - Compare always-strong, rule-based routing, and adaptive model routing on easy and hard task sets.

title: Chapter 15, Routing: 15.25 Chapter 15 checklist
text: - Routing allocates tasks to capabilities, workflows, models, or control paths. - Routing errors can have asymmetric cost and risk. - Router accuracy and end-to-end system quality are different metrics. - Model routing trades quality against cost and latency. - Cascades can replace perfect advance prediction with failure detection and escalation. - Route descriptions are interfaces and affect model-based routing. - Routing should be compared with simple baselines such as always-strong or deterministic rules.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.1 Sequential execution is the default
text: Many agent examples execute one action, wait, observe the result, and then execute the next action. Figure: Sequential execution waits for each task before starting the next. This is necessary when later work depends on earlier results. But if A, B, and C are independent, waiting for each one before starting the next wastes wall-clock time.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.2 Dependency determines parallelizability
text: Figure: Independent tasks can run together; dependent tasks must run in order. The key question is not whether several tasks exist. It is whether one task requires another task's output or side effect before it can proceed. First principle Parallelize independent work. Preserve ordering where dependencies exist. Experiment 29 — Parallel execution. Suppose an agent needs three independent facts from three services. Each call takes two seconds. The experiment simulates the services with asyncio.sleep, scaled so that one simulated second takes 0.01 real seconds, so the waits really do overlap. Elapsed time is read from a simulated clock rather than the wall clock: each call starts at the clock's current value and, when it finishes, advances the clock to its own finish time. The printed times are therefore exact and repeatable. Each fetch must be an async def coroutine: calling ordinary blocking functions inside gather would run them one after another before gather even starts, and gather would then reject their return values because they are not awaitable. Output: sequential: ['fact A', 'fact B', 'fact C'] calls=3 time=6 s concurrent: ['fact A', 'fact B', 'fact C'] calls=3 time=2 s dependency parallelized: RuntimeError('rate not available yet') dependency respected: 90.0 Both versions make three calls; only the elapsed time differs. The exact timing depends on the runtime and services, but the structural benefit is clear: independent waiting can overlap. The last two lines belong to the dependency experiment later in this chapter.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.3 Parallelism does not reduce total work
text: Three calls are still three calls. Parallelism primarily changes elapsed time, not necessarily tokens, API calls, or monetary cost. Sequential: work = A + B + C time ≈ tA + tB + tC Parallel: work = A + B + C time ≈ max(tA, tB, tC) + overhead Key distinction Lower latency ≠ lower compute or cost.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.4 Deliberately parallelize a dependency
text: Now make B depend on A. A: retrieve exchange rate B: convert price using exchange rate Running both at the same time means B begins before its required input exists. Experiment 29 does exactly this: it passes get_exchange_rate() and convert_price(100) to the same gather. The conversion reads the shared rate table before the rate arrives and fails with RuntimeError('rate not available yet'). Awaiting the rate first and converting afterwards returns 90.0. Failure mode Parallel execution can violate causal dependencies. Dependency analysis therefore precedes scheduling.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.5 A task graph makes dependencies visible
text: Figure: A task graph: D depends on A, B and C, so it cannot start until all three finish. A, B, and C can run concurrently. D must wait for all required predecessors. This is a directed acyclic graph when dependencies contain no cycles. The scheduler's job is simple in principle: execute nodes whose dependencies are satisfied.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.6 Concurrency has limits
text: Starting every possible task simultaneously can overwhelm APIs, databases, rate limits, memory, or budgets. Concurrency therefore needs a resource policy, not just an async keyword.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.7 The straggler problem
text: Suppose three branches take 1, 1, and 20 seconds. Figure: The straggler problem: fan-in waits for the slowest branch. If the final result requires all three, latency is dominated by the slowest branch. Parallelism cannot make a required 20-second dependency disappear. Latency principle Parallel latency is often governed by the critical path, not the average branch.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.8 Partial failure
text: Concurrent branches can succeed and fail independently. Figure: Partial failure: concurrent branches succeed or fail independently. The system now needs a policy: fail the whole task, retry B, continue with partial evidence, use a fallback, or return a degraded result. That decision belongs to orchestration, not to concurrency itself. The concurrency primitive you choose sets a default policy, so know what it is. - asyncio.gather(...) raises the first exception to the caller but does not cancel the other awaitables; they keep running, and their results are lost to the caller. - asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) returns each exception in place of its result, so the fan-in can see exactly which branch failed. - asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) cancels the remaining tasks when one fails and raises an ExceptionGroup: fail-fast as a structural default. - asyncio.timeout or asyncio.wait_for turns an unbounded wait into a timeout you can handle.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.9 Fan-out/fan-in
text: Parallel execution becomes an agentic pattern when one task is deliberately decomposed into several branches and their outputs are recombined. Figure: Fan-out/fan-in: one input is split into parallel branches whose outputs are recombined. Fan-out creates independent or semi-independent work. Fan-in aggregates the results. Experiment 30 — Fan-out/fan-in. Ask three workers to inspect the same proposal from different perspectives, then compare two fan-in policies on the same branch results. The bad policy over-summarizes: it keeps only issues that at least two reviewers raised. The complete policy keeps every finding with its reviewer and names any branch that failed. A second run makes the operations reviewer time out; return_exceptions=True turns that failure into a result the fan-in can report. Output: bad fan-in: Proposal looks acceptable. complete fan-in: revise, missing=[] financial: margin assumption unsupported risk: dependency on one supplier operations: timeline infeasible partial failure: incomplete, missing=['operations'] financial: margin assumption unsupported risk: dependency on one supplier The value is not merely speed. The branches intentionally create different evidence or viewpoints that one aggregator can combine, and the aggregator decides whether that evidence survives.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.10 Parallelism vs diversity
text: Pattern | Purpose Parallel execution | Reduce elapsed time for independent work Fan-out by partition | Split a large task into independent pieces Fan-out by perspective | Generate diverse analyses of the same input Fan-in | Combine branch outputs into a final state or decision These motives should not be conflated. Three identical workers may reduce neither latency nor error if they all perform the same unnecessary work.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.11 The aggregator is a critical component
text: In Experiment 30 all three reviewers identify valid issues, but the over-summarizing aggregator drops every one of them because no two reviewers raised the same issue. Financial reviewer: margin assumption unsupported Risk reviewer: dependency on one supplier Operations reviewer: timeline infeasible Bad fan-in: "Proposal looks acceptable." The branches succeeded. The system failed at aggregation. Failure mode Good parallel work can be destroyed by a bad fan-in policy.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.12 Aggregation is not always summarization
text: Fan-in operation | Example Concatenate | Combine independently generated sections Reduce | Sum partial numeric results Vote | Choose majority classification Rank | Select strongest candidate Merge | Combine non-overlapping evidence Judge | Use evaluator to synthesize conflicting outputs The correct aggregation operator depends on what the branches represent.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.13 Conflict at fan-in
text: Parallel branches may disagree. A: approve B: reject C: uncertain A fan-in policy must decide whether to vote, weight by expertise, verify against evidence, escalate to another evaluator, or ask a human. “Combine the answers” is not a sufficient specification.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.14 Shared state creates race conditions
text: Independent branches are easiest when they do not mutate the same state. Shared writes can make outcomes depend on timing. Two threads running worker can both read 0 and both write 1. Writing counter += 1 does not help: it is the same read-modify-write and is not atomic across threads. With asyncio the rule is different but not absent: code between two await points cannot be interleaved, so the race appears whenever a read and its dependent write are separated by an await, such as a tool call. Without appropriate coordination (a lock, a single owner, or an atomic operation), concurrent writes can overwrite or conflict. Agent systems that perform external actions face the same issue with files, tickets, transactions, and messages. State principle Parallel reads are easier than parallel writes.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.15 Side effects need stronger control
text: Running three research calls concurrently is different from running three payment actions concurrently. Safe-ish fan-out: search(source_A) search(source_B) search(source_C) Risky fan-out: send_payment(...) send_payment(...) send_payment(...) Permissions, idempotency, transaction semantics, and approval boundaries become more important as concurrent branches acquire side effects.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.16 Cancellation and early stopping
text: Sometimes one branch makes the remaining work unnecessary. Figure: Early stopping: once branch A finds a verified answer, the still-running branches B and C are cancelled. In asyncio this pattern looks like the following. Cancellation is cooperative: a coroutine stops at its next await, and a remote request that has already been sent may still complete and be billed. Threads cannot be interrupted at all; Future.cancel() in concurrent.futures only succeeds for work that has not started. Early cancellation can save resources, but only when incomplete branches are no longer required for correctness or safety.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.17 Speculative parallelism
text: A system can start several plausible paths before knowing which will be needed, then keep the first acceptable result. Figure: Speculative parallelism keeps the first verified result. This can reduce tail latency at the cost of duplicated work. It is therefore a deliberate exchange of resource efficiency for response time or reliability.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.18 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question Wall-clock latency | Did concurrency reduce elapsed time? Critical-path latency | Which dependency determines completion? Total work | How many calls/tokens/operations were consumed? Branch success | Which branches succeeded or failed? Aggregation quality | Did fan-in preserve useful branch information? Straggler rate | How often did one branch dominate latency? Cancellation savings | How much unnecessary work was avoided? Cost | Did parallelism duplicate expensive work? A speedup number without total work and failure behavior can be misleading.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.19 Compare against sequential baselines
text: Baseline A: sequential execution Candidate B: bounded parallel execution Candidate C: fan-out/fan-in Candidate D: speculative parallelism Use the same underlying work where possible. Otherwise a “parallel” architecture may appear faster simply because it performs a different task.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.20 Amdahl's intuition
text: Only the parallelizable fraction of a workflow can benefit from concurrency. If a long sequential dependency remains, adding workers eventually yields diminishing latency gains. workflow = parallelizable work + unavoidable sequential work Agentic systems are no exception. Architecture diagrams with many branches do not guarantee proportional speedup.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.21 Part III synthesis
text: Part III introduced six ways to allocate reasoning and work. Chapter | Pattern | Core allocation decision 11 | ReAct | When should feedback trigger another action? 12 | Planning | Which future sequence should be attempted? 13 | Reflection | Should an output receive another evaluation/revision? 14 | Search | Which candidate path deserves more compute? 15 | Routing | Which capability/model should receive the task? 16 | Parallelism | Which independent work should run concurrently? They look different, but each pattern allocates model calls, tools, time, and control under uncertainty. Part III conclusion Reasoning architectures are resource-allocation policies. More reasoning, more branches, more planning, or more concurrency are useful only when they improve outcomes enough to justify their costs and failure modes.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.22 From orchestration to multiple agents
text: So far, workers have mostly been functions, tools, or model calls inside one controller. But a worker can itself be an agent with its own context, tools, state, and control loop. What changes when an agent becomes another agent's tool? That opens Part IV — Agents Working Together.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.23 Exercises
text: - Draw a dependency graph with five tasks and identify the maximum set that can run concurrently. - Create three branches with latencies of 1, 3, and 10 seconds. Compare sequential and idealized parallel completion times. - Design a partial-failure policy for three retrieval branches where one source is optional and two are required. - Give an example where the correct fan-in operator is voting, and another where voting would be wrong. - Design a speculative-parallel architecture and state explicitly what resource it trades for lower latency.

title: Chapter 16, Parallelism: 16.24 Chapter 16 checklist
text: - Parallelism is valid only where dependencies permit it. - Concurrency can reduce wall-clock latency without reducing total work. - Critical-path and straggler latency matter. - Fan-out creates branches; fan-in defines how branch outputs become a result. - Aggregation quality must be evaluated separately from branch quality. - Shared writes and side effects require stronger coordination. - Parallel architectures need concurrency limits, failure policies, cancellation, and budgets.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.1 Multi-agent does not require new magic
text: We already know how a controller uses a tool: it selects a named capability, supplies arguments, receives a result, and continues. If another agent can be wrapped behind that same contract, the outer controller does not need a fundamentally new abstraction. Figure: An agent wrapped as a tool keeps the same input-to-output contract as an ordinary function. Core idea From the caller's perspective, an agent can be just another capability.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.2 A minimal specialist agent
text: Expose it to a parent controller: The parent can now choose researcher exactly as it chooses calculator. Experiment 31 — Agent as tool. Give the parent a goal that requires both research and arithmetic. Goal: Find the reported value of X, then calculate X * 1.10. The parent delegates the information subtask: ACTION: researcher(question="What is X?") OBSERVATION: "status": "complete", "answer": "80", "steps_used": 2 Then it uses a deterministic tool: ACTION: calculator(expression="80 * 1.10") OBSERVATION: 88.0 The experiment builds both levels from the Chapter 3 Agent loop. The child ResearchAgent has its own scripted model and its own search tool; the parent's policy reads each observation and decides the next action. The parent passes a step budget into the child, and the child reports a structured status instead of a bare string. The second run gives the child a model that searches forever, which the next sections discuss. Output: cooperative specialist researcher returned: "status": "complete", "answer": "80", "steps_used": 2 parent actions: ['researcher', 'calculator'] hidden child searches: 1 answer: X * 1.10 = 88.0 looping specialist, delegated max_steps=5 researcher returned: "status": "incomplete", "answer": null, "steps_used": 5 parent actions: ['researcher'] hidden child searches: 5 answer: escalate: research incomplete Nothing in the parent loop requires special multi-agent syntax. The specialist is simply an action whose implementation happens to contain another model-driven process.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.3 Encapsulation is the benefit
text: Why not give the parent every tool directly? Sometimes a specialist owns a coherent bundle of context, tools, instructions, and control logic. Figure: A research specialist encapsulates a coherent bundle of tools, rules and control logic. The parent does not need to manage those internal details. It delegates a subgoal and receives a result.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.4 The interface should hide implementation, not uncertainty
text: Encapsulation does not mean pretending the specialist is deterministic. A useful result can include structured metadata. "answer": "80", "sources": ["S1"], "confidence": 0.82, "status": "complete" The parent can use status, provenance, or confidence in its next decision rather than receiving an opaque string.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.5 Tool vs agent-tool
text: Property | Ordinary deterministic tool | Agent-tool Internal path | Usually fixed | May be dynamic Model calls | Often none | Potentially many Latency | Often predictable | Variable Cost | Often predictable | Variable Failure modes | Execution/API errors | Plus reasoning/trajectory errors Output variance | Often low | Potentially stochastic Internal autonomy | Low | Can be substantial The external contract can look identical while the operational behavior differs significantly.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.6 Deliberately hide an unbounded loop
text: Suppose the parent gives the specialist a simple task, but the specialist repeatedly searches. Parent: researcher("Find X") Inside researcher: search("X") search("X") search("X") ... The parent sees one tool call. The system may actually perform dozens of model and tool calls. In Experiment 31 the looping specialist's parent records a single researcher action while the child performs five searches; only the delegated limit stops it at five. Failure mode Delegation can hide resource consumption.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.7 Budgets must cross delegation boundaries
text: Experiment 31 delegates only a step limit, because that is what the Chapter 3 loop enforces. A production child would also accept a cost ceiling and a deadline, and charge its consumption to the parent's ledger rather than to a fresh budget of its own. A parent should be able to constrain the autonomy granted to a child agent. Otherwise nesting agents can make system-level budgets meaningless. Control principle Delegated autonomy should include delegated limits.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.8 Failure needs a contract
text: An agent-tool can fail because a source is unavailable, its own model makes a bad decision, its budget expires, or it cannot verify an answer. "status": "incomplete", "answer": null, "reason": "source unavailable", "steps_used": 5 Structured failure lets the parent retry, choose another specialist, ask the user, or stop. Returning a confident-looking guess destroys that control boundary.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.9 Delegation is not abdication
text: The parent remains responsible for deciding whether the specialist's result is sufficient for the larger goal. Figure: The parent validates a specialist result before deciding to accept, retry, delegate elsewhere or escalate. A child agent's completion signal means “I believe my subtask is complete,” not necessarily “the parent goal is satisfied.”

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.10 Context boundaries
text: A specialist does not necessarily need the parent's entire context. Parent context: goal + user history + budgets + other subtasks + private data Delegated context: specific subgoal + permitted evidence + constraints Passing only necessary context can reduce tokens, distraction, and information exposure. But under-sharing can remove constraints the child needs. Delegation is therefore also context engineering.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.11 Permission boundaries
text: A parent with permission to draft an email should not automatically grant a child permission to send it. parent permissions: ["read", "draft"] child permissions: ["read"] Capabilities should be explicitly delegated rather than inherited accidentally. Security principle Agent nesting must not become permission escalation.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.12 Recursive composition
text: Once an agent can be a tool, composition becomes recursive. Figure: A coordinator delegating to specialist agents, which may in turn use tools or further agents. This is powerful because complex systems can be assembled from smaller controlled units. It is dangerous because cost, latency, permissions, and failures can become difficult to see across layers.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.13 Trace across the boundary
text: Figure: A trace that crosses the agent boundary: the parent's step contains the child agent's own steps. Tracing should preserve parent-child relationships so a single top-level action can be expanded into the work it actually caused.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.14 Agent identity is architectural, not mystical
text: A component becomes useful to treat as an agent when it has meaningful local control: it can interpret a subgoal, choose among actions, maintain state, and decide when its subtask is complete. Agent = Model + Context + Actions + State + Control Wrapping a deterministic function in a class named Agent does not make the architecture meaningfully multi-agent. Conversely, a service may behave as an agent even if its API simply looks like a tool call.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.15 When is a specialist agent justified?
text: Use specialist agent when... | Prefer ordinary tool/workflow when... Subtask path is semantically uncertain | Execution path is fixed Specialist needs its own tools/context | One deterministic function suffices Local iteration adds value | Iteration adds overhead only Domain policy is reusable | Logic is tiny and application-specific Delegation boundary improves modularity | Boundary merely hides simple code Multi-agent architecture should not be the default. A specialist earns its existence by encapsulating useful local autonomy.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.16 Agent-as-tool vs handoff
text: There are at least two ways for one agent to involve another. Pattern | Control after delegation Agent as tool | Parent remains controller; child returns a result Handoff | Control responsibility moves to another agent This chapter focuses on agent-as-tool. Later communication patterns can support more peer-like or transferred control.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.17 Measure the hidden work
text: Metric | Question Top-level success | Did delegation help solve the parent goal? Child success | Did specialist complete its subtask? Delegation accuracy | Was the right subtask delegated? Nested calls | How much work occurred behind one parent action? Cost / latency | What did the child consume? Budget violations | Did child exceed delegated limits? Permission violations | Did child attempt unauthorized actions? Trace completeness | Can parent action be explained end to end? A top-level call count is no longer enough once calls can contain agents.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.18 Compare against a flat architecture
text: Flat: parent owns search + retrieval + calculator Hierarchical: parent owns calculator + ResearchAgent Compare both on the same tasks. The hierarchical version may improve modularity or specialist performance, but it may also add model calls, latency, and coordination failures. Part IV experimental rule More agents ≠ better intelligence. Every additional agent creates another interface, budget, failure mode, and coordination problem.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.19 The conceptual transition
text: The step from single-agent to multi-agent systems is smaller than it first appears. Figure: From Chapter 5 to Chapter 17: an agent behind a tool interface keeps the same select, invoke, observe contract. The novelty lies inside the capability: the delegated component can itself exercise model-driven control.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.20 Bridge to Chapter 18
text: One specialist is straightforward. What if a coordinator manages several specialists and decides who should work on which subtask? How should one agent coordinate a team of worker agents? That leads to supervisor-and-worker architectures and hierarchy.

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.21 Exercises
text: - Wrap a deterministic calculator and a model-driven researcher behind the same callable interface. List the operational differences the caller should still monitor. - Give a child agent a five-step budget and design the structured result returned when the budget expires. - Design a context-minimization rule for delegating a research subtask without exposing unrelated parent context. - Draw a three-level agent hierarchy and identify where permissions and cost budgets must be enforced. - Compare a flat single-agent system with an agent-as-tool version. Which metrics would determine whether the extra boundary is worthwhile?

title: Chapter 17, An Agent Is Just Another Tool: 17.22 Chapter 17 checklist
text: - An agent can be exposed through the same invocation contract as a tool. - Agent-tools differ operationally because their internal path, cost, latency, and failures can be variable. - Delegated autonomy should include explicit budgets and permissions. - Structured failure allows the parent to retain control. - Delegation is also context engineering and a security boundary. - Nested traces should expose the work hidden behind parent calls. - More agents are justified only when local autonomy provides measurable value.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.1 From one specialist to a team
text: Chapter 17 showed that a parent can invoke a specialist agent as a tool. With several specialists, a new problem appears: the system must decide how to divide a goal, which worker should receive each subtask, when work can proceed, and how results should be combined. Figure: A supervisor routes subtasks from one goal to specialized workers. The supervisor is not useful because it has a managerial title. It is useful only if these coordination decisions add value.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.2 What a supervisor actually does
text: Responsibility | Question Decompose | What subtasks are required? Assign | Which worker should handle each subtask? Schedule | What can run now, and what must wait? Monitor | Did each worker succeed? Integrate | How do worker results become one result? Recover | What happens when a worker fails? Operational definition A supervisor is a controller that allocates subtasks among workers and integrates their results toward a parent goal.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.3 The smallest supervisor
text: This is routing plus delegation plus aggregation. Multi-agent supervision is built from primitives we already know. Experiment 32 — Supervisor and workers. Give the system a goal with three distinct skills: Goal: Produce a short evidence-based comparison of A and B. The supervisor decomposes it: 1. Research comparable facts about A and B. 2. Analyze the differences. 3. Write the final comparison. Assignments: Figure: The supervisor's assignments: each worker receives one task. But task 2 depends on task 1, and task 3 depends on task 2. The supervisor must coordinate state as well as choose workers. Figure: Dependent workers: evidence flows from the researcher to the analyst, and findings flow to the writer. The experiment runs three scripted workers against a shared state. A plan is just an ordered list of worker names. The naive supervisor runs the plan in the given order; the dependency-aware supervisor runs, at each step, the first pending worker whose inputs already exist in state. The bad plan, which puts the writer first, is discussed in the next section. Output: good decomposition: order: researcher -> analyst -> writer draft: Comparison: A is cheaper; B is rated higher. bad decomposition: order: writer -> researcher -> analyst draft: A and B are broadly comparable. bad decomposition, dependency-aware supervisor: order: researcher -> analyst -> writer draft: Comparison: A is cheaper; B is rated higher.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.4 Decomposition quality matters
text: A supervisor can create a bad team trajectory before any worker acts. Bad decomposition: 1. Write final answer. 2. Research evidence. 3. Analyze evidence. Every worker may execute its assigned task competently, yet the overall ordering is defective. In Experiment 32 the naive supervisor runs the writer first; the writer has no findings and produces a fluent but unsupported draft, and nothing later revisits it. The same bad plan succeeds only when the supervisor itself checks dependencies before dispatching. The repair lives in the coordinator, not in the workers. Failure mode Worker competence cannot repair a structurally bad decomposition.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.5 Assignment quality matters too
text: Figure: Poor assignments: each subtask goes to a worker that lacks the right capability. The supervisor therefore needs an accurate model of worker capabilities, permissions, costs, and current availability.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.6 Worker descriptions are interfaces
text: ResearchAgent: retrieves and verifies external evidence AnalysisAgent: compares supplied evidence; no web access WritingAgent: turns supplied findings into final prose As with tools and routes, vague or overlapping descriptions make allocation harder. Team design is interface design.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.7 The supervisor needs shared task state
text: Workers should not have to rediscover everything from scratch. The supervisor can maintain an explicit state object. Each worker receives only the slice needed for its subtask and returns structured updates.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.8 Context isolation vs context continuity
text: Too little context | Too much context Worker misses constraints | Worker receives irrelevant history Duplicates prior work | Higher token/cost burden Produces incompatible result | Sensitive information spreads Cannot interpret predecessor output | Specialization becomes blurred The supervisor must preserve continuity without broadcasting the entire parent context to every worker.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.9 Worker failure is supervisor input
text: ResearchAgent: "status": "incomplete", "reason": "source unavailable" The supervisor can retry, reassign, reduce scope, ask for help, or stop. A worker failure is an observation for the coordination policy, not automatically a system failure.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.10 Supervisors can become bottlenecks
text: If every worker interaction passes through one supervisor, that controller may dominate latency, token usage, or decision errors. Figure: When every decision passes through one supervisor, it can become a bottleneck. Coordination cost Centralization simplifies control but concentrates failure and communication overhead.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.11 Parallel workers
text: Independent subtasks can reuse Chapter 16's fan-out/fan-in pattern. Figure: Parallel workers: the supervisor fans independent research out and integrates the results. A supervisor architecture does not imply sequential work. It defines who controls allocation and integration.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.12 Supervisor $\neq$ omniscient manager
text: The supervisor is another model-driven component. It can decompose poorly, misassign work, misunderstand worker results, or integrate them incorrectly. Part IV principle Adding a coordinator moves some failure modes; it does not remove them. Experiment 33 — Hierarchy. Now suppose one supervisor has too many heterogeneous workers. Introduce an intermediate layer. Figure: A two-level hierarchy: the root delegates to team leads, which delegate to workers. The root delegates broad subgoals. Leads coordinate local specialists. The architecture reduces the number of direct relationships the root must manage. The experiment compares a flat team, in which the root reads all four worker reports, with the two-level hierarchy above. It counts the root's span of control and the messages exchanged, and runs the hierarchy twice: once with leads that forward only findings and once with leads that also forward caveats in a separate field. One research worker reports that Option A is cheaper but that its source confidence is low. Output: flat: root span=4, messages=8 decision: verify before choosing: source confidence is low hierarchy, lossy leads: root span=2, messages=12 decision: choose Option A hierarchy, structured leads: root span=2, messages=12 decision: verify before choosing: source confidence is low The hierarchy halves the root's span of control and adds four messages. With lossy leads the root never sees the caveat and chooses Option A; the structured field carries it across both boundaries. The following sections examine each effect.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.13 Why hierarchy can help
text: Potential benefit | Mechanism Reduced coordination span | Each manager sees fewer workers Domain specialization | Local supervisor understands its worker group Context isolation | Subteams receive only relevant state Reusable subteams | A whole team can become an agent-tool Local recovery | Subteam can retry without involving root Hierarchy is therefore a compression mechanism for coordination: higher layers interact with abstractions rather than every low-level action.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.14 Information is compressed at every boundary
text: Figure: Information is compressed at every boundary on its way up the hierarchy. Each layer can remove detail. This resembles Chapter 9's context compression, but now compression occurs across organizational boundaries.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.15 Deliberately lose a critical fact
text: Suppose a worker reports: Finding: Option A is cheaper, BUT source confidence is low. The team lead forwards only: Option A is cheaper. The root now receives a cleaner message and a worse representation of reality. Hierarchy failure Every abstraction boundary can become an information-loss boundary.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.16 Hierarchy adds hops
text: Figure: Hierarchy adds hops: a flat round trip versus one routed through a lead. Extra hops can add latency, tokens, interpretation errors, and duplicated summaries. Hierarchy earns its cost only when the coordination problem is large enough.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.17 Flat vs hierarchical teams
text: Flat team | Hierarchical team Fewer communication hops | Smaller local coordination spans Root sees detailed outputs | Root sees abstractions Simple for small teams | Can scale organizational complexity Root may become overloaded | Intermediate supervisors can fail Less summary loss | More compression boundaries There is no universally optimal topology. Team structure is another architecture choice to benchmark.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.18 Delegation depth needs a limit
text: Figure: Unbounded delegation: each agent can spawn another, so depth needs an explicit limit. Recursive delegation can make cost and control difficult to bound. A system can limit depth just as it limits steps.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.19 Budgets across a hierarchy
text: A root can allocate portions of its budget to subteams. root budget: 1.00 research team: 0.40 build team: 0.40 reserve: 0.20 A child budget should not silently create new system-level resources. Budget conservation keeps local autonomy compatible with global limits.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.20 Permissions across hierarchy
text: The same principle applies to capabilities. Root permissions: read, draft, approve Research team: read Writing team: read, draft A child should receive the minimum capability set required for its delegated role.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.21 Trace the organization
text: Figure: A trace that follows the organization: the root task, its teams and their workers. Hierarchical traces should preserve delegation lineage, budgets, results, and failures. Otherwise organizational complexity becomes operational opacity.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.22 What should we measure?
text: Metric | Question End-to-end success | Did the team solve the parent goal? Decomposition quality | Were necessary subtasks identified and ordered? Assignment accuracy | Were subtasks sent to suitable workers? Worker success | Did specialists complete delegated work? Integration quality | Were worker results combined correctly? Information retention | Did critical facts survive hierarchy? Coordination calls | How much management work was added? Cost / latency | What did the topology consume? Delegation depth | How deep did control recurse? A multi-agent benchmark should attribute failures to the layer that caused them rather than reporting only final success.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.23 Compare topology, not just agent count
text: A: one general agent B: supervisor + 3 workers C: flat coordinator + tools D: root + 2 leads + 4 workers Hold the task and underlying capabilities as constant as possible. Otherwise gains attributed to “multi-agent” may actually come from extra models, extra tools, or extra compute.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.24 When hierarchy is justified
text: Hierarchy is most plausible when the work naturally decomposes into semi-independent domains, local specialists require different context or permissions, and a single controller's coordination burden becomes material. For a three-step task, hierarchy is likely architecture theater.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.25 Chapter principle
text: Coordination must earn its layer A supervisor is valuable only when decomposition, assignment, monitoring, or integration are real problems. A hierarchy is valuable only when reducing coordination complexity outweighs extra hops and information loss.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.26 Bridge to Chapter 19
text: Supervisor architectures assume one controller decides how work is allocated. But some problems can be approached by several agents independently and then resolved through voting, judging, or debate. Can disagreement between agents improve a decision? That leads to debate and voting.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.27 Exercises
text: - Design a supervisor for research, analysis, and writing. Identify the dependency edges between subtasks. - Create a bad decomposition that competent workers cannot repair. Explain why the failure belongs to the supervisor. - Convert a flat team of six specialists into a two-level hierarchy. What information should each lead return to the root? - Construct a hierarchy where one critical uncertainty is lost during summarization. Add a structured field that preserves it. - Compare one general agent, a supervisor-worker team, and a two-level hierarchy under the same system-level cost budget.

title: Chapter 18, Supervisor and Workers: 18.28 Chapter 18 checklist
text: - Supervision combines decomposition, assignment, scheduling, monitoring, integration, and recovery. - Worker competence cannot compensate for every supervisor error. - Shared task state should preserve continuity without broadcasting unnecessary context. - Central supervisors can become bottlenecks and single points of coordination failure. - Hierarchy reduces coordination span by introducing abstraction boundaries. - Abstraction boundaries can lose critical information. - Budgets, permissions, delegation depth, and traces should remain enforceable across hierarchy.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: 19.1 Why ask several agents?
text: A single model can make an error. One response is to sample several answers and combine them. The hope is that errors differ while correct reasoning converges. Figure: Independent agents produce answers that are combined into one decision. This can work. It can also create expensive consensus around the same mistake.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: 19.2 Voting is an aggregation rule
text: For a discrete decision, the simplest fan-in operator is majority vote. Voting does not inspect why the agents chose A or B. It assumes the distribution of votes contains useful information. Experiment 34 — Voting. Use a binary question with known ground truth, B. Each scripted worker answers from the one source it reads: a filing and an analyst note both say B, and a promotional blog says A. When the three workers read three different sources, one is wrong and the vote repairs its error. Then change the error structure so that two workers read the same blog. The experiment also reports Oracle@N (was at least one worker right?) and the number of distinct sources behind the votes, and it reports an exact tie instead of breaking it arbitrarily. Output: ground truth: B independent errors: votes=['B', 'B', 'A'] majority=B correct=True oracle@3=True unique sources=3 correlated errors: votes=['A', 'A', 'B'] majority=A correct=False oracle@3=True unique sources=2 nine correlated voters: votes=['A', 'A', 'A', 'A', 'A', 'A', 'A', 'B', 'B'] majority=A correct=False oracle@9=True unique sources=2 even split: votes=['A', 'B'] majority=tie correct=False oracle@2=True unique sources=2 In the correlated case the correct answer was present (Oracle@3 is true), but the vote selected the wrong one. The vote itself has no mechanism for recognizing that the minority worker is correct.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: 19.3 Independence is the hidden assumption
text: If three workers use the same model, prompt, context, evidence, and decoding behavior, their errors may be strongly correlated. Figure: Shared model, prompt, evidence and blind spot lead to repeated error. Key principle Three correlated opinions are not equivalent to three independent sources of evidence.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: 19.4 False consensus
text: Suppose all agents receive a source containing the same incorrect fact. Figure: False consensus: every agent repeats the same wrong shared evidence, so the vote confirms the error. Unanimity is high. Accuracy is zero. Failure mode Consensus can amplify shared upstream errors.

title: Chapter 19, Debate and Voting: 19.5 Diversity can be engineered
